lessons.title: Separating mixtures
objectives: Explain the key ideas in this chapter.
Apply the ideas to the worked examples and exercises.
paragraphs: A mixture contains two or more substances that are physically combined. Its components retain their properties. A solution is a homogeneous mixture: dissolved salt is distributed throughout water. A suspension, such as muddy water, has particles that can settle. A pure substance has a fixed composition; visual clarity alone does not prove purity.

Choose a separation method using a difference in physical properties. Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid. The solid left on the paper is the residue; the liquid passing through is the filtrate. Dissolved salt passes through filter paper with water, so filtration cannot recover it.

Evaporation removes a solvent to leave a dissolved solid. Crystallisation allows crystals to form from a concentrated solution, often on cooling. Simple distillation boils a liquid and condenses its vapour to collect the solvent. Never heat a sealed apparatus, taste laboratory chemicals or point a heated tube at anyone. School practical work requires teacher supervision.
examples: Muddy water: allow large particles to settle, then filter. Mud is the residue and the water is the filtrate. Filtration alone does not make water safe to drink.
Salt water: evaporation can recover salt, but loses the water. Distillation collects water as a distillate while non-volatile salt remains behind.
Sand and salt: add water to dissolve salt, filter off sand, then evaporate the filtrate to obtain salt. The order matters because dry filtration cannot separate two powders.
lessons.summary: A mixture contains two or more substances that are physically combined.

lessons.title: Particles and changes of state
objectives: Explain the key ideas in this chapter.
Apply the ideas to the worked examples and exercises.
paragraphs: Matter is modelled as particles. In a solid, particles vibrate near fixed positions. In a liquid, particles remain close but move past one another. Gas particles are widely separated and move randomly. The model explains shape and compressibility; particles themselves do not expand when a substance is heated.

Melting changes a solid into a liquid. Freezing reverses melting. Boiling occurs throughout a liquid at its boiling temperature for a given pressure; evaporation occurs at a surface over a range of temperatures. Condensation changes gas to liquid. In a physical change, the chemical identity remains the same.

Diffusion is the net spreading of particles from a region of higher concentration to lower concentration due to random motion. It usually becomes faster as temperature rises. A smell spreading through air illustrates diffusion, but airflow may also move it.
examples: Ice melts to water: H₂O molecules remain H₂O; the arrangement and movement change. This is a physical change.
A syringe containing air can be compressed because there is much space between gas particles. A sealed liquid-filled syringe is much harder to compress.
Water droplets outside a cold bottle come from water vapour in the surrounding air condensing on the cold surface, rather than water passing through the bottle.
lessons.summary: Matter is modelled as particles.

lessons.title: Measurement and density
objectives: Explain the key ideas in this chapter.
Apply the ideas to the worked examples and exercises.
paragraphs: A measurement compares a quantity with a unit. Length has SI unit metre (m), mass kilogram (kg), and time second (s). Read a scale with your eye perpendicular to it to reduce parallax error. Record the unit as well as the number; 12 alone is not a complete length measurement.

Density is mass divided by volume: ρ = m/V. A material of mass 200 g occupying 100 cm³ has density 2 g/cm³. Compare densities only in compatible units. Since 1 g = 0.001 kg and 1 cm³ = 0.000001 m³, 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.

For a regular block, measure length, width and height and multiply them to obtain volume. For an insoluble irregular solid, measure the increase in water level when fully submerged in a measuring cylinder. Avoid trapped bubbles and ensure water does not overflow. Repeat readings when possible.
examples: A block is 5 cm × 2 cm × 3 cm. Volume = 5 × 2 × 3 = 30 cm³. If its mass is 90 g, density = 90/30 = 3 g/cm³.
A cylinder reads 40 cm³ before immersion and 65 cm³ after. Object volume = 65 − 40 = 25 cm³. For mass 50 g, density = 2 g/cm³.
Convert 2.5 g/cm³ to SI density: 2.5 × 1000 = 2500 kg/m³. Convert both mass and volume units, rather than just one.
lessons.summary: A measurement compares a quantity with a unit.

lessons.title: Speed and distance–time graphs
objectives: Explain the key ideas in this chapter.
Apply the ideas to the worked examples and exercises.
paragraphs: Distance is the length of a path travelled. Average speed is total distance divided by total time: v = d/t. Speed is a scalar: it has magnitude but no direction. Velocity includes a direction, so a journey returning to its starting point can have positive average speed but zero average velocity.

A distance–time graph places time on the horizontal axis and accumulated distance on the vertical axis. Its gradient represents speed. A horizontal section means the object is at rest. A steeper rising section indicates a greater speed if the axes use the same scales.

Convert units before substituting. To change km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6. For multiple journey sections, add all distances and all times, including stops, then divide. Averaging two speeds directly is generally wrong when the times spent at them differ.
examples: A student travels 600 m in 120 s. Average speed = 600/120 = 5 m/s.
A cyclist travels 2 km in 10 min and stops for 5 min. Overall speed = 2000/900 = 2.22 m/s, including the stop.
Convert 36 km/h: 36 × 1000/3600 = 10 m/s. In 8 s at this speed, distance = vt = 10 × 8 = 80 m.
lessons.summary: Distance is the length of a path travelled.

lessons.title: Cells and organisation
objectives: Explain the key ideas in this chapter.
Apply the ideas to the worked examples and exercises.
paragraphs: A cell is the basic structural and functional unit of living organisms. The cell membrane regulates movement of substances into and out of the cell. Cytoplasm is the region where many chemical reactions occur. In typical plant and animal cells, the nucleus contains genetic material and helps control cell activities.

Plant cells usually have a cellulose cell wall outside the cell membrane and a large permanent vacuole containing cell sap. Photosynthetic plant cells contain chloroplasts with chlorophyll. Not every plant cell has chloroplasts: many root cells do not. Animal cells have no cellulose cell wall or chloroplasts.

Similar specialised cells form a tissue; tissues cooperate in an organ; organs cooperate in an organ system. A leaf is an organ containing several tissues. Use a microscope carefully: begin with low power, focus safely, and keep lenses clean. A diagram should have clear lines, a title and labels that do not cross.
examples: A leaf palisade cell contains many chloroplasts. These absorb light for photosynthesis, connecting its structure to its function.
A root hair cell has an elongated extension that increases surface area for absorption. It usually lacks chloroplasts because it is underground.
Cardiac muscle cell → cardiac muscle tissue → heart → circulatory system → organism. Each level includes interacting components.
lessons.summary: A cell is the basic structural and functional unit of living organisms.

lessons.title: Food chains and ecosystems
objectives: Explain the key ideas in this chapter.
Apply the ideas to the worked examples and exercises.
paragraphs: An ecosystem includes organisms and their physical surroundings interacting together. A habitat is the place where an organism lives. Producers, such as green plants, make organic food using light energy. Consumers obtain food by eating organisms or their products.

A food-chain arrow points from the food to the feeder, showing energy transfer. Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake begins with a producer. Decomposers break down dead material and release nutrients that can be used again. Energy flows through the system and is dissipated as heat; nutrients cycle.

A food web links many food chains. Removing one species can affect several others, but the exact effect depends on alternative foods, disease and habitat. Burning vegetation can destroy habitats and expose soil. Conservation includes protecting habitats and using resources sustainably.
examples: In maize → mouse → owl, maize is a producer, mouse a primary consumer and owl a secondary consumer. Arrows show the direction of energy transfer.
If insect numbers fall, an insect-eating bird may have less food. A bird that also eats seeds may be less affected than a specialist insect feeder.
Fungi break down dead leaves. Nutrients return to soil and can be absorbed by plants; this does not mean that energy is recycled.
lessons.summary: An ecosystem includes organisms and their physical surroundings interacting together.

lessons.title: Fractions and proportional reasoning
objectives: Explain the key ideas in this chapter.
Apply the ideas to the worked examples and exercises.
paragraphs: A fraction a/b represents a divided by b, where b ≠ 0. Equivalent fractions represent the same quantity: multiplying numerator and denominator by the same nonzero number preserves the value. Simplify using a common factor. A denominator describes the size of equal parts; it is not added when combining like fractions.

To add or subtract fractions, first express them with a common denominator. To multiply, multiply numerators and denominators, cancelling common factors where helpful. To divide by a nonzero fraction, multiply by its reciprocal. Check whether the result is reasonable.

A ratio compares quantities in the same units. To divide a total in ratio a:b, calculate a+b equal shares, then allocate a and b shares. A proportion states equal ratios. Percent means per hundred, so 15% = 15/100 = 0.15.
examples: 2/3 + 1/4 = 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12. The least common denominator is 12.
3/5 ÷ 9/10 = 3/5 × 10/9 = 30/45 = 2/3. Multiplication by the reciprocal reverses division.
Divide TSh 24,000 in ratio 2:3. Total shares = 5. One share = 4800. The amounts are TSh 9600 and TSh 14,400; their sum is 24,000.
lessons.summary: A fraction a/b represents a divided by b, where b ≠ 0.

lessons.title: Linear equations
objectives: Explain the key ideas in this chapter.
Apply the ideas to the worked examples and exercises.
paragraphs: An equation states that two expressions have equal values. A solution is a value that makes the equation true. To preserve equality, perform the same operation on both sides. Expressions such as 3x + 2 contain a variable; 3x means 3 multiplied by x.

Solve a linear equation by simplifying brackets and collecting like terms, then isolating the variable. The distributive rule a(b+c)=ab+ac applies to every term inside the brackets. When a negative multiplier is outside brackets, it affects each sign inside.

Translate words carefully. Three more than twice a number is 2x+3; twice the sum of a number and three is 2(x+3). After solving, substitute into the original equation. A plausible-looking value is not enough: both sides must be equal.
examples: 3x + 5 = 20. Subtract 5 from both sides: 3x = 15. Divide by 3: x = 5. Check: 3(5)+5 = 20.
2(x − 4) = 10. Divide by 2: x − 4 = 5. Add 4: x = 9. Alternatively expand first to get 2x − 8 = 10.
A rectangle has perimeter 30 cm and length 9 cm. 2(9+w)=30; 9+w=15; w=6 cm. Check: 2(9+6)=30 cm.
lessons.summary: An equation states that two expressions have equal values.

lessons.title: Mawasiliano na ufahamu
objectives: Eleza dhana kuu za sura hii.
Tumia dhana katika mifano na mazoezi.
paragraphs: Mawasiliano ni mchakato wa kupeana na kupokea ujumbe. Mtumaji huwasilisha ujumbe kwa mpokeaji kupitia njia fulani. Lugha, ishara na picha zinaweza kufikisha ujumbe. Muktadha husaidia kuelewa maana: maneno yanayofaa kwa rafiki yanaweza kuhitaji kubadilishwa unapozungumza na mwalimu.

Usikilizaji makini unahitaji kuzingatia msemaji, kutambua hoja kuu na kuuliza swali la ufafanuzi bila kukatiza ovyo. Kelele na ujumbe usio wazi ni vikwazo vya mawasiliano. Mrejesho humsaidia mtumaji kutambua kama ujumbe umeeleweka.

Soma kifungu hiki: Asha aliona vitabu vimetapakaa darasani. Aliwaomba wenzake wamsaidie kuvipanga. Baada ya kazi, kila kitabu kilikuwa kwenye sehemu yake na wanafunzi walikipata kwa urahisi. Hoja kuu ni manufaa ya ushirikiano na utunzaji wa vifaa. Jibu swali kwa kutumia ushahidi wa kifungu, si kubuni tukio jipya.
examples: Ujumbe: Tafadhali fika maktabani saa nne. Mtumaji ni anayetoa ombi; mpokeaji ni anayeombwa; ujumbe unaeleza mahali na wakati.
Swali: Kwa nini Asha aliomba msaada? Jibu: Vitabu vilikuwa vimetapakaa na alitaka vipangwe. Jibu linategemea kifungu.
Mwanafunzi anasema: Samahani mwalimu, naomba ufafanue hoja ya pili. Huu ni mrejesho wenye heshima unaoonyesha hitaji la maelezo zaidi.
lessons.summary: Mawasiliano ni mchakato wa kupeana na kupokea ujumbe.

lessons.title: Uandishi wa aya na barua
objectives: Eleza dhana kuu za sura hii.
Tumia dhana katika mifano na mazoezi.
paragraphs: Aya ni mkusanyiko wa sentensi zinazojenga wazo moja kuu. Sentensi ya mada huanzisha wazo; sentensi zinazofuata hutoa maelezo, sababu au mifano. Aya nzuri ina mshikamano, yaani mawazo yanafuatana kwa namna inayoeleweka.

Kabla ya kuandika, tambua kusudi na msomaji. Panga hoja, andika rasimu, kisha hariri. Viunganishi kama kwa sababu, hata hivyo na kwa hiyo huonyesha uhusiano wa mawazo. Usitumie kiunganishi bila kuelewa kama kinaonyesha sababu, tofauti au matokeo.

Barua ya kirafiki inaweza kuwa na anwani ya mwandishi, tarehe, salamu, ujumbe na hitimisho. Ujumbe ubaki wazi na wenye heshima. Barua rasmi huhitaji mtindo unaolingana na taasisi na kusudi lake; hakiki maelekezo ya kazi kabla ya kuchagua muundo.
examples: Sentensi ya mada: Maktaba yetu ina manufaa mengi. Maelezo: Tunapata vitabu vya rejea na mahali tulivu pa kusoma. Sentensi hizi zinajenga wazo moja.
Rasimu: Tulichelewa. Mvua ilinyesha. Uhariri: Tulichelewa kwa sababu mvua kubwa ilinyesha. Kiunganishi kinaonyesha sababu.
Ombi kwa rafiki: Nakuomba uniletee kitabu changu Jumamosi. Linaeleza kitu kinachohitajika na wakati unaotarajiwa.
lessons.summary: Aya ni mkusanyiko wa sentensi zinazojenga wazo moja kuu.

lessons.title: Maps, direction and scale
objectives: Explain the key ideas in this chapter.
Apply the ideas to the worked examples and exercises.
paragraphs: A map represents an area using selected symbols and a scale. A title states what is shown, a key explains symbols and a direction indicator helps orient the reader. North, east, south and west are the cardinal directions. Check the north indicator instead of assuming every page has north at the top.

A representative fraction such as 1:50,000 means one unit on the map represents 50,000 of the same units on the ground. Thus 1 cm represents 50,000 cm = 500 m. A larger denominator corresponds to a smaller scale, showing less detail over a larger area.

For a straight-line distance, measure between locations with a ruler and apply the scale. A winding route may be measured with a thread or short segments, then converted. Map distance and ground distance must use the same units before forming a ratio.
examples: On a 1:50,000 map, 4 cm represents 4 × 50,000 = 200,000 cm = 2 km.
A school lies east of a clinic. From the school, the clinic is west. Reverse direction when changing the starting point.
A 1:25,000 map shows more detail than a 1:100,000 map for the same paper area. One centimetre represents 250 m rather than 1000 m.
lessons.summary: A map represents an area using selected symbols and a scale.

lessons.title: Weather observations
objectives: Explain the key ideas in this chapter.
Apply the ideas to the worked examples and exercises.
paragraphs: Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a particular place and time. Climate describes long-term weather patterns. Temperature, rainfall, humidity, pressure, wind and cloud cover are weather elements. A single rainy day does not establish a climate trend.

A rain gauge measures precipitation depth in millimetres. Place it upright at a suitable open site away from obstructions and splashing. A thermometer measures temperature; suitable shelter protects an air-temperature sensor from direct solar radiation while allowing airflow.

Record observations with date, time, location and units. Daily temperature range is maximum minus minimum temperature. A mean requires adding readings and dividing by their count. Missing observations should be marked missing, not invented as zero.
examples: Maximum temperature 31°C and minimum 19°C give a daily range of 31 − 19 = 12°C.
Rainfall readings 8, 0 and 10 mm total 18 mm over three days. A zero records an observed dry day; a missing reading is not the same thing.
Temperatures 20, 24 and 28°C have mean (20+24+28)/3 = 24°C. Equal weighting assumes the specified readings are being averaged.
lessons.summary: Weather is the condition of the atmosphere at a particular place and time.

lessons.title: Needs, wants and scarce resources
objectives: Explain the key ideas in this chapter.
Apply the ideas to the worked examples and exercises.
paragraphs: A need is something essential for well-being, such as adequate food, safe water and shelter. A want is something a person would like beyond basic needs. The classification depends on context: a phone may support essential work, while an expensive upgrade may mainly satisfy a preference.

Resources such as time, labour, land and capital are limited. Scarcity means choices must be made because available resources cannot satisfy every competing use. Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone, not the sum of every possible alternative.

A budget lists expected income and planned spending over a stated period. Separate necessary spending from optional spending and allow for saving or emergencies where possible. A balanced budget has planned spending no greater than available funds. Money saved remains a use of income, rather than extra income.
examples: A student has TSh 5000 and chooses a dictionary instead of a football. If the football was the next best option, it is the opportunity cost of the choice.
Weekly income is TSh 20,000. Food 9000 + transport 6000 + saving 3000 = 18,000. Unallocated balance = 2000.
A household compares repair and replacement. A cheaper purchase is not always cheaper overall if running and maintenance costs are higher. Compare costs over the relevant time.
lessons.summary: A need is something essential for well-being, such as adequate food, safe water and shelter.

lessons.title: Revenue, costs and simple records
objectives: Explain the key ideas in this chapter.
Apply the ideas to the worked examples and exercises.
paragraphs: A business keeps records to understand what it receives, spends, owns and owes. Revenue is money earned from sales before deducting costs. Profit is revenue minus the relevant total costs over the same period. A cash receipt is evidence of payment; it is not itself a profit calculation.

For identical items sold at one price, sales revenue = selling price × quantity sold. Cost of goods sold relates to the items sold; unsold stock should not automatically be treated as if it generated sales. For an introductory example with no opening or closing stock, profit can be calculated by subtracting purchase and operating costs from sales.

A simple cash record has date, description, money in, money out and running balance. Credit sales and purchases involve payment later, so profit and cash on hand can differ. Keep supporting documents and reconcile the record with actual cash.
examples: A trader sells 20 notebooks at TSh 1500 each. Revenue = 20 × 1500 = TSh 30,000.
All notebooks cost TSh 18,000 and transport costs TSh 2000. If all are sold for TSh 30,000, profit = 30,000 − 18,000 − 2000 = TSh 10,000.
Opening cash 5000; cash received 8000; cash paid 6500. Closing cash = 5000+8000−6500 = TSh 6500.
lessons.summary: A business keeps records to understand what it receives, spends, owns and owes.

lessons.title: Vyanzo vya historia na ushahidi
objectives: Eleza dhana kuu za sura hii.
Tumia dhana katika mifano na mazoezi.
paragraphs: Historia huchunguza maisha na matukio ya binadamu katika nyakati zilizopita kwa kutumia ushahidi. Vyanzo vinaweza kuwa simulizi, maandishi, picha, vitu vya kale na mabaki ya majengo. Kila chanzo kina uwezo na mipaka; kutaja chanzo pekee hakuthibitishi kila dai linalotolewa.

Chanzo cha msingi kinatokana moja kwa moja na kipindi au tukio linalochunguzwa, kama barua ya mshiriki. Chanzo cha pili huchanganua au kueleza vyanzo vingine. Uainishaji hutegemea swali la utafiti: kitabu cha zamani kinaweza kuwa ushahidi wa mawazo ya kipindi kilipoandikwa.

Mtafiti huuliza: Nani alitengeneza chanzo? Lini? Kwa kusudi gani? Analinganisha ushahidi kutoka vyanzo tofauti badala ya kutegemea kumbukumbu moja. Simulizi zinahifadhi maarifa muhimu lakini kumbukumbu na mitazamo zinaweza kutofautiana. Heshimu mtoa taarifa na pata ridhaa kabla ya kurekodi mahojiano.
examples: Barua iliyoandikwa wakati wa tukio inaweza kuwa chanzo cha msingi kuhusu mawazo ya mwandishi. Hata hivyo, huenda mwandishi hakushuhudia kila jambo alilotaja.
Wazee wawili wakitoa tarehe tofauti ya tukio, linganisha simulizi zao na kumbukumbu nyingine. Usichague tarehe kwa sababu msemaji mmoja anaongea kwa kujiamini zaidi.
Chungu cha kale kinaweza kutoa ushahidi kuhusu teknolojia au matumizi ya vyombo. Mahali kilipopatikana na mazingira yake ni muhimu; kukiondoa bila kumbukumbu hupoteza taarifa.
lessons.summary: Historia huchunguza maisha na matukio ya binadamu katika nyakati zilizopita kwa kutumia ushahidi.

lessons.title: Maadili, uwajibikaji na utunzaji wa urithi
objectives: Eleza dhana kuu za sura hii.
Tumia dhana katika mifano na mazoezi.
paragraphs: Maadili ni kanuni na mitazamo inayosaidia kutathmini mwenendo wa watu. Uaminifu unahusisha kusema ukweli na kutotumia vibaya mali au taarifa. Uwajibikaji unahusisha kutimiza wajibu na kueleza maamuzi na matokeo yake.

Urithi wa kihistoria unaweza kuwa majengo, maeneo, nyaraka, sanaa, lugha na maarifa yanayorithishwa. Kuuhifadhi kunahitaji kuheshimu jamii zinazouhusisha na historia yao. Usiharibu wala kuondoa vitu kwenye eneo la kihistoria; fuata sheria na maelekezo ya mamlaka husika.

Katika mjadala, tofautisha ukweli unaoungwa mkono na ushahidi na maoni. Sikiliza hoja tofauti kwa heshima. Kutatua mgogoro kwa amani kunahitaji kubaini tatizo, kusikiliza pande zote na kutafuta suluhu inayoheshimu haki badala ya vitisho.
examples: Mwanafunzi akipata kitabu cha mwenzake, anakirudisha badala ya kukificha. Huu ni mfano wa uaminifu na kuheshimu mali.
Kikundi kinapanga kusafisha mazingira ya eneo la urithi kwa ushauri wa wahusika. Hakigusi vitu vya kale bila ruhusa au utaalamu.
Wanafunzi wanapogombania kifaa cha kujifunzia, wanaweza kukubaliana ratiba ya matumizi baada ya kila mmoja kueleza hitaji lake.
lessons.summary: Maadili ni kanuni na mitazamo inayosaidia kutathmini mwenendo wa watu.

lessons.title: Reading for meaning
objectives: Explain the key ideas in this chapter.
Apply the ideas to the worked examples and exercises.
paragraphs: Good readers identify the purpose, main idea and supporting details of a text. Skimming gives an overview; scanning locates a particular detail such as a date or name. Close reading examines the words and their relationships carefully. Choose the strategy that matches the task.

Read this original passage: Neema planted three seedlings near her home. During the dry week, she watered them each evening using water left from rinsing vegetables. Her brother made a small fence to protect them from goats. Two months later, all three seedlings had new leaves. The passage describes practical care for young plants.

A literal question asks for information stated directly. An inference combines clues with reasoning, but should not contradict the text. The passage suggests teamwork, because Neema watered the plants and her brother protected them. It does not state the species of tree or the exact volume of water used.
examples: Question: How many seedlings did Neema plant? Answer: Three. This detail is explicitly stated in the first sentence.
Question: Why was a fence useful? Answer: It protected the seedlings from goats. The passage supplies this reason directly.
Question: What suggests cooperation? Answer: Neema watered the seedlings while her brother built a fence. Both contributed different kinds of care.
lessons.summary: Good readers identify the purpose, main idea and supporting details of a text.

lessons.title: Paragraphs and tense consistency
objectives: Explain the key ideas in this chapter.
Apply the ideas to the worked examples and exercises.
paragraphs: A paragraph develops one main idea. A topic sentence introduces it, supporting sentences explain it with details or examples, and a closing sentence can complete the thought. Use connectors to show relationships, rather than listing unrelated sentences.

The simple past describes completed events at a past time: visited, walked, wrote. Some verbs are irregular: go becomes went, not goed. The present perfect uses has or have with a past participle and can connect a past event to the present: She has written a letter. Avoid changing tense without a reason.

When revising, check subject–verb agreement, tense, punctuation and clarity. He walks uses a singular present-tense verb; they walk uses the plural form. A complete sentence normally contains a subject and a finite verb. Read a draft aloud to hear missing words or awkward connections.
examples: Draft: Yesterday we go to the library. Correction: Yesterday we went to the library. The time marker yesterday calls for the past tense.
Topic: Our school garden supports learning. Detail: We observe plant growth and practise measuring beds. The detail develops the topic rather than changing it.
Combine: It rained. We stayed indoors. Result: It rained, so we stayed indoors. The connector so expresses the result.
lessons.summary: A paragraph develops one main idea.

lessons.title: Elements, compounds and the periodic table
objectives: Distinguish elements, compounds and mixtures.
Read symbols and simple formulae.
Identify periods, groups and the first twenty elements.
paragraphs: An element contains only one kind of atom. Copper wire, oxygen gas and a piece of pure carbon are examples. Some elements occur as single atoms, while others occur as molecules: O₂ has two oxygen atoms joined together. An element is therefore not the same thing as a single atom. A compound contains atoms of different elements chemically joined in a fixed ratio. Water is a compound because each H₂O molecule contains two hydrogen atoms for every oxygen atom.

A chemical symbol identifies an element. The first letter is capital and a second letter, if present, is lower case: C is carbon, Ca calcium, Co cobalt and Cl chlorine. A formula identifies the kinds and relative numbers of atoms in a substance. CO₂ has one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms per molecule. The small lower number is a subscript; a number written before a formula counts complete units. Thus 2H₂O contains four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms altogether.

In a compound the properties can differ greatly from those of its elements. Hydrogen is a combustible gas and oxygen supports combustion, but water is a liquid at ordinary room conditions and can extinguish some fires. This comparison does not mean water is safe for every fire: never use water on live electrical equipment or burning cooking oil. Separating a compound into its elements requires chemical change; a mixture can usually be separated using physical differences.

The periodic table orders elements by atomic number. Its horizontal rows are periods and its vertical columns are groups. For the first twenty elements the order is H, He, Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F, Ne, Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, Ar, K, Ca. Most metals are on the left and centre; most non-metals are towards the right. Metals generally conduct electricity well, are malleable and form positive ions, but statements about materials need exceptions: graphite, a form of carbon, conducts electricity although carbon is a non-metal.
examples: Count atoms in CO₂: C has no subscript, so it contributes 1 atom; O has subscript 2, so there are 2 oxygen atoms. Total = 3 atoms per molecule.
Classify air and pure water: air is a mixture with variable proportions of gases; pure water is a compound with a fixed hydrogen-to-oxygen ratio of 2:1.
Interpret 3MgO: each formula unit contains 1 magnesium and 1 oxygen atom. Three units contain 3 magnesium and 3 oxygen atoms. The coefficient multiplies the whole formula.
lessons.summary: An element contains only one kind of atom.

lessons.title: Atomic structure and electron arrangements
objectives: Calculate proton, neutron and electron numbers.
Use first-twenty shell arrangements.
Relate arrangements to period and group.
paragraphs: An atom has a small, dense nucleus containing positively charged protons and uncharged neutrons. Negatively charged electrons occupy regions around the nucleus. Most of the atomic volume is outside the nucleus. The shell diagrams used in this chapter are useful models for counting electrons; they are not photographs of tiny balls following fixed circular paths.

The atomic number Z is the number of protons. It identifies the element. The mass number A is the total number of protons and neutrons in a particular atom, so neutron number = A − Z. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons. An ion forms when electrons are lost or gained; ordinary ion formation does not change the number of protons in the nucleus.

For introductory arrangements of the first twenty elements, fill the first shell with up to 2 electrons, then the second with up to 8, and use the school-level arrangements 2,8,8,1 for potassium and 2,8,8,2 for calcium. Sodium has 11 electrons arranged 2,8,1. Chlorine has 17 arranged 2,8,7. These simple shell counts describe the first twenty elements and should not be extended as a universal rule for all elements.

Atoms of the same element can have different neutron numbers: these are isotopes. Carbon-12 and carbon-14 both have six protons but have six and eight neutrons respectively. Their shared proton number makes them carbon. Electron arrangements connect to the periodic table: the occupied-shell count gives the period for these elements. Atoms in groups 1 and 2 have one and two outer electrons; groups 13–18 usually have three to eight outer electrons, with helium an exception having two.
examples: For sodium-23, Z = 11 and A = 23. Protons = 11; neutrons = 23 − 11 = 12; a neutral atom has 11 electrons, arranged 2,8,1.
An oxygen atom has Z = 8 and A = 16. It has 8 protons, 8 neutrons and 8 electrons. If it gains two electrons to form O²⁻, it has 10 electrons but still 8 protons.
Calcium has arrangement 2,8,8,2. Four occupied shells place it in period 4, and two outer electrons place it in group 2.
lessons.summary: An atom has a small, dense nucleus containing positively charged protons and uncharged neutrons.
lessons.diagramAlt: Sodium-23 shell-count model: 11 protons, 12 neutrons and electron arrangement 2,8,1.

lessons.title: Force, pressure, work and energy
objectives: Calculate pressure, work, power and efficiency.
Distinguish force balance from being at rest.
Use units consistently.
paragraphs: A force is a push or pull measured in newtons (N). It can change an object’s motion or shape. Several forces may act together: the resultant is their combined effect, taking direction into account. Two opposite forces of 8 N and 3 N have a resultant of 5 N towards the larger force. Balanced forces give zero resultant; this can occur while an object is at rest or moving at constant velocity.

Pressure is normal force per unit area: p = F/A. Its SI unit is the pascal, equivalent to N/m². A smaller contact area produces more pressure for the same force. A sharp blade therefore cuts more readily than a blunt one. In a stationary liquid, pressure increases with depth; liquid pressure acts in all directions at a point. When using p = ρgh for pressure due to a liquid, use density in kg/m³ and depth in metres.

Work is done when a force causes displacement in its direction. For a constant force parallel to motion, W = Fs, in joules (J). Holding a heavy bag stationary may feel tiring, but the simple mechanical work on the bag is zero because it has no displacement. Energy is the capacity to do work and can be transferred between stores or pathways. Near Earth, gravitational potential energy gained = mgh.

Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy: P = W/t, measured in watts (W). A machine doing 600 J of useful work in 3 s has useful power 200 W. Efficiency compares useful output with total input: useful energy output/input energy × 100%. Energy is conserved, but not all input becomes the intended useful output; some usually warms the surroundings. Always state which output is considered useful.
examples: A 120 N force acts normally on 0.04 m². Pressure = 120/0.04 = 3000 Pa. If the area doubles with the same force, pressure halves to 1500 Pa.
A horizontal force of 25 N moves a box 4 m along the force. Work = 25 × 4 = 100 J. If this takes 5 s, average power = 100/5 = 20 W.
Raise a 3 kg load through 2 m. Using g = 10 N/kg, potential energy gain = 3 × 10 × 2 = 60 J. If input energy is 100 J, efficiency = 60/100 × 100% = 60%.
lessons.summary: A force is a push or pull measured in newtons (N).

lessons.title: Light, reflection and refraction
objectives: Draw normals and apply reflection angles.
Describe plane-mirror images.
Explain refraction and basic lens action.
paragraphs: A luminous object emits its own light; a non-luminous object is seen when light reaches it and is reflected towards the eye. In a uniform transparent medium, light travels approximately in straight lines. A ray is a line used to show the direction of travel. Transparent materials transmit light with clear images, translucent materials transmit scattered light, and opaque materials prevent most light from passing through.

Reflection occurs when light returns from a surface. Draw a normal perpendicular to the surface at the point where the ray meets it. The angle of incidence and angle of reflection are measured between the rays and this normal, not the surface. The laws of reflection state that these angles are equal and that the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane. Smooth surfaces give regular reflection; rough surfaces scatter reflected rays because their local normals differ.

A plane mirror forms an upright, virtual image of the same size as the object. The image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. A virtual image cannot be projected directly onto a screen: the rays only appear to come from behind the mirror. Lateral inversion describes reversal across the mirror’s perpendicular direction; use diagrams to reason rather than treating it as a literal exchange of every left and right direction.

Refraction is a change in direction associated with a change of speed when light crosses obliquely between media. Entering glass from air, a ray usually bends towards the normal; leaving glass for air, it bends away. At normal incidence it changes speed without bending. A convex lens can converge parallel rays to a focus. For a converging lens, an object beyond the focal length can form a real image; an object inside the focal length produces a virtual magnified image. Never look at the Sun through a lens or focus sunlight near eyes or flammable materials.
examples: An incident ray makes 35° with the normal. The reflected ray also makes 35° with the normal. The angle between the incident and reflected rays is 70°.
An object is 12 cm in front of a plane mirror. Its image is 12 cm behind it, so the object–image separation is 24 cm.
A ray makes 30° with a flat mirror surface. Its angle to the normal is 90° − 30° = 60°, so the angle of reflection is 60°.
lessons.summary: A luminous object emits its own light; a non-luminous object is seen when light reaches it and is reflected towards the eye.
lessons.diagramAlt: Incident and reflected rays make equal 45-degree angles with the normal to a plane mirror.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis and leaf structure
objectives: Explain food production in green plants.
Relate leaf structures to their functions.
Interpret supervised starch-test evidence safely.
paragraphs: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use light energy to make organic food from carbon dioxide and water. Chlorophyll in chloroplasts absorbs light. A school-level word equation is carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, with light and chlorophyll as conditions. Glucose is a starting material for other substances; it can be used in respiration, converted to starch for storage or used to make cellulose. Plants do not obtain their main food supply by absorbing ready-made food from soil.

A leaf’s broad surface intercepts light, while its thin shape keeps diffusion distances short. The upper epidermis and cuticle protect it while allowing light through. Palisade cells commonly have many chloroplasts. Spongy mesophyll contains air spaces that help gas movement. Stomata are pores controlled by guard cells; they allow gas exchange but also permit water vapour to escape. Veins supply water through xylem and carry sugars through phloem.

Water is taken up by roots and carbon dioxide enters mainly through stomata. Light intensity, carbon dioxide availability and temperature can limit photosynthesis. Increasing one factor will not keep increasing the rate if a different factor has become limiting. Mineral ions are needed for healthy growth: magnesium contributes to chlorophyll and nitrates help plants make amino acids and proteins. A mineral deficiency is not the same as a lack of light.

An investigation should change one factor while keeping other important conditions similar. For a school starch test, a teacher removes leaf chlorophyll using hot ethanol in a water bath, then applies iodine solution; a blue-black colour indicates starch. Ethanol is flammable and must not be heated over a flame. This procedure requires teacher supervision, eye protection and appropriate handling of hot liquids. A paper-based interpretation of observations can be completed independently; do not perform this chemical test unsupervised.
examples: A leaf kept in darkness has little opportunity to make new food by photosynthesis. Comparing it with an otherwise similar illuminated leaf helps investigate the need for light, provided stored starch has been considered.

In a variegated-leaf starch investigation, the green regions may test blue-black while non-green regions do not. Under controlled conditions this supports the role of chlorophyll; record the original pattern before removing the colour.
If a plant has adequate light but little carbon dioxide, adding more light may not increase its photosynthesis rate. Carbon dioxide is then a limiting factor.
lessons.summary: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use light energy to make organic food from carbon dioxide and water.
lessons.diagramAlt: Light-driven photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water to produce glucose and oxygen.

lessons.title: Human nutrition and digestion
objectives: Trace digestion and absorption through the human gut.
Distinguish nutrient roles and digestive processes.
Interpret food-test observations safely.
paragraphs: A balanced diet supplies adequate nutrients in suitable proportions for a person’s needs. Carbohydrates and fats can supply energy; proteins provide amino acids for growth and repair. Vitamins and minerals support body processes. Water is essential for transport and chemical reactions, and dietary fibre helps normal bowel movement. Energy requirements vary with age, activity and other circumstances, so a single menu is not automatically suitable for everyone.

Digestion breaks large, insoluble food molecules into smaller molecules that can be absorbed. Mechanical digestion, such as chewing, breaks food into smaller pieces without changing their chemical identity. Chemical digestion uses enzymes, which are biological catalysts. In the mouth, teeth break food up and saliva helps swallowing; salivary amylase begins the digestion of starch. Food moves through the oesophagus by coordinated muscle contractions called peristalsis.

The stomach churns food and provides acidic conditions in which a protease begins protein digestion. Most digestion and nutrient absorption occur in the small intestine. The pancreas supplies digestive enzymes; bile is made by the liver, stored in the gall bladder and released into the small intestine. Bile emulsifies fats into small droplets and helps neutralise acid, but is not an enzyme. Lipase breaks fats down chemically.

The small intestine has folds and villi that provide a large absorptive surface. Villi have thin surfaces and a good blood supply, helping nutrients move away after absorption. The large intestine absorbs water and forms faeces from remaining material. Egestion removes undigested food; excretion removes metabolic waste, so they are different processes. A ruminant such as a cow has a multi-compartment stomach, and microbes help digest cellulose; humans do not have the same cellulose-digesting system.

Food-test observations support conclusions only when methods and controls are appropriate. Iodine can test starch; Benedict’s test can test reducing sugars with supervised heating; the biuret test can test protein. Chemical reagents are not food and must never be tasted. These tests require a teacher and laboratory precautions. For independent study, interpret supplied result tables and explain what the results support rather than attempting unsupervised chemical testing.
examples: A sample turns blue-black with iodine. This supports the presence of starch. It does not by itself establish that the sample contains every nutrient needed in a balanced diet.
Chewing bread increases its surface area, helping enzymes contact the starch. Mechanical breakdown and chemical enzyme action work together, but are not the same process.
Compare a small intestine with many villi and one with damaged villi. Less effective surface area can reduce nutrient absorption even if digestion has broken food down normally.
lessons.summary: A balanced diet supplies adequate nutrients in suitable proportions for a person’s needs.

lessons.title: Real numbers, inequalities and approximation
objectives: Classify and compare real numbers.
Convert recurring decimals and solve simple inequalities.
Round and estimate with stated precision.
paragraphs: A rational number can be written as a/b, where a and b are integers and b is nonzero. Integers, terminating decimals and recurring decimals are rational. An irrational number cannot be written in this form; its decimal expansion neither terminates nor repeats. √2 is irrational but √9 = 3 is rational. The real numbers include both rational and irrational numbers and can be represented on a number line.

On a number line, numbers increase towards the right. Thus −2 is greater than −5 even though 5 has a greater magnitude than 2. Absolute value is distance from zero, so |−5| = 5 and |5| = 5. For inequalities, adding the same quantity to both sides preserves the direction. Multiplying or dividing by a negative number reverses the inequality sign: if −2x < 8, dividing by −2 gives x > −4.

To turn a recurring decimal into a fraction, let x equal the decimal, multiply by a suitable power of ten, and subtract equations so the repeating tails cancel. For x = 0.333…, 10x = 3.333…, so 9x = 3 and x = 1/3. For x = 0.272727…, 100x − x = 27 and x = 27/99 = 3/11. The number of repeated digits determines the useful power of ten.

Decimal places count digits after the decimal point, whereas significant figures count from the first nonzero digit. To round, inspect the next digit: in the usual school convention, increase the last retained digit if the next is 5 or more. Leading zeros are not significant. For example 0.00486 to two significant figures is 0.0049. Rounding introduces an approximation, so use ≈ when appropriate and avoid rounding every intermediate calculation unnecessarily.
examples: Compare −7 and −3: −3 lies farther right, so −7 < −3. Their absolute values are 7 and 3 respectively.
Round 28.746 to two decimal places: retain 28.74 and inspect the next digit 6, giving 28.75. To two significant figures it becomes 29 instead.
Solve −3x ≥ 12: divide by −3 and reverse the sign, obtaining x ≤ −4. Check x = −5: 15 ≥ 12 is true.
lessons.summary: A rational number can be written as a/b, where a and b are integers and b is nonzero.

lessons.title: Quadratic equations and indices
objectives: Solve quadratics by factorisation, completing the square and formula.
Apply index laws correctly.
Convert numbers to standard form.
paragraphs: A quadratic equation has a highest variable power of two and can be written ax² + bx + c = 0, with a ≠ 0. Always put the equation in this form before identifying a, b and c. The sign belongs with the coefficient: in x² − 5x + 6 = 0, b is −5. A root or solution is a value that makes the original equation true.

Factorisation writes a quadratic expression as a product. To factor x² + bx + c, look for two numbers whose sum is b and product is c. Since −2 and −3 sum to −5 and multiply to 6, x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 2)(x − 3). If a product is zero, at least one factor must be zero; therefore the roots are 2 and 3. Do not use the zero-product rule on a product that equals a nonzero number.

Completing the square rewrites an expression using a perfect square. For x² + 6x + 5 = 0, move 5, add 9 to both sides and obtain (x + 3)² = 4. Taking both square roots gives x + 3 = ±2, so x = −1 or −5. More generally the quadratic formula is x = [−b ± √(b² − 4ac)]/(2a). The entire numerator is divided by 2a. A negative discriminant means no real roots.

For a nonzero base a, a^m × a^n = a^(m+n), a^m/a^n = a^(m−n), (a^m)^n = a^(mn), a^0 = 1 and a^(−n) = 1/a^n. These rules require the same base when combining exponents by addition or subtraction. Standard form writes a number as A × 10^n with 1 ≤ A < 10 and n an integer. Thus 540,000 = 5.4 × 10^5 and 0.00072 = 7.2 × 10^−4.
examples: Solve x² − 7x + 12 = 0. The numbers −3 and −4 have sum −7 and product 12, so (x−3)(x−4)=0 and x=3 or 4. Substitution confirms both.
Simplify 2³ × 2⁴ / 2² = 2^(3+4−2) = 2⁵ = 32. Combine exponents only because the base is consistently 2.
lessons.summary: A quadratic equation has a highest variable power of two and can be written ax² + bx + c = 0, with a ≠ 0.

lessons.title: Aina za maneno na mpangilio wa sentensi
objectives: Tambua kazi za aina za maneno.
Tunga sentensi na aya zenye uhusiano sahihi.
Hariri herufi kubwa na alama za uandishi.
paragraphs: Maneno hutimiza kazi tofauti katika sentensi. Nomino hutaja mtu, kitu, mahali, hali au wazo, kwa mfano Amina, kitabu na furaha. Kiwakilishi husimama badala ya nomino katika muktadha, kwa mfano yeye katika Amina amefika; yeye amebeba kitabu. Kivumishi hutoa maelezo kuhusu nomino au kiwakilishi, kama kidogo katika kitabu kidogo. Usihukumu aina ya neno bila kuangalia matumizi yake katika sentensi.

Kitenzi hueleza tendo au hali: anasoma, wamefika na ni katika matumizi ya kuwa kiunganishi cha kiarifu. Vielezi hueleza zaidi kuhusu tendo au sifa, kwa mfano polepole katika anatembea polepole na jana katika alifika jana. Kihusishi huonyesha uhusiano, kwa mfano chini ya meza. Kiunganishi huunganisha vipashio, kama na, lakini na kwa sababu. Kihisishi huonyesha hisia, kama Lo! au Hongera!, kutegemea muktadha.

Sentensi yenye maana inahitaji uhusiano unaoeleweka baina ya maneno yake. Mtoto mdogo anasoma kitabu ina nomino mtoto, kivumishi mdogo, kitenzi anasoma na nomino kitabu. Kubadilisha mpangilio kiholela kunaweza kuficha maana. Kiswahili kinaweza kutumia kiambishi cha nafsi katika kitenzi bila kurudia kiima kwa neno tofauti: Ninasoma tayari huonyesha msemaji mmoja.

Unapoandika hadithi, chagua maneno yanayolingana na tukio na hadhira. Unganisha sentensi katika aya zenye wazo kuu, epuka kurukaruka muda bila sababu na tumia alama za uandishi. Majina mahsusi huanza kwa herufi kubwa. Nukta huonyesha mwisho wa sentensi ya taarifa; alama ya kuuliza hutumika kwa swali. Soma rasimu tena ili kukagua maana, upatanisho na mpangilio kabla ya kuwasilisha.
examples: Katika sentensi Mwanafunzi hodari ameandika vizuri, mwanafunzi ni nomino, hodari kivumishi, ameandika kitenzi na vizuri kielezi. Uchambuzi unaangalia kazi ya kila neno hapa.
Sentensi Asha alisoma na Juma aliandika hutumia na kuunganisha taarifa mbili. Asha alisoma lakini hakumaliza hutumia lakini kuonyesha tofauti na matarajio.
Rasimu: juma alifika jana je alileta kitabu. Uhariri: Juma alifika jana. Je, alileta kitabu? Tumeweka herufi kubwa na kutofautisha taarifa na swali.
lessons.summary: Maneno hutimiza kazi tofauti katika sentensi.

lessons.title: Ngeli na upatanisho wa kisarufi
objectives: Tumia upatanisho katika umoja na wingi.
Hariri virejeshi, vivumishi na vitenzi.
Tofautisha sentensi ambatani na changamani.
paragraphs: Upatanisho wa kisarufi ni uhusiano wa kimaumbo kati ya nomino na vipashio vinavyoirejelea, kama vivumishi, viwakilishi na vitenzi. Katika kitabu kizuri kimepotea, ki- katika kizuri na kimepotea kinahusiana na kitabu. Katika vitabu vizuri vimepotea, umbo la wingi linaonekana katika vi-. Ngeli zinaweza kuchambuliwa kwa viambishi vya nomino au vya upatanisho; katika sura hii tunazingatia maumbo yanayotumika katika sentensi.

Nomino nyingi za watu na viumbe hai hupatana kwa a- katika umoja na wa- katika wingi wa vitenzi: mtoto anacheza; watoto wanacheza; paka amekula; paka wamekula. Hata hivyo, maumbo ya vivumishi na viwakilishi yanahitaji kuangaliwa katika matumizi husika. Usichukue kila neno linaloanza kwa ki- kuwa la ngeli moja bila kuchunguza maana na upatanisho wake: kipofu, akimaanisha mtu, anaweza kuhitaji upatanisho wa viumbe hai.

Mifano mingine ni mti mrefu umeanguka na miti mirefu imeanguka; jicho kubwa linauma na macho makubwa yanauma; nyumba nzuri imejengwa na nyumba nzuri zimejengwa. Nomino inaweza kubaki na umbo lilelile katika umoja na wingi lakini upatanisho ukabadilika, kama nyumba. Soma sentensi nzima ili kujua idadi na uhusiano, badala ya kutegemea umbo la nomino peke yake.

Sentensi ambatani huunganisha vishazi huru, kwa mfano Asha anasoma na Juma anaandika. Sentensi changamani ina kishazi kinachotegemea kingine, kwa mfano Mwanafunzi aliyefika mapema amepata nafasi. Katika uandishi, hakikisha virejeshi vinaendana na vinavyorejelewa: kitabu kilichopotea; vitabu vilivyopotea. Ukibadili nomino kuwa wingi, kagua kila kipashio kinachohusika katika sentensi, si kitenzi pekee.
examples: Umoja: Kitabu hiki kipya kimefika. Wingi: Vitabu hivi vipya vimefika. Nomino, kionyeshi, kivumishi na kitenzi vimebadilika kwa kuzingatia wingi.
Umoja: Mti huu mrefu umeanguka. Wingi: Miti hii mirefu imeanguka. Usitumie vi- kwa sababu tu nomino iko katika wingi.
Makosa: Watoto mdogo amefika. Uhariri: Watoto wadogo wamefika. Tumeoanisha kivumishi na kitenzi na nomino ya wingi.
lessons.summary: Upatanisho wa kisarufi ni uhusiano wa kimaumbo kati ya nomino na vipashio vinavyoirejelea, kama vivumishi, viwakilishi na vitenzi.

lessons.title: Earth in the solar system
objectives: Locate Earth within the solar system.
Explain shape, rotation, revolution and seasons.
Use latitude, longitude and ideal local-time differences.
paragraphs: The solar system includes the Sun and the objects that move under its gravity, including planets, moons, asteroids and comets. Earth is the third planet from the Sun. In order outwards the eight planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. The Sun is a star that emits light; planets are seen mainly by reflected sunlight. The Moon is Earth’s natural satellite, not a planet orbiting independently around the Sun in the same sense as Earth.

Earth is approximately spherical, with slight flattening near the poles and a bulge near the equator. Its mean radius is about 6371 km and its equatorial circumference about 40,075 km. These are approximate measurements, not values every school map needs at full precision. Evidence for its curved shape includes photographs from space, Earth’s curved shadow during lunar eclipses and changes in visible stars with latitude.

Earth rotates about its axis from west to east, completing a rotation relative to the Sun in about twenty-four hours. This produces the cycle of day and night: the part facing the Sun is illuminated while the other part is dark. Earth also revolves around the Sun in about 365¼ days. Its tilted axis and revolution cause changing day lengths and seasons; seasons are not mainly caused by changes in Earth’s distance from the Sun.

Latitude describes angular position north or south of the equator, from 0° to 90°. Longitude describes angular position east or west of the prime meridian, up to 180°. Parallels join points of equal latitude and meridians join the poles through points of equal longitude. Tanzania lies south of the equator, but exact coordinates depend on the location. A coordinate needs both its number and direction: 6°S is different from 6°N.

Earth turns roughly 360° in 24 hours, equivalent to 15° per hour or 1° in four minutes. This supports ideal local solar-time calculations, where a place farther east reaches solar noon earlier. Official civil time zones are chosen for practical and political reasons and do not always follow every 15° line. In a school calculation, first state whether the question asks for ideal local time or an official time-zone reading.
examples: At a place with latitude 5°S, the angular position is five degrees south of the equator. Its longitude is still needed to locate it fully.
Two locations differ by 30° of longitude. Ideal local time differs by 30/15 = 2 hours. If B is east of A and A is at 10:00, B is at 12:00 local solar time.
Distinguish rotation and revolution: rotation is turning about Earth’s own axis and explains day/night; revolution is its orbit around the Sun and, together with axial tilt, helps explain seasons.
lessons.summary: The solar system includes the Sun and the objects that move under its gravity, including planets, moons, asteroids and comets.

lessons.title: Earth’s layers and interacting systems
objectives: Compare crust, mantle, core and lithosphere.
Describe atmosphere, hydrosphere and biosphere.
Explain interactions through water-cycle and pollution examples.
paragraphs: Earth has a thin outer crust, a much thicker mantle and a central core. Continental crust is generally thicker and less dense than oceanic crust. The mantle is mainly solid rock, but over long timescales some regions can flow slowly. Describing the whole mantle as a sea of liquid is misleading. The outer core is liquid and the inner core is solid, consisting mainly of iron with nickel and other constituents.

Temperature generally increases with depth, but pressure also increases and affects whether material is solid or liquid. The inner core remains solid despite its high temperature because of enormous pressure. The lithosphere consists of the crust and the rigid uppermost mantle, rather than the crust alone. Plates are sections of this rigid outer region. A classroom layered model simplifies a complex planet and is not a perfectly scaled representation.

The atmosphere is the envelope of gases around Earth. Most weather occurs in the lowest layer, the troposphere. The hydrosphere includes Earth’s water in oceans, rivers, lakes, ice, groundwater and water vapour. The biosphere includes life and the regions where organisms occur. These systems overlap and interact: water evaporates into air, rain enters soil and plants take up water through roots.

Water cycles through evaporation, condensation, precipitation, infiltration and runoff. Solar energy supports evaporation and gravity drives falling water and much surface flow. Removing vegetation can reduce interception and change runoff and erosion. Pollution released in one part of a catchment can affect water and living things elsewhere. A sound geographical explanation connects processes and evidence rather than presenting each system as isolated.
examples: Compare crust and lithosphere: crust is a compositional layer; lithosphere includes the crust plus rigid upper mantle. Calling them identical loses the distinction.

Rain falls on a hillside. Some water infiltrates soil, some moves as runoff into a stream and some may later evaporate or be transpired by plants. The same event links water, land, air and living organisms.
A factory releases waste into a river. The immediate change is in the hydrosphere, but aquatic organisms in the biosphere may be affected and people downstream may lose a safe water source.
lessons.summary: Earth has a thin outer crust, a much thicker mantle and a central core.
lessons.diagramAlt: Schematic crust, mantle, liquid outer core and solid inner core, not to scale.

lessons.title: Entrepreneurship and sole proprietorship
objectives: Explain goods, services and business links.
Evaluate entrepreneurial opportunities and skills.
Compare advantages and risks of sole proprietorship.
paragraphs: Business studies examines how people organise activities to produce, distribute and exchange goods and services. A good is a tangible item, such as a notebook; a service is an activity, such as bicycle repair or transport. Business decisions connect with mathematics through costing, languages through communication, geography through locations and transport, and science through products and production methods.

An entrepreneur identifies an opportunity, organises resources and accepts the uncertainty of starting or improving an enterprise. Useful skills include planning, keeping records, communicating, solving problems and adapting to evidence. Risk-taking does not mean gambling blindly: a careful entrepreneur estimates possible losses, tests demand and chooses affordable experiments. Profit can reward success, but it is not guaranteed.

An opportunity is more than an idea that sounds attractive. Investigate who needs the product, what alternatives they already use, whether they can pay and whether the business can deliver safely and lawfully at a sustainable cost. For example, many students may want low-cost stationery, but sales depend on school rules, competing sellers, purchasing times and reliable supply. Ask neutral questions rather than encouraging only the answer you hope to hear.

A sole proprietorship is owned by one person. The owner normally makes decisions and receives profits, but also carries responsibility for losses and business debts. Advantages can include simple decision-making and direct customer contact; disadvantages can include limited capital, heavy workload and lack of continuity if the owner cannot work. Ordinary sole proprietorship should not be confused with a limited-liability company. Before starting, an owner must check applicable registration, tax and sector requirements with the responsible authorities rather than assume a classroom example grants legal permission.
examples: An entrepreneur notices that cyclists travel far for repairs. Before renting a workshop, she counts local bicycles, interviews potential customers and tests a small repair service. This reduces uncertainty without pretending it removes all risk.

A sole trader buys stock on credit and later cannot sell it. The debt is not automatically erased because the business name is different from the owner’s name; personal responsibility is a key disadvantage of ordinary sole proprietorship.

A notebook costs TSh 800 to buy and TSh 100 per unit in transport and handling. At a price of TSh 1000, the amount left before other costs is TSh 100. Ignoring the handling cost would overstate the margin.
lessons.summary: Business studies examines how people organise activities to produce, distribute and exchange goods and services.

lessons.title: Production, capital and small-business resources
objectives: Explain production and its factors.
Compare capital sources and repayment obligations.
Calculate and check simple inventory records.
paragraphs: Production creates or increases the usefulness of goods and services. Growing maize, milling it, transporting flour and selling it all contribute to usefulness in different ways. Primary production obtains resources from nature, secondary production processes or manufactures products, and tertiary production supplies services. A service can be productive even when it creates no physical object.

The traditional factors of production are land, labour, capital and enterprise. Land includes natural resources; labour is human physical and mental effort; capital includes tools, equipment and other produced resources used to produce further output; enterprise coordinates resources and bears uncertainty. Money can finance productive capital, but money itself does not plough a field or repair a bicycle. A useful plan distinguishes finance from the assets and skills it will purchase.

A small business can obtain finance from personal savings, family contributions, loans or supplier credit. Loans require repayment under agreed terms and may involve interest, fees, collateral or group obligations. Supplier credit postpones payment but does not make goods free. Compare the full amount repayable, repayment dates and likely cash flow; do not judge an offer from the advertised instalment alone.

Cooperatives are member-owned organisations formed to meet shared needs, for example marketing crops or obtaining inputs. A savings and credit cooperative can help members save and obtain credit under its rules. Microfinance may provide small-scale financial services, but a small loan can still be costly or unsuitable. Membership obligations, charges, risks and governance should be understood before borrowing. This chapter explains concepts and is not a recommendation for any specific lender.

Warehousing involves safe storage until goods are needed. It can protect stock, support seasonal supply and allow larger purchases, but costs money and carries risks such as spoilage, theft and damage. Inventory records track stock received, issued and remaining. First-in, first-out handling can help move older dated stock before newer stock, but safe expiry rules still take priority. Reconcile recorded stock with physical counts to identify errors or loss.
examples: Maize growing is primary production, milling flour is secondary production and transporting flour to customers is a tertiary service. Each activity adds usefulness to the chain.

A loan gives TSh 100,000 now and requires twelve payments of TSh 10,000 with no other charges. Total repayment is TSh 120,000 and finance cost is TSh 20,000. The example does not establish an annual percentage rate.

Opening stock is 40 bags, deliveries add 25 and sales remove 38. Expected closing stock = 40+25−38 = 27 bags. If only 24 are counted, investigate the difference of 3 rather than silently altering the record.
lessons.summary: Production creates or increases the usefulness of goods and services.

lessons.title: Jamii za Tanzania kabla ya ukoloni
objectives: Eleza tofauti na mwingiliano wa jamii kabla ya ukoloni.
Husisha uchumi na mifumo ya kisiasa na kijamii.
Tathmini teknolojia na maadili kwa ushahidi.
paragraphs: Historia ya jamii za Tanzania kabla ya ukoloni inaonyesha mwingiliano, uhamaji na mabadiliko ya muda mrefu. Makundi yanayotajwa kwa lugha au asili si visiwa visivyohusiana. Watu walibadilishana maarifa, kuoana, kufanya biashara na kubadili shughuli za maisha kulingana na mazingira. Istilahi kama Wabantu na Wanilo zinaweza kusaidia kueleza uhusiano wa lugha na historia ya uhamaji, lakini hazimaanishi kila kundi lilikuwa na tabia, kazi au uwezo uleule.

Shughuli za kiuchumi zilihusisha kilimo, ufugaji, uvuvi, uwindaji, ukusanyaji, ufundi na biashara. Mazingira, teknolojia na mahitaji yaliathiri mchanganyiko wa shughuli hizo. Mfugaji angeweza kubadilishana mazao ya mifugo na nafaka kutoka kwa mkulima; jamii moja ingeweza kufanya kilimo na ufugaji kwa pamoja. Usihusishe shughuli moja na watu wote wa kundi fulani bila ushahidi wa mahali na kipindi.

Mifumo ya kisiasa ilitofautiana. Baadhi ya jamii zilikuwa na mamlaka iliyojikita kwa machifu au wafalme, huku nyingine zikitumia mabaraza ya wazee, ukoo au mifumo ya rika. Mamlaka ya kisiasa na mahusiano ya kijamii yaliathiri uamuzi kuhusu ardhi, migogoro, ulinzi na ushirikiano. Kutokuwa na ufalme mkuu hakumaanishi kutokuwa na utaratibu wa uongozi au sheria.

Utengenezaji wa vyombo, usindikaji wa chuma, ujenzi, tiba za jadi, uhifadhi wa chakula na maarifa ya mazingira ni mifano ya sayansi na teknolojia za jamii. Maarifa yalienezwa kupitia mafunzo ya vitendo, familia, mafundi na biashara. Mawasiliano na wageni yalileta bidhaa na mawazo mapya lakini pia yaliweza kuhusisha unyonyaji, vita na biashara ya watumwa. Tathmini mabadiliko kwa ushahidi na athari zake kwa makundi tofauti, badala ya kuyasifu au kuyakataa yote kwa kauli moja.
examples: Jamii ya wakulima na wafugaji zinapobadilishana nafaka na maziwa, kila upande unapata bidhaa ambayo unaweza kukosa. Biashara hiyo huonyesha utegemeano, si kutengwa kabisa.
Mfua chuma anapofundisha mwanafunzi kuchagua na kutengeneza zana, maarifa ya kiufundi yanapitishwa kwa mazoezi. Bidhaa ya mwisho pekee haielezi hatua zote za teknolojia hiyo.
Baraza la wazee linaweza kusikiliza mgogoro wa matumizi ya ardhi. Huu ni mfano wa utaratibu wa kisiasa hata kama hakuna mfalme mwenye mamlaka juu ya eneo kubwa.
lessons.summary: Historia ya jamii za Tanzania kabla ya ukoloni inaonyesha mwingiliano, uhamaji na mabadiliko ya muda mrefu.

lessons.title: Ukoloni, upinzani na harakati za uhuru
objectives: Eleza mifumo na athari za ukoloni.
Linganisha mbinu za upinzani na harakati za uhuru.
Panga matukio muhimu bila kuyachanganya.
paragraphs: Ukoloni ni mfumo ambao dola ya nje hutawala jamii na eneo jingine kwa manufaa yake. Katika Afrika ya karne ya kumi na tisa, upanuzi wa himaya za Ulaya ulihusishwa na mashindano ya kisiasa, masoko, rasilimali na maslahi mengine. Mkutano wa Berlin wa 1884–1885 uliweka taratibu zilizosaidia mashindano ya kikoloni ya Ulaya; haukuwa mkutano ambao kila mpaka wa sasa wa Tanzania uliamuliwa mara moja wala ambao jamii za Afrika zilipewa nafasi sawa ya kuamua hatima yao.

Sehemu kubwa ya eneo la Tanganyika iliingia katika ukoloni wa Kijerumani mwishoni mwa karne ya kumi na tisa. Baada ya Vita Kuu ya Kwanza ya Dunia, Tanganyika iliwekwa chini ya utawala wa Uingereza katika mfumo wa mamlaka ya Shirikisho la Mataifa, baadaye udhamini wa Umoja wa Mataifa. Zanzibar ilikuwa na historia tofauti ya usultani na ulinzi wa Uingereza. Usichukulie Tanganyika na Zanzibar kuwa na historia ileile ya utawala katika kila kipindi.

Utawala wa kikoloni uliathiri ardhi, kazi, kodi, uzalishaji na elimu. Mahitaji ya kodi na kazi yanaweza kuonyesha namna uchumi ulivyoelekezwa kukidhi maslahi ya utawala na wafanyabiashara wa kikoloni. Jamii ziliitikia kwa njia mbalimbali, ikiwemo upinzani wa silaha, kukataa masharti, kuhama, mazungumzo na ushirikiano wa kimkakati. Njia iliyochaguliwa ilihusiana na mazingira na uwezo wa jamii, hivyo kukosekana kwa vita vya wazi si ushahidi wa kukubali kila sharti.

Vita vya Maji Maji vya 1905–1907 vilikuwa upinzani mkubwa dhidi ya utawala wa Kijerumani katika maeneo kadhaa ya kusini na mashariki ya Tanganyika. Sera za kazi na kilimo, ikiwemo masharti ya uzalishaji wa pamba, zilichangia malalamiko. Ukandamizaji wa kijeshi na uharibifu wa maisha na chakula ulileta mateso makubwa. Kujifunza harakati hizi kunahitaji kuheshimu waathiriwa na kutofautisha madai ya wakati huo, ushahidi wa kihistoria na tafsiri za baadaye.

Harakati za baadaye za uhuru zilijumuisha vyama, wafanyakazi, wakulima, viongozi wa jamii na mijadala ya kisiasa. TANU ilianzishwa mwaka 1954 na Tanganyika ilipata uhuru tarehe 9 Desemba 1961. Zanzibar ilipata uhuru tarehe 10 Desemba 1963 na Mapinduzi yalitokea tarehe 12 Januari 1964. Tanganyika na Zanzibar ziliungana tarehe 26 Aprili 1964. Tarehe hizi ni matukio tofauti; usiziunganishe kana kwamba uhuru, Mapinduzi na Muungano vilikuwa tukio moja.
examples: Linganisho la maeneo: Tanganyika ilikuwa chini ya utawala wa Kijerumani na baadaye Uingereza; historia ya Zanzibar ilihusisha usultani na ulinzi wa Uingereza. Ufafanuzi sahihi unataja eneo na kipindi.
Mfanyakazi anapokataa sharti la kazi na mwingine akihama ili kuliepuka, wote wanaweza kuwa wanapinga hali fulani, ingawa mbinu zao si sawa na vita vya silaha.
Mpangilio wa matukio: TANU 1954 → uhuru wa Tanganyika 1961 → uhuru wa Zanzibar 1963 → Mapinduzi Januari 1964 → Muungano Aprili 1964. Mfuatano husaidia kuzuia kuchanganya matukio.
lessons.summary: Ukoloni ni mfumo ambao dola ya nje hutawala jamii na eneo jingine kwa manufaa yake.

lessons.title: Grammar for everyday communication
objectives: Use simple present, present progressive and simple past in context.
Apply articles and possession correctly.
Give clear directions using landmarks.
paragraphs: The simple present often describes routines, facts and states. With I, you, we and they, use the base form for most verbs: I read; they walk. With he, she or it, add the appropriate ending: she reads; he watches. Questions and negatives normally use do or does with a base verb: Does she read? She does not read. Do not write does she reads, because does already carries the agreement.

The present progressive describes an activity in progress around the relevant present time: am/is/are + the -ing form. I am reading now contrasts with I read every evening. Use a form of be that agrees with the subject: we are studying, not we is studying. Some verbs for states, such as know in I know the answer, are usually expressed in the simple present rather than the progressive.

The simple past describes a completed event at a past time. Regular verbs often end in -ed, but many common verbs are irregular: go–went, write–wrote, see–saw and buy–bought. Past questions and negatives normally use did with the base form: Did you go? I did not go. A sentence can change tense when the time changes, but changing randomly makes a story confusing.

Articles and pronouns help the reader identify people and things. Use a/an for one non-specific countable item: a book, an egg. The choice depends on the following sound: an hour but a university. Use the when the reference is identified or otherwise specific in context. Possession can be shown with have/has, possessive pronouns or an apostrophe: Asha has a bag; the bag is hers; Asha’s bag. Possessive its has no apostrophe; it’s means it is or it has.

Directions combine clear sequence with location words: Walk past the library, turn left at the gate, and stop beside the office. Prepositions such as near, behind, between and opposite express relationships. Give a useful starting point and landmarks; avoid directions that depend on private knowledge. In spoken communication, listen to the request and check whether the person needs a repeated or simpler explanation.
examples: Routine: Neema walks to school every day. Question: Does Neema walk to school every day? The main verb returns to walk after does.
Now: They are playing football. Yesterday: They played football. The time expressions explain why the tense changes.
Possession: This is Juma’s book. It is his. The apostrophe marks possession in Juma’s, while his is a possessive pronoun.
lessons.summary: The simple present often describes routines, facts and states.

lessons.title: Inference, summaries and connected ideas
objectives: Distinguish stated facts, inferences and unsupported assumptions.
Write concise summaries and paraphrases.
Use vocabulary and cohesive devices accurately.
paragraphs: An inference is a conclusion supported by clues and reasoning. It goes beyond repeating a stated fact, but it must remain consistent with the text. If a character closes a window as dark clouds approach, we may infer that rain is expected. We cannot infer the exact time the rain will begin unless the text supplies evidence. Separate what is stated, what is reasonably inferred and what remains unknown.

Read this original passage: The village library opened earlier during examination week. Halima arrived before sunrise, but several seats were already occupied. She chose a desk near the window and placed her notes beside a borrowed dictionary. When her friend asked her to leave for the market, she smiled and pointed to the revision timetable on the wall. After an hour, they compared answers to a science exercise. The passage suggests that preparation matters to Halima, without claiming that she studies every hour of every day.

A summary selects the main ideas and expresses them concisely in your own words. It omits minor details, repetitions and personal opinions unless the task asks for evaluation. Paraphrasing restates a particular idea, often at a similar level of detail; summarising reduces a larger text to its essentials. Preserve the meaning and avoid inventing motives or events. Use an appropriate word limit and check the summary against the source.

Word meanings can be inferred from surrounding ideas, but context may not provide a precise dictionary definition. In the passage, occupied suggests the seats were already being used. Prefixes and suffixes can help build vocabulary: un- can express the opposite, as in kind–unkind, and -ly can form some adverbs, as in careful–carefully. Not every word beginning with un or ending with ly follows a simple rule, so verify unfamiliar words in a suitable reference.

Cohesive devices make relationships clear. Moreover adds a supporting point, however introduces contrast, because gives a reason and therefore signals a result. Choose a connector that fits the logic. A summary should not simply string together every sentence with and. When combining accounts from several speakers, identify agreement and differences and keep track of who supplied each claim.
examples: Literal detail: Halima used a borrowed dictionary. Inference: she had access to reference material for studying. Unsupported claim: she owned the dictionary; the passage says it was borrowed.

Possible summary: During examination week, Halima used the library early, followed a revision plan and worked with a friend on science answers. This keeps the main learning activities without every location detail.

Combine two ideas: The library opened early. Many seats were already occupied. Contrast: The library opened early; however, many seats were already occupied. The connector highlights an unexpected contrast.
lessons.summary: An inference is a conclusion supported by clues and reasoning.

lessons.title: Bonding, formulae and balanced reactions
objectives: Explain ionic and covalent models.
Derive simple neutral formulae and empirical ratios.
Balance equations without changing substances.
paragraphs: Chemical bonds hold particles together. In ionic, or electrovalent, bonding, electron transfer produces oppositely charged ions whose electrostatic attraction holds a structure together. A sodium atom can lose one electron to become Na⁺, while chlorine gains one to become Cl⁻. Sodium chloride is an extended ionic structure, not a collection of separate NaCl molecules. Its formula describes a 1:1 ratio of ions.

In a covalent bond, atoms share one or more pairs of electrons. H₂ has a shared pair between hydrogen atoms, O₂ is represented with a double bond and N₂ with a triple bond in introductory models. Many simple covalent substances consist of molecules; network structures such as diamond are exceptions. Ionic substances often conduct when molten or dissolved because ions can move, but do not normally conduct as solids. These patterns depend on structure rather than a label alone.

A compound formula must balance charges when it represents an electrically neutral ionic substance. Calcium is Ca²⁺ and chloride is Cl⁻, so the ratio is one calcium to two chloride ions: CaCl₂. For aluminium oxide, Al³⁺ and O²⁻ require two aluminium ions and three oxide ions, giving Al₂O₃. An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms; a molecular formula gives actual atom numbers in a molecule. Glucose has molecular formula C₆H₁₂O₆ and empirical formula CH₂O.

A chemical equation represents a reaction while conserving atoms. Change coefficients before formulae to balance it; changing a subscript changes the substance. For hydrogen burning, 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O has four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on each side. Combination reactions join reactants into a product; decomposition breaks a reactant into products; displacement replaces one element in a compound. A reaction can fit more than one useful description, so define the classification being used.
examples: Balance Mg + O₂ → MgO: put 2 before MgO to obtain two oxygen atoms on the right, then 2 before Mg. Result: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.
Derive magnesium chloride: Mg²⁺ needs two Cl⁻ ions to make zero net charge. Write MgCl₂, not Mg₂Cl. The ratio follows the charges.
C₂H₆ has ratio C:H of 2:6. Divide by 2 to obtain empirical formula CH₃. The molecular formula still contains two carbon and six hydrogen atoms.
lessons.summary: Chemical bonds hold particles together.

lessons.title: Current, voltage and resistance
objectives: Use current, voltage and resistance relations.
Compare series and parallel circuits.
Calculate electrical energy and apply safe boundaries.
paragraphs: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge: I = Q/t, measured in amperes (A). Conventional current is described in the direction positive charge would move. In a metal, electrons drift in the opposite direction. A simple circuit needs a complete conducting path and an energy source. Current is not used up by a lamp; energy is transferred in the lamp while charge continues around the circuit.

Potential difference, or voltage, is energy transferred per unit charge: V = E/Q. A voltmeter is connected across a component in parallel. An ammeter measures current and is connected in series. Resistance describes opposition to current, R = V/I, measured in ohms (Ω). For an ohmic conductor at constant temperature, V is proportional to I. A lamp filament can heat up and change resistance, so not every component gives a straight-line V–I graph.

In a series path, the same current passes through each component and potential differences add across the supply. For resistors, total series resistance is R₁ + R₂ + …. In parallel branches, the voltage is the same across each branch and branch currents add to the supply current. These statements require a correctly identified circuit; drawing components near each other does not prove they are in series or parallel.

Electrical power can be calculated as P = VI. Energy transferred at constant power is E = Pt. Use seconds for joules, or use kilowatts and hours for kilowatt-hours. Household mains electricity is dangerous. Independent school-level experiments should use only teacher-approved low-voltage supplies; never experiment on wall sockets, household wiring or damaged appliances. Fuses and circuit breakers can interrupt excessive current, but are not permission to handle live equipment.
examples: A charge of 120 C passes in 30 s. Current I=120/30=4 A.
