A resistor has 6 V across it and 0.5 A through it. R=6/0.5=12 Ω. Power P=6×0.5=3 W.
A 60 W lamp operates for 2 h. Energy = 0.060 kW × 2 h = 0.12 kWh. In joules, 60 × 7200 = 432,000 J.
lessons.summary: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge: I = Q/t, measured in amperes (A).

lessons.title: Transport in flowering plants and humans
objectives: Explain transport tissues and transpiration.
Trace double circulation and blood components.
Interpret controlled transport and pulse observations.
paragraphs: Flowering plants use xylem to transport water and dissolved mineral ions mainly from roots towards leaves. Root hairs increase contact area with soil water. Osmosis is net water movement through a partially permeable membrane from a region of higher water potential to lower water potential. Mineral-ion uptake and water uptake should not be treated as exactly the same process; active transport can contribute to ion uptake.

Transpiration is water-vapour loss from aerial plant parts, especially leaves. Evaporation from leaf surfaces and diffusion out through stomata contribute to the process. A transpiration pull helps move a continuous water column through xylem. Warmer, drier or windier conditions often increase water loss, while stomatal closure can limit it. Phloem transports sugars and other organic substances between sources and sinks, not simply water upwards.

In humans, the heart pumps blood through a double circulation: blood passes through the lungs and through the rest of the body in separate circuits. The right side receives blood returning from the body and pumps it to the lungs; the left side receives blood from the lungs and pumps it to the body. The left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall because the systemic circuit requires higher pressure. Valves help prevent backward flow.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry it towards the heart; these definitions concern direction, not oxygen content. The pulmonary artery carries blood low in oxygen to the lungs, while pulmonary veins return oxygenated blood. Capillaries have thin walls for exchange with tissues. Red blood cells carry oxygen with haemoglobin, white blood cells support defence, platelets support clotting and plasma transports dissolved substances.

A pulse is the pressure wave felt in an artery when the heart beats. To compare pulse rate before and after ordinary activity, use the same measurement duration and conditions, count carefully and allow recovery. Avoid strenuous exercise tests for anyone with health concerns; use supplied data instead. A short classroom observation is not a medical diagnosis, and unexpected symptoms should be addressed by a responsible adult and a qualified health professional.
examples: A pulse count of 18 beats in 15 s corresponds to 18×4=72 beats/min. Multiplying is appropriate only if that short interval represents the rate being estimated.

A leafy shoot loses water faster in moving dry air than in still humid air under otherwise similar conditions. This supports a role for diffusion conditions, but does not isolate wind if humidity also changed.
Trace circulation: body → right heart → lungs → left heart → body. Place oxygen uptake at the lungs and delivery to tissues in the systemic circulation.
lessons.summary: Flowering plants use xylem to transport water and dissolved mineral ions mainly from roots towards leaves.

lessons.title: Sets and right-triangle trigonometry
objectives: Perform and explain two-set operations.
Count overlapping set memberships.
Use right-triangle ratios and elevation/depression diagrams.
paragraphs: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct elements. Write A={1,2,3}; repeating an element does not increase the set size. The empty set has no elements, and a universal set U gives the context in which complements are taken. Equal sets have exactly the same elements; equivalent finite sets have the same number of elements but need not contain the same things. A subset contains only elements of another set.

The union A∪B includes elements in either set or both. The intersection A∩B includes elements common to both. The complement A′ includes elements of U that are not in A, so its meaning depends on the chosen universal set. For two finite sets, n(A∪B)=n(A)+n(B)−n(A∩B). Subtract the intersection because it was counted twice. A Venn diagram should show overlapping regions and the relevant universe clearly.

In a right-angled triangle, choose an acute angle θ. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is the longest side; the opposite and adjacent sides are named relative to θ. Define sin θ=opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ=adjacent/hypotenuse and tan θ=opposite/adjacent. Changing the chosen acute angle changes which shorter side is opposite and which is adjacent.

An angle of elevation is measured upwards from the horizontal line of sight; an angle of depression is measured downwards from a horizontal line. Draw the horizontal explicitly rather than measuring from a vertical wall. Choose a ratio that uses the known and required sides. These ratios apply directly to right triangles; do not apply them blindly to a triangle with no right angle. If a calculator is used for ordinary angle problems, ensure its angle mode matches degrees.
examples: If A={1,2,3} and B={3,4}, then A∪B={1,2,3,4} and A∩B={3}. Their sizes are 4 and 1, and 3+2−1=4.
In a 3–4–5 right triangle, choose θ opposite the side of length 3. Then sin θ=3/5, cos θ=4/5 and tan θ=3/4.

A vertical pole is observed from 10 m away at 45° elevation on level ground. tan45°=height/10=1, so the height above the observation level is 10 m. Add observer eye height only if the question requires height above ground.
lessons.summary: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct elements.

lessons.title: Photograph interpretation and geographical evidence
objectives: Distinguish photographic views and image regions.
Separate observation from interpretation.
Explain scale, timing and comparison limitations.
paragraphs: A geographical photograph records a selected view at a particular time and location. Ground photographs are taken near ground level; aerial photographs are taken from above and can be vertical or oblique. A photograph is not a map with a single uniform scale. Perspective, camera angle and distance can make apparent sizes misleading, especially in oblique views.

In a ground or oblique view, the foreground is nearest the camera, the middle ground lies farther away and the background is most distant. Describe location using these regions and relative positions before interpreting features. A river, terrace, road or settlement may be recognised through shape, pattern and associations, but a single image may not reveal names, exact dimensions or the date of an activity.

Observation states what is visible; interpretation proposes its geographical meaning. Parallel lines of plants may suggest cultivated land, but the crop species should not be named without sufficient evidence. Roof clusters connected by paths may suggest a settlement; their existence alone does not prove income level or population size. Use cautious claims and compare with maps, field information or other images when possible.

Photographs can support studies of land use, erosion, transport, vegetation and change. A before-and-after comparison needs comparable viewpoints, dates and seasonal conditions. A dry-season image and a wet-season image might show vegetation differences without proving permanent deforestation. Cropping can hide important context, so record the source, date if known and limitations instead of treating a photograph as a complete account.
examples: Visible parallel rows and cleared soil support an interpretation of cultivation. Without closer evidence, identifying the field as maize rather than another crop is an unsupported extra claim.
A road appears wider in the foreground than in the background. Perspective can explain the difference; it does not necessarily mean the real road narrows by the same proportion.
Two images of a river taken at different seasons show different water levels. Check dates and rainfall before concluding that the change was caused by a dam.
lessons.summary: A geographical photograph records a selected view at a particular time and location.

lessons.title: Business records, budgets and local opportunities
objectives: Keep basic cash and credit records.
Compare budgets and actual outcomes.
Evaluate local opportunities using evidence and responsibilities.
paragraphs: Management coordinates people, money, materials and activities to reach a business objective. Planning decides what should be done, organising arranges resources, directing supports implementation and controlling compares actual results with the plan. These functions overlap in a small enterprise, where the owner may perform several roles. A written plan is useful only if it is checked against real results.

Records should distinguish cash received, cash paid, credit transactions, goods held and debts. A simple receipt record does not reveal every cost or obligation. For a credit customer, write the date, amount owed, agreed payment date and later payments so the balance can be checked. Keep evidence securely and respect customer privacy. Never invent receipts or erase differences to make a record appear correct.

A budget estimates income and spending for a stated period. A cash-flow plan pays attention to when money is received and paid, not just total profit. A business may expect profitable sales but run short of cash if suppliers must be paid before customers pay. Compare actual figures with budgeted figures and investigate significant differences. Use the comparison to improve estimates rather than treat a budget as a guaranteed prediction.

Local opportunities can arise from unmet needs, changes in transport, seasonal demand, repair needs or improved ways of doing existing work. Assess demand, resources, competitors, likely costs and relevant requirements. Social and environmental effects also matter: a low-cost business that creates unsafe waste or exploits customers is not automatically a sound opportunity. An evidence-based small test can reveal whether the opportunity is practical before committing all available resources.
examples: A shop starts with TSh 25,000, receives 18,000 cash and pays 31,000. Closing cash=25,000+18,000−31,000=12,000. Credit sales unpaid at this date are not added as cash receipts.
A customer owes TSh 15,000 and pays 6000. Outstanding debt=9000. Recording the payment twice would falsely reduce the balance.
Budgeted transport was TSh 8000 and actual cost 9500. Actual spending exceeded budget by TSh 1500. Investigate price, distance and trip count before assigning a cause.
lessons.summary: Management coordinates people, money, materials and activities to reach a business objective.

lessons.title: Uhuru, Mapinduzi na ujenzi wa Taifa
objectives: Panga matukio ya uhuru, jamhuri, Mapinduzi na Muungano.
Chunguza changamoto na mikakati ya 1961–1966.
Tofautisha malengo, ushahidi na matokeo.
paragraphs: Uhuru hubadili mamlaka ya kisiasa lakini hauondoi mara moja matatizo yote ya uchumi na jamii. Tanganyika ilipopata uhuru mwaka 1961, serikali na wananchi walikabiliwa na mahitaji ya elimu, afya, miundombinu, watumishi wenye ujuzi na kupunguza tofauti zilizorithiwa. Kuchunguza kipindi cha 1961–1966 kunahitaji kutofautisha malengo, hatua zilizochukuliwa na matokeo yake badala ya kudhani kila lengo lilitimia mara moja.

Maendeleo ya utaifa yalihusisha kuimarisha ushirikiano wa watu wa maeneo, lugha na dini tofauti. Kiswahili kilichangia mawasiliano ya kitaifa, huku taasisi na shughuli za pamoja zikitoa nafasi za kujenga mshikamano. Utaifa unaoheshimu watu hauhitaji kudharau tofauti zao. Maadili kama uadilifu, uwajibikaji na usawa ni muhimu wakati wa kutumia rasilimali na kujenga huduma kwa wote.

Tanganyika ilikuwa jamhuri kuanzia tarehe 9 Desemba 1962, mwaka mmoja baada ya uhuru. Zanzibar ilipata uhuru tarehe 10 Desemba 1963 na Mapinduzi yakatokea tarehe 12 Januari 1964. Chimbuko la Mapinduzi linahitaji kuchunguzwa katika muktadha wa tofauti za kijamii na kiuchumi, mashindano ya kisiasa na malalamiko kuhusu utawala na uwakilishi. Eleza madai kwa ushahidi na epuka kuwahusisha watu wote wa kundi fulani na msimamo mmoja.

Muungano wa Tanganyika na Zanzibar ulifanyika tarehe 26 Aprili 1964. Kuunganisha maeneo hayo kulifungua hatua mpya katika ujenzi wa Taifa, lakini si kila suala la maisha na utawala lilikuwa sawa pande zote. Tathmini mchango wa umoja na changamoto zake kwa vyanzo vinavyotaja wakati na eneo. Usihamishe sera za baadaye na kuzitaja kana kwamba zilitangazwa kabla ya 1966: kwa mfano Azimio la Arusha lilitangazwa mwaka 1967, nje ya kipindi hicho cha awali.
examples: Mpangilio: uhuru wa Tanganyika 1961 → jamhuri 1962 → uhuru wa Zanzibar 1963 → Mapinduzi na Muungano 1964. Mfuatano unaonyesha tofauti za matukio yanayokaribiana.
Tathmini ya huduma za elimu inaanza kwa kutaja hitaji, hatua na ushahidi wa matokeo. Kutangaza lengo la kujenga shule si sawa na kuthibitisha kwamba kila mtoto alipata nafasi mara moja.
Kauli Azimio la Arusha lilikuwa sehemu ya hatua za 1961–1966 ina kosa la kipindi. Azimio lilitangazwa 1967; linaweza kutajwa kama tukio linalofuata, si la ndani ya kipindi hicho.
lessons.summary: Uhuru hubadili mamlaka ya kisiasa lakini hauondoi mara moja matatizo yote ya uchumi na jamii.

lessons.title: Insha za hoja, wasifu na muhtasari
objectives: Jenga insha zenye hoja na mpangilio.
Andika wasifu unaoheshimu ukweli na faragha.
Fupisha matini na rekodi maamuzi bila kubuni.
paragraphs: Insha ya hoja huwasilisha msimamo kuhusu suala na kuujenga kwa sababu, mifano na ushahidi. Utangulizi hutambulisha suala; kiini huendeleza hoja katika aya; hitimisho huunganisha msimamo na hoja bila kuleta mada mpya isiyojadiliwa. Mwandishi anaweza kutaja hoja pinzani kwa haki, kisha kueleza kwa nini ushahidi wake unaunga mkono msimamo aliouchagua.

Insha ya wasifu humweleza mtu, mahali, kitu au hali kwa vipengele vinavyojenga picha yenye mpangilio. Maelezo yawe na kusudi badala ya kuwa orodha ya vivumishi. Kwa mtu, chagua taarifa zinazofaa na zinazoheshimu faragha; usibuni sifa au matendo na kuyawasilisha kama ukweli. Kwa mahali, unaweza kufuata mpangilio kutoka eneo pana kwenda sehemu maalumu au kutoka nje kwenda ndani.

Soma matini hii asilia: Shule yetu ilianzisha kikundi cha kusoma wakati wa mapumziko. Mwanzoni wanafunzi wachache walihudhuria kwa sababu wengi hawakujua mpango huo. Wanakikundi waliweka ratiba ubaoni na kuomba ruhusa ya kutumia kivuli karibu na maktaba. Baada ya wiki mbili, walipata washiriki zaidi. Hata hivyo, baadhi walilalamika kwamba muda ulikuwa mfupi. Kikundi kikapendekeza vipindi viwili kwa wiki badala ya kipindi kimoja. Mabadiliko hayo yalihitaji makubaliano ili yasiingiliane na shughuli nyingine za shule.

Muhtasari huchagua mawazo makuu na kuyaeleza kwa ufupi bila kubadili maana. Katika matini ya kikundi, hoja kuu ni kuanzishwa kwa kikundi, hatua za kufahamisha wengine, ongezeko la washiriki na pendekezo la kuboresha muda. Kutaja kwamba kikundi kilikuwa na washiriki mia moja kungebuni taarifa ambayo haikutolewa. Kumbukumbu za mjadala zinaweza kuonyesha suala, hoja kuu, uamuzi na kazi iliyokabidhiwa; zitofautishe pendekezo ambalo bado halijakubaliwa na uamuzi wa mwisho.
examples: Hoja: Ratiba iliyo wazi husaidia ushiriki. Sababu: wanafunzi wanajua muda na mahali. Ushahidi wa matini: washiriki waliongezeka baada ya ratiba kuwekwa na taarifa kutolewa.
Muhtasari: Kikundi cha kusoma kiliongeza ushiriki kwa kutoa taarifa na ratiba, kisha kikapendekeza vipindi zaidi ili kukabiliana na muda mfupi. Hatujatoa idadi ya washiriki ambayo haikutajwa.
Kumbukumbu sahihi: Pendekezo la vipindi viwili litatathminiwa. Kumbukumbu isiyo sahihi: Vipindi viwili vimeidhinishwa. Matini imetaja pendekezo linalohitaji makubaliano, si kibali cha mwisho.
lessons.summary: Insha ya hoja huwasilisha msimamo kuhusu suala na kuujenga kwa sababu, mifano na ushahidi.

lessons.title: Requests, claims and email messages
objectives: Write clear requests, claims and email subjects.
Distinguish proposals from agreements.
Use respectful language and protect private information.
paragraphs: A formal request states who is writing, what is needed and why the request is reasonable. Use a suitable greeting, an organised message and a respectful closing. Being formal does not require long or difficult words. A school request for equipment should identify the items, their purpose and any relevant timing; it should not imply approval has already been given.

A claim letter raises an issue and asks for a remedy based on evidence. Explain the transaction or event, describe the problem accurately, include relevant details such as a date or receipt reference and state the action requested. Avoid threats or unsupported accusations. Keep personal details to what is necessary. A copy of a receipt can support a claim, but the original should normally be retained safely.

An email needs a clear subject line as well as its body. Check the recipient, spelling, attachments and whether private information should be sent. A subject such as Request for footballs for the school team is more useful than Hello. Do not write Attached is the list if no list is actually attached. Messages in group contexts also need turn-taking: acknowledge the previous point before changing topics or disagreeing.

Read this original model: Dear Head Teacher, Our science club requests permission to use the classroom on Friday from 3 p.m. to 4 p.m. We plan to revise measurement questions in small groups. A club leader will record attendance and ensure the room is left tidy. Please let us know whether the room is available. Yours faithfully, The Science Club. The message gives a purpose, time, responsibility and a clear request; it does not assume permission.

Polite negotiation uses clear proposals and reasons: Could you offer a lower price if we buy several items? A seller may accept, refuse or propose another amount. Agreement requires both sides to understand the item, quantity, price and terms. Politeness supports communication but does not oblige another person to accept an offer. Keep a request distinct from a demand and a proposal distinct from a confirmed agreement.
examples: Unclear subject: Request. Improved subject: Request to use classroom on Friday, 3–4 p.m. The improved version lets the recipient identify the action quickly.

Accusatory claim: You cheated me. Evidence-based claim: The notebook has several missing pages. I bought it yesterday and would like a replacement; the receipt number is 18. The second states the problem and requested remedy.

Negotiation: Could you sell three notebooks for TSh 4200? Seller: I can offer three for TSh 4500. Buyer: Thank you; I accept that price. The final acceptance, not the first proposal, establishes agreement here.
lessons.summary: A formal request states who is writing, what is needed and why the request is reasonable.

lessons.title: Number skills: prerequisite revision
objectives: Review compatible prerequisite skills.
Use the original source question and independent solution carefully.
paragraphs: Legacy Form Two papers can revisit number skills now introduced earlier in the curriculum. This supplemental revision chapter supports arithmetic, approximation, ratio and percentages. It does not add a new official Form Two syllabus requirement or claim complete curriculum coverage.

Evaluate brackets first, then powers, multiplication and division at the same precedence from left to right, then addition and subtraction from left to right. The word of in a fraction expression means multiplication. Keep the sign of a bracketed result: multiplying a positive fraction by a negative number gives a negative result.

For rounding to thousands, compare the remainder after complete thousands with 500. For a percentage loss, use loss divided by the original cost price, then multiply by 100%. In a ratio division, add the ratio terms to find the total number of equal shares before multiplying by the required term.
examples: A total of 78,650 rounded to the nearest thousand is 79,000 because the final 650 is at least 500.
Divide 24 kg in ratio 1:2:3: total terms 6, one share 4 kg; the largest share is 12 kg.
lessons.summary: Legacy Form Two papers can revisit number skills now introduced earlier in the curriculum. This supplemental revision chapter supports arithmetic, approximation, ratio and percentages. It does not add a new official Form Two syllabus requirement or claim complete curriculum coverage.

lessons.title: Angles and algebra: prerequisite revision
objectives: Review compatible prerequisite skills.
Use the original source question and independent solution carefully.
paragraphs: This supplemental chapter revisits parallel-line angle reasoning and elementary algebra used in legacy examination questions. Use the original diagram when identifying an angle: labels and marked right angles are part of the mathematical information, not decoration.

Vertically opposite angles are equal. Angles on a straight line sum to 180°. A transversal crossing parallel lines creates equal corresponding angles and equal alternate angles. Name the angle relationship before inserting a value; a visual estimate of a drawing is not a proof.

For a perimeter problem, add all side expressions, equate the sum to the stated perimeter and solve. For expressions, distribute a negative multiplier across every bracket term before collecting like terms. Check numerical solutions in the original conditions, including whether proposed side lengths can form a triangle.
examples: An angle adjacent on a straight line to 65° is 180°−65°=115°; its vertically opposite partner is also 115°.
If triangle sides are x+1, x+3 and 6 with perimeter 18, then 2x+10=18, x=4 and the sides are 5,7,6.
lessons.summary: This supplemental chapter revisits parallel-line angle reasoning and elementary algebra used in legacy examination questions. Use the original diagram when identifying an angle: labels and marked right angles are part of the mathematical information, not decoration.

lessons.title: Straight lines: prerequisite revision
objectives: Review compatible prerequisite skills.
Use the original source question and independent solution carefully.
paragraphs: Legacy assessment questions on coordinate geometry are provided as labelled prerequisite revision. A line y=mx+c has gradient m and vertical-axis intercept c. The intercept is the value of y when x=0; it is not necessarily the constant appearing in an unsimplified equation.

If an equation is ky=kx+x+d, first consider k=0 separately. When that case is incompatible with a stated finite gradient, divide by nonzero k to obtain y=((k+1)/k)x+d/k. Only then compare its coefficients with y=mx+c.

A line containing a stated point must satisfy its equation when the coordinates are substituted. Two points can provide two equations in unknown coefficients. Solve simultaneously, then verify both original point conditions. Keep negative coordinates and signs intact when substituting.
examples: For 2y=6x+8, divide by 2: y=3x+4. The gradient is 3 and y-intercept is 4.
If y=mx+2 passes through (3,8), then 8=3m+2 and m=2.
The line y=2x−1 contains (0,−1) and (2,3), because both substitutions satisfy the equation.
lessons.summary: Legacy assessment questions on coordinate geometry are provided as labelled prerequisite revision. A line y=mx+c has gradient m and vertical-axis intercept c. The intercept is the value of y when x=0; it is not necessarily the constant appearing in an unsimplified equation.

lessons.title: Laboratory skills and scientific investigation
objectives: Choose apparatus and read measurements appropriately.
Plan a controlled investigation.
Follow laboratory and emergency boundaries.
paragraphs: Chemistry investigates substances, their properties and the changes they undergo. It connects with farming through fertilisers and soils, health through medicines and diagnostics, industry through materials and fuels, and environmental work through water and pollution analysis. A benefit must be considered alongside safe handling and waste disposal; producing a useful substance does not make every use harmless.

A laboratory is a controlled workplace, not a place to taste or casually mix substances. Read instructions before starting, wear the required eye protection and clothing, tie back long hair and keep exits clear. Report broken apparatus, spills and injuries promptly. Never pipette by mouth. Heating, concentrated chemicals, unfamiliar reactions and fire response require a teacher or competent supervisor. In an emergency, alert the responsible adult and follow the school emergency procedure instead of improvising a chemical treatment.

Choose apparatus to match the task. A beaker holds and mixes liquids but is not usually the best instrument for an accurate volume. A measuring cylinder measures liquid volume more closely; a balance measures mass. A funnel supports transfer or filtration, a test tube holds small samples and a thermometer measures temperature. Inspect apparatus for damage and read scales at an appropriate eye level. Where a clear liquid forms a curved surface, the bottom of the meniscus is commonly read at eye level; the instrument and liquid determine the correct convention.

An investigation begins with a clear question and a testable prediction. Change the independent variable, observe or measure the dependent variable, and keep relevant controlled variables similar. Repeat observations to identify variation, record units and distinguish observations from conclusions. A fair test of dissolving rate could vary water temperature while keeping water volume, solute mass, particle size and stirring conditions comparable. A result supports a conclusion only within the tested conditions.
examples: Question: Does temperature affect dissolving time? Independent variable: temperature. Dependent variable: time to dissolve. Controls include water volume and solute amount. Do not change temperature and stirring at the same time.
A beaker suggests about 50 mL while a suitable measuring cylinder allows a finer reading. Choose the cylinder for a volume measurement and a balance if the task asks for mass.
Observation: a solid remains on the filter. Conclusion: an insoluble component was retained. The observation alone does not identify the substance or prove the filtrate is safe to drink.
lessons.summary: Chemistry investigates substances, their properties and the changes they undergo.

lessons.title: Measurements, graphs and experimental evidence
objectives: Select suitable measurement tools.
Calculate and interpret means and ranges.
Present evidence in labelled tables and graphs.
paragraphs: A useful measurement states a quantity, a numerical value and a unit. Select an instrument with a suitable range and resolution: a metre rule for ordinary length, a stopwatch for time, a balance for mass and a measuring cylinder for liquid volume. The smallest scale division influences how finely the result can be read. More decimal digits do not automatically mean a more accurate measurement.

Check zero readings and view scales carefully. A zero error shifts readings even when nothing should register. Parallax results from viewing a scale from the wrong angle. Repeated readings can reveal random variation, but repeating a biased method does not remove systematic error. Record what was actually observed, including an unexpected value; investigate a suspected mistake rather than quietly replacing it.

Organise data in a table with a clear heading and units for each column. The mean is the sum of values divided by their number; the range is maximum minus minimum. Values should be combined only when they describe comparable quantities and conditions. A missing reading is not zero. A large difference between repeats is a reason to examine technique, timing or conditions.

Graphs show relationships. Put the independent variable on the horizontal axis and the dependent variable on the vertical axis unless the task specifies otherwise. Choose convenient scales, label units and plot points accurately. A best-fit line or curve represents the overall pattern rather than forcing every point into a zigzag. The gradient is vertical change divided by horizontal change, with units inherited from both axes. State the limits of what the graph supports; extrapolating far beyond observations can be unreliable.
examples: Time readings 12.1 s, 11.9 s and 12.0 s have mean 36.0/3=12.0 s and range 0.2 s. Retain the unit in both results.
A distance–time line passes through (2 s,6 m) and (6 s,18 m). Gradient=(18−6)/(6−2)=3 m/s, representing speed for that straight section.
A balance reads 2 g when empty. This suggests a zero error; simply averaging many similarly shifted readings will not remove that bias.
lessons.summary: A useful measurement states a quantity, a numerical value and a unit.

lessons.title: Classification, organisms and microscopes
objectives: Use scientific names correctly.
Compare major school-level organism groups.
Calculate magnification and follow observation conventions.
paragraphs: Biology studies living organisms and their processes. Classification groups organisms using selected characteristics so that similarities, differences and relationships can be studied and information communicated. An artificial system may use a few convenient visible traits; a natural system aims to reflect a broader set of relationships. One superficial similarity does not prove close relationship: a bird and an insect both fly but differ in many major features.

Scientific names reduce confusion between local names. In binomial naming, the first word is the genus and begins with a capital letter; the second is the specific epithet and begins with a lower-case letter. Both are written in italics in print or separately underlined when handwritten. Homo sapiens is an example. A species name is the two-word combination, not the second word alone.

The school classification framework in this syllabus includes Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia, with viruses considered separately. Monera includes organisms such as bacteria that lack a membrane-bound nucleus. Protists are diverse; fungi absorb nutrients and do not photosynthesise like green plants. Most familiar plants make food by photosynthesis, while animals ingest organic food. Viruses are not cellular organisms and reproduce only within host cells. Modern classification systems may organise these groups differently, so identify the framework being used.

A microscope makes small structures visible, but good use requires preparation. Begin with low power, place and secure the slide, illuminate appropriately and focus without striking the slide with the objective. Total magnification is eyepiece magnification multiplied by objective magnification. Keep observations separate from assumptions about identity. Draw clear labelled structures actually seen; do not add organelles simply because a textbook diagram includes them. Slides and biological material should be prepared and handled under the required school guidance.
examples: For a 10× eyepiece and 4× objective, total magnification=10×4=40×. Changing to a 10× objective gives 100×.
A wing is not enough to classify an animal as a bird: insects also have wings. Consider body organisation and other features before deciding.
Write Homo sapiens, not homo Sapiens. The genus starts with a capital; the specific epithet starts lower case, and the full name is treated as a two-word unit.
lessons.summary: Biology studies living organisms and their processes.

lessons.title: Simultaneous equations and straight lines
objectives: Solve and check simultaneous equations.
Calculate gradients and line equations.
Interpret graphical solutions and inequalities.
paragraphs: Two simultaneous equations describe conditions that must hold for the same unknowns. A solution pair must satisfy both equations, not just one. Substitution replaces a variable with an equivalent expression from the other equation. Elimination adds or subtracts suitable multiples so one variable cancels. Keep equality by applying the same operation to both sides.

For x+y=11 and x−y=3, adding gives 2x=14, so x=7 and y=4. Check 7+4=11 and 7−4=3. If equations are proportional, they may describe the same line and have infinitely many solution pairs; if they are inconsistent, there is no common solution. Not every pair of linear equations has exactly one solution.

Coordinates (x,y) locate a point using horizontal and vertical positions relative to chosen axes. For a line through distinct points, gradient m=(y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁), provided x₂≠x₁. In y=mx+c, m is gradient and c the vertical-axis intercept. A vertical line has undefined finite gradient in this formula and is written x=a, not y=mx+c with an ordinary numerical m.

To draw a line, choose convenient x values, calculate the corresponding y values and plot at least two points accurately. Their intersection can show a simultaneous solution. The accuracy depends on scale and plotting; use algebra to obtain an exact result when possible. For inequalities, remember to reverse the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number. A solution interval contains many values, not just one number at its boundary.
examples: Solve x+y=9 and x−y=1. Add: 2x=10, x=5; substitute to get y=4. Both equations are satisfied.
For points (1,4) and (3,10), gradient=(10−4)/(3−1)=3. Using y=3x+c and (1,4), c=1, so the line is y=3x+1.
Solve −2x+3>11. Subtract 3: −2x>8; divide by −2 and reverse the inequality: x<−4. For example x=−5 gives 13>11.
lessons.summary: Two simultaneous equations describe conditions that must hold for the same unknowns.

lessons.title: Kusoma kwa uelewa, msamiati na kamusi
objectives: Soma matini na toa majibu yenye ushahidi.
Chagua maana sahihi kwa msaada wa kamusi.
Andika muhtasari na shiriki mazungumzo kwa heshima.
paragraphs: Usomaji wenye uelewa unahusisha kutambua ujumbe mkuu, taarifa saidizi na uhusiano wa mawazo. Kabla ya kusoma, angalia kichwa na kusudi la kazi. Unaposoma, zingatia alama za uandishi na muktadha wa maneno. Kusoma kwa sauti kunahitaji kasi inayoeleweka na kiimbo kinachoendana na tungo, lakini kuigiza sauti bila kuelewa maana hakutoshi.

Soma matini hii asilia: Mwanaidi alikopa kamusi maktabani ili kuandaa maonesho ya darasa. Alipokutana na neno lisilojulikana, hakuchukua maana ya kwanza tu. Alisoma maana tofauti na kuangalia sentensi aliyokuwa akiandika. Baadaye alimwonyesha Baraka rasimu yake. Baraka alipendekeza afafanue maneno mawili ambayo yangeweza kuwachanganya wasikilizaji. Walipomaliza, walirudisha kamusi kwa wakati na kuweka nakala ya maelezo yao kwenye ubao wa darasa.

Kamusi hupanga vidahizo kwa utaratibu maalumu, mara nyingi wa alfabeti. Kidadisi cha neno kinaweza kuonyesha tahajia, aina ya neno, maana zaidi ya moja, mfano wa matumizi na taarifa nyingine. Taarifa hutofautiana kwa aina ya kamusi. Chagua maana inayolingana na muktadha; si kila maana inafaa kila sentensi. Katika mawasiliano ya kidijitali, tumia kamusi au chanzo kinachotambulika badala ya kuamini tafsiri ya kwanza bila kukagua.

Muhtasari wa matini huchagua hoja kuu na kuziunganisha kwa lugha yako bila kuongeza tukio jipya. Katika mazungumzo, sikiliza hadi uelewe hoja kabla ya kujibu, toa nafasi kwa wengine na uliza ufafanuzi kwa heshima. Kumbukumbu fupi zinaweza kusaidia kufuatilia mawazo, lakini zisigeuze maoni ya mtu kuwa ukweli uliothibitishwa. Mazoezi haya yanaweza kufanywa kwa kusoma matini; mazoezi halisi ya kusikiliza yanahitaji sauti au msomaji.
examples: Kwa nini Mwanaidi hakuchukua maana ya kwanza tu? Kwa sababu alitaka maana inayolingana na sentensi na kusudi lake. Jibu linatokana na matini.
Mpangilio wa alfabeti: amani, bahari, darasa, elimu. Linganisha herufi ya kwanza; ikiwa inafanana, endelea kwenye herufi zinazofuata.
Muhtasari: Mwanaidi alitumia kamusi kwa kuzingatia muktadha, akaboresha rasimu kwa msaada wa Baraka na kurudisha kitabu kwa wakati. Hakuna taarifa kwamba alinunua kamusi.
lessons.summary: Usomaji wenye uelewa unahusisha kutambua ujumbe mkuu, taarifa saidizi na uhusiano wa mawazo.

lessons.title: Geography, landforms, water bodies and vegetation
objectives: Distinguish physical and human geography.
Identify major land and water features.
Explain vegetation and people–environment relationships.
paragraphs: Geography studies places, environments and relationships between people and the Earth. Physical geography examines features and processes such as landforms, water and climate; human geography considers activities such as settlement, farming, transport and trade. These branches overlap: a river affects settlement and transport, while land use can affect the river’s water quality. Maps, field observations and photographs help investigate such relationships.

The commonly used seven-continent model names Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Europe, North America, South America and Australia. Different naming conventions may refer to the wider region of Oceania, so state the model being used. The five commonly recognised oceans are the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern and Arctic. Tanzania lies on the eastern side of Africa with a coast on the Indian Ocean. A continent is a large landmass; an ocean is a major body of salt water.

Relief describes variations in the height and shape of the land. A mountain rises prominently above nearby land; a plateau is an elevated area with a relatively broad level surface; a plain has relatively low relief; a valley is an elongated depression. Definitions describe patterns rather than a guarantee that every surface fits one perfect shape. In Tanzania, Mount Kilimanjaro is a prominent mountain and the surrounding lower land has different relief characteristics.

Inland water bodies include lakes, rivers, wetlands and reservoirs. Lake Victoria, Lake Tanganyika and Lake Nyasa/Malawi are major East African lakes shared across national borders. Rivers flow through drainage basins and can connect upstream activities with downstream effects. Vegetation zones reflect interacting influences including rainfall, temperature, soils, altitude, fire and human activity. Forest, woodland, grassland/savanna and sparse dryland vegetation are broad categories; boundaries vary rather than forming identical bands everywhere.

A geographical explanation links a feature to its significance with evidence. Plains may make some transport routes easier, but floods or soft soils can still create difficulties. Mountains can influence rainfall, water sources and tourism, but also bring steep-slope hazards. Treat a benefit or challenge as dependent on place and conditions. During observation, record location, visible features and human activities without entering unsafe water, unstable slopes or restricted land.
examples: A coastal settlement may depend on fishing and transport links. Explaining it well combines a physical setting, human activities and evidence rather than calling it only physical or only human geography.
Classify three features: Mount Kilimanjaro is a mountain, Lake Tanganyika an inland lake and the Indian Ocean a major ocean. They are not interchangeable kinds of water/land feature.

If bare soil appears after vegetation is removed, investigate runoff, slope and rainfall before predicting erosion. The vegetation change is one part of a connected system, not a complete explanation alone.
lessons.summary: Geography studies places, environments and relationships between people and the Earth.

lessons.title: Planning and starting a sole-trader enterprise
objectives: Separate start-up resources from operating needs.
Calculate practical small-business costs.
Use a trial and records to improve decisions.
paragraphs: A business plan explains a proposed enterprise: the customer need, product or service, resources, operations, expected costs and revenue, and risks. Planning does not guarantee success, but it makes assumptions visible so they can be tested. An entrepreneur should distinguish an attractive idea from evidence that enough customers will buy at a workable price.

Calculate start-up needs separately from running costs. A sewing machine bought to begin tailoring is a start-up asset; thread, rent and transport may recur. Working capital supports day-to-day operations while money is tied up in stock or unpaid sales. If all available cash is spent on equipment, a business may be unable to buy the materials needed to use it.

A sole trader can make decisions directly, but personal capacity and resources limit the operation. Check access to skills, time, suppliers, storage and customers. Keep business transactions recorded even when the owner supplies the money. Money taken for personal use is not evidence of a business expense, and cash put in by the owner is not sales revenue.

A small trial helps test demand and practical problems. Specify what will count as evidence, such as the number of paid orders, full cost per item and customer feedback. Review quality, waste and complaints as well as sales totals. Before operating, check the requirements that apply to the location and activity with the responsible authorities; a school exercise is not a licence or a financial promise.
examples: Equipment costs TSh 40,000 and opening materials TSh 15,000. At least TSh 55,000 is needed for those items, before other costs and cash reserves. Counting equipment alone understates the plan.

A trader buys ten items at TSh 700 each and spends TSh 1000 on transport. Total batch cost=8000, so relevant unit cost before other expenses is 800. At a selling price of 1000, 200 per sold item remains before other costs.

A trial sells six of ten products. Record six sales and four remaining items; do not record ten sales merely because ten were produced. Unsold stock and customer comments both inform the next decision.
lessons.summary: A business plan explains a proposed enterprise: the customer need, product or service, resources, operations, expected costs and revenue, and risks.

lessons.title: Urithi, maadili na ushirikiano wa jamii
objectives: Tambua aina na thamani za urithi.
Husisha maadili na utunzaji unaoheshimu watu.
Chunguza fursa na ushirikiano kwa uwajibikaji.
paragraphs: Urithi wa jamii unajumuisha vitu vinavyoonekana kama majengo, maeneo na zana, na mambo yasiyoshikika kama lugha, simulizi, sanaa na maarifa. Urithi hutusaidia kuchunguza maisha ya vizazi vilivyotangulia na kuelewa utambulisho wa sasa. Hata hivyo, maelezo ya urithi yanahitaji ushahidi; simulizi moja au jina la kitu halithibitishi kila dai linalotolewa kuhusu asili yake.

Maadili yanahusiana na namna watu wanavyotathmini matendo na wajibu wao kwa wengine. Uaminifu, uwajibikaji, heshima na ushirikiano vinaweza kusaidia kujenga maisha ya pamoja. Mila zinapotathminiwa, zingatia heshima ya binadamu na haki badala ya kudai kwamba kila desturi ya zamani ilikuwa nzuri au kwamba kila jambo jipya ni bora. Jamii zinaweza kuhifadhi maarifa yenye thamani huku zikirekebisha matendo yenye madhara.

Utunzaji wa urithi unahitaji ushirikiano wa jamii, wataalamu na mamlaka husika. Usichimbe, kuondoa, kuandika juu au kuuza vitu vya kihistoria bila kufuata taratibu zinazotumika. Kupiga picha au kurekodi maarifa ya mtu kunahitaji kuzingatia ridhaa, faragha na masharti yake. Kuhamisha kitu bila rekodi kunaweza kupoteza muktadha unaosaidia kuelewa matumizi na kipindi chake.

Urithi unaweza kusaidia uchumi kupitia ufundi, maonesho, utalii unaowajibika na elimu. Fursa itathminiwe pamoja na manufaa kwa wenye urithi na gharama za kuutunza. Biashara isiwasilishe vitu vipya kama vya kale kwa udanganyifu au kutoa maarifa ya jamii bila heshima. Shughuli za pamoja kama usafi wa mazingira, kujenga huduma na kubadilishana stadi zinaweza kukuza mshikamano na uwezo wa kiuchumi zinapopangwa kwa uwazi na ushiriki wa haki.
examples: Kikundi cha wanafunzi kinaomba ruhusa ya kusaidia kusafisha eneo la urithi na kinafuata maelekezo ya msimamizi. Huu ni ushiriki unaolenga kuhifadhi, si ruhusa ya kuhamisha vitu vya kale.
Mfundi anatengeneza bidhaa mpya kwa kutumia mbinu za jadi. Anaweza kuieleza kama kazi mpya ya ufundi wa jadi, badala ya kudai kwa uongo kwamba ni kitu cha karne zilizopita.
Jamii inapoweka rekodi ya mapato na matumizi ya maonesho, wanachama wanaweza kujadili manufaa na gharama kwa ushahidi. Uwazi husaidia uwajibikaji.
lessons.summary: Urithi wa jamii unajumuisha vitu vinavyoonekana kama majengo, maeneo na zana, na mambo yasiyoshikika kama lugha, simulizi, sanaa na maarifa.

lessons.title: Finding information and writing friendly messages
objectives: Search with clear questions and relevant terms.
Evaluate source cards and vocabulary in context.
Write complete friendly messages and invitations.
paragraphs: Information search begins with a clear question. Choose keywords describing the topic and the kind of information needed rather than typing a very long vague sentence. A search engine helps locate sources; it is not itself proof that a result is correct. Look for the author or institution, date, purpose and evidence. In offline practice, compare prepared source cards and decide which would answer a stated question; no internet connection is needed for that exercise.

Consider two original source cards. Card A: School library notice, issued Monday, says the library will open at 8 a.m. during revision week. Card B: An undated message says someone heard that all school rooms are closed. For the question about library opening time, Card A is more directly relevant and attributable. It can still be checked with the school if circumstances change. A confident tone and a large number of forwarded messages do not replace a named, relevant source.

When learning vocabulary, record the word, its meaning in context and your own example. A word may have more than one meaning: light can refer to illumination or to low weight. A useful vocabulary game pairs words with suitable contexts rather than treating every dictionary meaning as interchangeable. Retelling a story requires a clear sequence; a summary keeps its main events and omits minor detail without inventing an ending.

A friendly letter normally includes the sender’s address where required, date, greeting, message and closing. Its tone should suit the relationship and purpose. A clear invitation states the activity, place, date and time and asks for a response where needed. Follow the stages of planning, drafting, revising and editing. A timetable records activities and times consistently so that it can be followed by someone who did not help write it.
examples: Question: When does the library open during revision week? Useful keywords might be school library revision week opening time. A current school notice is more relevant than an unrelated general article about libraries.
Context contrast: The bag is light means not heavy; the lamp gives light means illumination. Use the sentence to choose a meaning.

Invitation: Dear Asha, Please join our reading group in the library on Friday at 3 p.m. We will discuss a short story. Let me know whether you can come. Best wishes, Neema. The key practical details are present.
lessons.summary: Information search begins with a clear question.

lessons.title: Mathematical models and graphing software
objectives: Translate a practical rule into a linear model
Use a spreadsheet or graphing tool to compare two models
Check a graphical solution against algebra and context
paragraphs: A mathematical model selects quantities and states assumptions. For a delivery charge, let x be distance in kilometres and C be cost in shillings. A fixed starting charge plus a constant charge per kilometre gives C=ax+b. The intercept b describes the starting charge; a has units shillings per kilometre. State whether fractional distances are allowed and whether the rule applies beyond the advertised area.

A spreadsheet can generate a table from a model. Put x values in column A and, for C=600x+1500, enter =600*A2+1500 in B2 if the first distance is in A2. Copy the formula down so each row refers to its own distance. Use an XY scatter chart because both coordinates are numerical. Label both axes with units; a category chart can conceal unequal distance intervals.

To compare two charges, calculate both costs for the same x values. An intersection represents equal costs. A display window can hide an intersection or make nearby lines appear identical. Zoom sensibly, inspect numerical coordinates and substitute the proposed point into both original rules. Software gives evidence; an algebraic equality gives an exact solution for linear rules.

A model is useful only within its assumptions. A negative distance solution has no meaning for a delivery journey. A bus count must be a whole number even if a graph allows fractions. Rounding can alter a comparison near an intersection, so retain exact values until the final decision. Record the formulas, units and allowed range so someone else can reproduce the investigation.
examples: A bicycle courier charges C=400x+1200. At x=3.5 km, C=400×3.5+1200=2600 shillings. The rate is 400 shillings/km and the fixed charge is 1200 shillings.

Compare A=300x+1800 with B=500x+1000. Equal costs give 300x+1800=500x+1000, hence 800=200x and x=4 km. Both cost 3000 shillings. At 2 km A costs 2400 and B 2000, so B is cheaper below 4 km within the model.
A spreadsheet uses distances 0, 2, 5 km. For y=2x+1 the outputs are 1, 5, 11. An XY scatter chart plots (0,1), (2,5), (5,11) with unequal horizontal gaps; the gradient is (11−1)/(5−0)=2.
lessons.summary: A mathematical model selects quantities and states assumptions.

lessons.title: Rates, direct and inverse variation
objectives: Distinguish a rate from a ratio
Find constants of direct and inverse variation
Test a model before using it for prediction
paragraphs: A rate compares quantities with different units, such as litres per minute or shillings per kilogram. Divide the amount by the corresponding number of units. Conversion must preserve the same physical quantity: 72 km/h is 72000 m in 3600 s, or 20 m/s. A unit rate makes fair comparisons possible when packages or journey times differ.

Direct variation means y=kx for a constant k. The ratio y/x is constant for nonzero x, and its graph is a straight line through the origin. Doubling x doubles y. A straight line with a nonzero intercept is a linear relationship but is not direct variation; a fixed service fee is one reason a cost does not vary directly with usage.

Inverse variation means y=k/x, so xy=k for nonzero x. Doubling x halves y. For a fixed job, the time may vary inversely with the number of equally productive workers, provided they can work independently without delays. Real teams may not satisfy these assumptions. The graph is a curve, and x=0 is excluded.

Variation can also involve powers or two inputs: y=kx² or y=kx/z. Determine k using one complete set of data, then retain it when substituting new inputs. Check units and whether a prediction is sensible. Two isolated measurements that look proportional do not prove a universal physical law; further measurements should test the proposed model.
examples: A tap fills 42 L in 3 minutes at a steady rate. Rate=42/3=14 L/min. In 8 minutes it fills 14×8=112 L, assuming the flow remains steady.
If y varies directly as x and y=35 when x=5, k=35/5=7. Thus y=7x; when x=12, y=84. The ratio stays 7.
Six equally productive workers finish a fixed task in 10 days. Under an inverse model nt=60 worker-days. With 15 workers, t=60/15=4 days; the prediction assumes no interference or change in hours.
lessons.summary: A rate compares quantities with different units, such as litres per minute or shillings per kilogram.

lessons.title: Similarity and scale factors
objectives: Match corresponding sides and angles
Use length, area and volume scale factors
Measure inaccessible lengths with explicit assumptions
paragraphs: Similar shapes have the same shape: corresponding angles are equal and corresponding lengths are in a constant ratio. Name corresponding vertices in the same order. If triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF, AB corresponds to DE, BC to EF, and AC to DF. A scale factor from the first shape to the second is a second-shape length divided by its corresponding first-shape length.

Triangles can be shown similar by two equal corresponding angles (AA), three proportional corresponding sides (SSS similarity), or two proportional sides with equal included angle (SAS similarity). A visual resemblance is not proof. Parallel lines often create equal corresponding or alternate angles, allowing a similarity argument before any length calculation.

If lengths scale by k, areas scale by k² and volumes of similar solids scale by k³. These are different multipliers. A drawing twice as wide and twice as high covers four times the area. Units remain essential: a map scale 1:25000 compares lengths in the same units, so 1 cm represents 25000 cm, or 250 m.

Shadow measurements can estimate height using similar right triangles when objects stand vertically on level ground and sunlight reaches both at the same angle at the same time. Divide height by shadow length for the reference object and apply the same ratio. Uneven ground, leaning objects and measurements taken at different times weaken the model. Never enter roads or climb structures to measure them.
examples: Triangle sides 3,4,5 cm correspond to 9,12,15 cm. Each ratio is 3, so the triangles are similar with scale factor 3. Their area ratio is 3²=9.
A 1.5 m vertical pole casts a 2 m shadow while a tree casts an 8 m shadow on level ground. h/8=1.5/2, so h=6 m under the shared-angle assumption.
On a 1:40000 map a path measures 3.2 cm. Actual length=3.2×40000=128000 cm=1280 m=1.28 km.
lessons.summary: Similar shapes have the same shape: corresponding angles are equal and corresponding lengths are in a constant ratio.

lessons.title: Congruent triangles and proof
objectives: Select valid congruence tests
Write a correspondence-based proof
Distinguish congruence evidence from similarity evidence
paragraphs: Congruent figures have the same shape and size. A rotation, reflection or translation can move one onto the other without stretching. In triangles, proving congruence allows us to conclude that all corresponding sides and angles are equal. A correct vertex correspondence is necessary before making these conclusions.

The SSS test uses equality of all three corresponding sides. SAS uses equality of two sides and the angle included between them. ASA uses two corresponding angles and the side between them; two angles also determine the third angle, so an appropriate AAS argument works as well. For right triangles, RHS uses a right angle, equal hypotenuses and one equal corresponding leg.

AAA shows shape but does not determine size: triangles with sides 3,4,5 and 6,8,10 have equal angles but are not congruent. Two sides and a non-included angle (SSA) do not provide a general congruence rule, because different triangles can satisfy such information. Identify where an angle lies instead of choosing a test from a count of marks alone.

A proof separates facts, reasons and conclusions. Given equal lengths may be combined with a common side, vertically opposite angles or angles established by parallel lines. State a test, list the triangle correspondence, then use corresponding parts. A diagram supports reasoning but cannot certify a length or angle merely because it looks equal.
examples: Triangles ABC and DEF satisfy AB=DE=5 cm, BC=EF=7 cm and AC=DF=8 cm. All corresponding sides match, so ABC≅DEF by SSS. Therefore angle A=angle D.

In isosceles triangle ABC, AB=AC. Let D be the midpoint of BC. Compare ABD and ACD: AB=AC, BD=DC and AD is common. They are congruent by SSS, so angle BAD=angle DAC and angle ADB=angle ADC. The latter sum to 180°, so each is 90°.
Right triangles PQR and XYZ have right angles at Q and Y, hypotenuses PR=XZ=13 cm, and legs PQ=XY=5 cm. RHS proves PQR≅XYZ. The remaining legs are each √(169−25)=12 cm.
lessons.summary: Congruent figures have the same shape and size.

lessons.title: Binary operations and algebraic structure
objectives: Evaluate an explicitly defined operation
Test closure, commutativity and associativity
Find an identity and an inverse when they exist
paragraphs: A binary operation combines two elements of a stated set to produce one result. The symbol is a label whose meaning must be defined: if a★b=2a+b, then 3★4=10. It is not ordinary multiplication. Substitute the first input for a and the second for b, keeping their positions and using brackets when an input is negative or is itself an expression.

Closure means the result stays in the stated set for every allowed pair. Subtraction is closed on integers but not on nonnegative integers, because 2−5=−3. Division on real numbers cannot accept a zero second input. Always state the domain before declaring that a rule is an operation on a set; the same formula may work on one set and fail on another.

An operation is commutative if a★b=b★a for every allowed pair. It is associative if (a★b)★c=a★(b★c) for every allowed triple. A counterexample disproves a universal claim, but one matching numerical example does not prove it. Compare general expressions where possible. Associativity controls regrouping; commutativity controls order.

An identity e satisfies a★e=e★a=a for all a. An inverse of a, relative to identity e, is an element b with a★b=b★a=e. Solve these conditions using the defined rule and then check membership of the result in the set. A rule may have no two-sided identity, and without a specified identity the usual inverse question is not meaningful.
examples: For a★b=2a+b, 4★(−3)=2×4−3=5. But (−3)★4=−6+4=−2, so this operation on real numbers is not commutative.
Define a∘b=a+b+2 on integers. Then (a∘b)∘c=a+b+c+4=a∘(b∘c), so it is associative. An identity satisfies a+e+2=a, giving e=−2, which also works on the left.
For a∘b=a+b+2 with identity −2, the inverse of 5 solves 5+b+2=−2, giving b=−9. Check 5∘(−9)=−2 and (−9)∘5=−2.
lessons.summary: A binary operation combines two elements of a stated set to produce one result.

lessons.title: Logarithms as inverse powers
objectives: Convert between exponential and logarithmic statements
Apply logarithm laws with valid domains
Solve and check elementary logarithmic equations
paragraphs: For base b>0 and b≠1, log_b(x)=y means b^y=x, with x>0. A logarithm asks for an exponent. Since 10³=1000, log₁₀(1000)=3. The common logarithm uses base 10. A real logarithm of zero or a negative number is undefined; negative logarithm values are allowed when the positive argument is between zero and one and the base exceeds one.

For positive M and N, log_b(MN)=log_b M+log_b N and log_b(M/N)=log_b M−log_b N. These laws come from adding and subtracting exponents. They do not turn a sum inside a logarithm into a sum of logarithms: log_b(M+N) generally has no such split. Keep the base fixed throughout a law application.

The power law is log_b(M^r)=r log_b M for positive M and real r. In particular log_b 1=0 and log_b b=1. When using a calculator, enter brackets around the full argument and round only at the end. If a calculator only has common logarithms, log_b x=log₁₀ x/log₁₀ b, with b valid and x positive.

Solve logarithmic equations by respecting domains first, applying laws or converting to exponential form, and checking the original expressions at the end. Algebra may produce a value that makes an original argument nonpositive. Such a value must be rejected even if it satisfies an equation obtained after transformation.
examples: log₂ 32 asks for y with 2^y=32. Since 2⁵=32, y=5. Similarly log₁₀ 0.01=−2 because 10^(−2)=0.01.
Evaluate log₃ 27+log₃ 9−log₃ 3. The values are 3+2−1=4. Equivalently combine the arguments: log₃(27×9/3)=log₃ 81=4.
Solve log₁₀(x−1)+log₁₀(x+1)=log₁₀ 8. Domain x>1. Combine to obtain (x−1)(x+1)=8, so x²=9 and x=±3. Only x=3 is valid; its arguments are 2 and 4 with product 8.
lessons.summary: For base b>0 and b≠1, log_b(x)=y means b^y=x, with x>0.

lessons.title: Radicals and rational denominators
objectives: Simplify radicals using square factors
Combine and multiply radical expressions
Rationalise simple and binomial denominators
paragraphs: The principal square root √a is the nonnegative number whose square is a, for a≥0. Thus √25=5, while solving x²=25 gives x=5 or x=−5. For real x, √(x²)=|x|. These statements prevent a common sign error when variables might be negative.

For nonnegative a and b, √(ab)=√a√b. Factor out a perfect square to simplify a radical: √72=√(36×2)=6√2. Only like radicals combine by addition or subtraction, just as like algebraic terms combine. The rule √(a+b)=√a+√b is generally false; test a=b=1 to see √2 differs from 2.

Multiply radicals using distribution and simplify each resulting term. A conjugate pair has the form p+q and p−q; their product p²−q² removes the middle terms. In particular, (√a+√b)(√a−√b)=a−b when both square roots are real. Check that a proposed denominator is nonzero before manipulating a fraction.

Rationalising a denominator rewrites an equivalent fraction with no radical in that denominator. Multiply numerator and denominator by the same nonzero expression. For 1/√a with a>0, multiply by √a/√a. For a denominator √a+√b, its conjugate may remove the radicals. The numerical value does not change, and a negative denominator can be tidied by multiplying both parts by −1.
examples: Simplify √108. Factor 108=36×3, so √108=6√3. Then √108+2√3=8√3 because both terms have the same radical part.
Expand (√5+2)(√5−1). Distribution gives 5−√5+2√5−2=3+√5. Squaring a sum would also require the middle term.
Rationalise 3/(√7−2). Multiply by (√7+2)/(√7+2). The denominator becomes 7−4=3, so the result is 3(√7+2)/3=√7+2. The original denominator is nonzero.
lessons.summary: The principal square root √a is the nonnegative number whose square is a, for a≥0.

lessons.title: Floating, sinking and displaced water
objectives: Relate upthrust to displaced liquid
Predict floating using average density
Test and improve a safe floating prototype
paragraphs: A liquid exerts pressure on every submerged surface. Pressure increases with depth, so the upward force on the lower parts of an object exceeds the downward force on its upper parts. The resultant upward fluid force is upthrust. Archimedes' principle states that the upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced by the object: U=ρgV, where V is the submerged volume, not necessarily the whole object volume.

A freely floating object at rest has balanced vertical forces: upthrust equals its total weight. A fully submerged object released from rest sinks if its weight exceeds the upthrust, rises if upthrust exceeds weight, and can remain neutrally buoyant if they balance. Comparing average object density with fluid density gives the same prediction when trapped air and all parts are included in the average.

A solid steel block sinks in water, but a hollow steel boat can float because the mass of steel and enclosed air is spread over a larger external volume. A floating boat displaces its own weight of water. Adding cargo makes it settle deeper until it displaces more water; if water enters and displaces the enclosed air, its average density increases and it may sink. Stability also matters, so a floating design is not automatically safe for carrying people.

Test a small foil boat in a shallow tray on a stable table. Use counters or washers as cargo, add them slowly near the centre, record total supported mass and compare different hull shapes made from equal foil areas. Keep electrical equipment away and dry spilled water. These are tabletop models; never use a student prototype to support a person or enter deep water. Use g=10 N/kg and water density 1000 kg/m³ in this chapter unless stated otherwise.
examples: A submerged block displaces 0.002 m³ of water. U=1000×10×0.002=20 N. If its weight is 30 N, the initial resultant force is 30−20=10 N downward, so it sinks when released.
A 0.6 kg object floats. Its weight is 0.6×10=6 N, so U=6 N. Displaced volume V=6/(1000×10)=0.0006 m³=600 cm³.
A uniform block has density 750 kg/m³ and floats in water. From ρ_water g V_sub=ρ_block g V_total, V_sub/V_total=750/1000=0.75. Therefore 75% of its volume is submerged and 25% remains above water.
lessons.summary: A liquid exerts pressure on every submerged surface.

lessons.title: Mechanical properties and spring investigations
objectives: Distinguish elasticity, plasticity and stiffness
Use Hooke’s law within its limits
Calibrate a safe spring-based measuring prototype
paragraphs: Materials respond differently to forces. An elastic material returns to its original dimensions after unloading within its elastic range. Plastic deformation remains after unloading. Stiffness describes resistance to deformation: a stiffer spring extends less for the same force. Strength concerns resistance to failure, while brittleness concerns fracture with little plastic deformation; these are not synonyms for stiffness.

For a spring obeying Hooke's law, F=kx, where F is applied force in newtons, x is extension in metres and k is spring constant in N/m. Extension is loaded length minus original length, not the total spring length. The law applies only over the proportional range; increasing a load indefinitely can permanently stretch or break the spring.

A force-versus-extension graph is straight through the origin in the Hooke's-law range. Its gradient ΔF/Δx is k. If extension is plotted vertically instead, the gradient is 1/k, so read axis labels before interpreting a slope. Elastic energy stored in an ideal Hooke's-law spring is E=½Fx=½kx², equal to the triangular area under its force–extension graph during loading.

A simple force-meter prototype can use a teacher-approved spring, a paper scale and small known masses. Clamp it securely, place a tray below the masses and keep faces away from suspended loads. Add loads gradually, record extensions on loading and unloading, and stop at the approved maximum. Recheck the zero after removal of loads; a shifted zero may reveal permanent deformation and invalidate calibration. Use g=10 N/kg for numerical work here.
examples: An unloaded spring is 8 cm long and reaches 11 cm under 1.5 N. Extension=3 cm=0.03 m. Thus k=1.5/0.03=50 N/m; using 11 cm as extension would be wrong.
For k=80 N/m and load 2.4 N, x=F/k=2.4/80=0.03 m=3 cm. This prediction is valid only if the load is in the spring's proportional range.
A spring with k=200 N/m extends 0.04 m. Force=200×0.04=8 N. Stored energy=½×200×0.04²=0.16 J, the same as ½×8×0.04.
lessons.summary: Materials respond differently to forces.

lessons.title: Magnets, fields and a compass prototype
objectives: Describe poles and magnetic fields
Explain magnetisation and demagnetisation
Collect evidence using a safe compass prototype
paragraphs: A magnet has north-seeking and south-seeking poles. Like poles repel and unlike poles attract. Some materials, notably iron and many steels, can be magnetised; many other metals such as aluminium and copper are not strongly attracted by an ordinary school magnet. Attraction alone does not prove that an unknown object is already a magnet because unmagnetised iron is also attracted. Repulsion from a known pole is stronger evidence of an existing magnetic pole.

A magnetic field is a region where magnetic forces can act. A small compass indicates the local field direction through its north-seeking end. Outside a bar magnet, field lines are drawn from north to south; closer spacing represents a stronger field. Field lines do not cross because the field has one direction at each point. The lines are a model, not physical strings inside the space.

A domain model explains magnetisation by increased alignment of many small magnetic regions. Stroking a steel needle repeatedly in one direction with one pole can align it sufficiently for a compass demonstration; lift the magnet away on each return stroke. Soft iron magnetises and loses magnetism readily, while steel often retains it better. Heating or mechanical shock can disrupt alignment, but learners should not heat, strike or damage magnets in class. Storage with suitable keepers helps preserve some bar magnets.

A teacher can prepare a magnetised needle and secure it flat on a small cork disk floating in a shallow tray, with its sharp point covered. Away from magnets and steel furniture it turns approximately north–south in Earth's field. Compare its direction with a known compass before labelling the ends. Record repeated headings, disturbances and limitations; nearby magnetic materials can distort readings. Keep small magnets away from mouths, electronic devices and medical implants; use a commercial compass when a needle prototype is unsuitable.
examples: The north pole of a known magnet repels end A of a freely suspended unknown bar. Like poles repel, so A is a north pole and the opposite end is south. Attraction alone would not support that identification.

A compass is placed near the middle region outside a bar magnet, between its north and south ends. Its north-seeking end points along the local field from the magnet's north towards its south, not automatically towards geographic north.

A prototype compass points east on a desk but approximately north when moved away from a steel cabinet. Repeat at several clear locations. The changed heading suggests a local magnetic disturbance; it is not evidence that Earth's magnetic direction changed.
lessons.summary: A magnet has north-seeking and south-seeking poles.

lessons.title: Static charge, conductors and capacitors
objectives: Explain charge transfer and induction
Distinguish conductors, insulators and earthing
Interpret electroscope evidence and basic capacitor quantities
paragraphs: Static electricity concerns electric charge that accumulates rather than flowing steadily around a circuit. Atoms contain positive nuclei and negative electrons. In ordinary rubbing experiments electrons transfer between materials; protons do not move from object to object. An object gaining electrons becomes negatively charged and one losing electrons becomes positively charged. Rubbing separates charge rather than creating a net supply of it.

Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. A charged object can also attract a neutral object by polarisation: opposite charge is displaced slightly closer than like charge. In a conductor, some electrons move readily; an insulator restricts large-scale electron movement. Charging by contact transfers charge, while induction can redistribute charge without touching. Earthing connects an object to the Earth so electrons can move in the direction required by the electrical conditions.

An electroscope can show the presence of charge through separation of similarly charged leaves. An initially uncharged electroscope's divergence alone does not reveal whether the nearby charge is positive or negative. A known initial charge and controlled procedure are needed to compare signs. On an isolated conducting body at electrostatic equilibrium, excess charge lies on its outer surface; sharp regions can produce stronger nearby fields. A lightning protection system provides an engineered path to earth; its installation is professional work.

A capacitor stores separated charge on two conductors separated by an insulator. Its capacitance C=Q/V measures stored charge magnitude per potential difference; the SI unit is the farad (F), with Q in coulombs and V in volts. A capacitor has equal and opposite plate charges rather than a net charge Q on the whole ideal device. Study school-approved low-voltage components only: never open mains appliances or handle unknown charged capacitors. Static demonstrations should use dry plastic and paper, away from flammable vapours and electronic equipment.
examples: A plastic ruler gains electrons when rubbed. It becomes negatively charged; the other material loses the same number of electrons and becomes positive. The total charge of the isolated pair remains unchanged.

A charged balloon attracts a neutral wall. The wall's charges shift slightly, making the nearer region effectively opposite in sign. Attraction therefore does not prove the wall carried an opposite net charge before the balloon approached.
A capacitor stores charge magnitude Q=0.000024 C at V=12 V. C=Q/V=0.000002 F=2 μF. If the same ideal capacitor is used at 6 V, Q=CV=0.000012 C=12 μC.
lessons.summary: Static electricity concerns electric charge that accumulates rather than flowing steadily around a circuit.

lessons.title: Optical instruments and experimental design
objectives: Explain a pinhole camera, simple magnifier and periscope
Use magnification ratios with units
Analyse optical data and communicate a prototype test
paragraphs: An optical instrument controls light to make an image or redirect a view. In a pinhole camera, rays travel approximately straight from the top and bottom of an object through a small hole to opposite parts of a screen, producing a real inverted image. A smaller hole can sharpen the image but reduces brightness; making it extremely small introduces diffraction, so smaller is not always better. A dark enclosure reduces unwanted light.

A simple magnifier uses a converging lens with the object inside its focal length. The emerging rays diverge and the eye traces them back to an upright, magnified virtual image. A camera lens instead forms a real image on a sensor or screen when the object is beyond the focal length. A real image can be received on a screen; a virtual image cannot be projected directly there. Never view the Sun or intense light through any optical instrument.

A simple periscope uses two parallel plane mirrors, commonly placed at 45° to the tube direction. Two successive reflections redirect rays around an obstruction. The law of reflection applies at each mirror: angles are measured from the normal. Aligning and securing the mirrors matters more than decorating the housing. Teacher-provided unbroken mirrors or suitable mirror sheet should be used; learners should not cut glass.

For a pinhole camera viewing a perpendicular object, similar triangles give image height/object height=image distance/object distance, using positive magnitudes. Measure all lengths in compatible units. A spreadsheet can hold object distance, image distance and image height, calculate ratios, and display a labelled XY graph. Repeat measurements and report their spread; compare a prediction with observations rather than inventing perfect data. An oral report should state the question, method, evidence, conclusion and limitations. Safe bright classroom objects or an LED target may be used, never the Sun.
examples: A 30 cm high object is 150 cm from a pinhole and the screen is 10 cm behind it. Image height/30=10/150, so image height=2 cm. The image is inverted and real.
A camera image is 8 mm high for an object 400 mm high. Linear magnification magnitude=8/400=0.02. The small image does not imply poor focus; size and sharpness are different observations.

At fixed object distance 200 cm and object height 40 cm, screen distances 5,10,15 cm predict image heights 1,2,3 cm. A plot of image height against screen distance is a line through the origin with gradient 40/200=0.2, using the same length units for both axes.
lessons.diagramAlt: Schematic rays from an upright object cross at a pinhole to form a real inverted image on a screen; u and v label object and screen distances.
lessons.summary: An optical instrument controls light to make an image or redirect a view.

lessons.title: Recurring decimals with a non-repeating prefix
objectives: Separate a decimal prefix from its repeating block
Convert mixed recurring decimals into reduced fractions
Predict terminating and recurring expansions from reduced denominators
paragraphs: Write recurring decimals so the repeating block is unambiguous. In 0.1666… the initial digit 1 does not repeat and only 6 repeats; in 0.161616… the whole block 16 repeats. These are different numbers. In this chapter, brackets identify the block: 0.1(6) means 0.1666…, while 0.(16) means 0.161616…. The digits before the brackets form the non-repeating prefix.

To eliminate a prefix, first multiply by a power of ten that moves all its digits left of the decimal point. If x=0.1(6), then 10x=1.(6). Multiply again by ten because the block has one digit: 100x=16.(6). Subtracting these aligned equations cancels the infinite tails, giving 90x=15. The important condition is matching tails, rather than merely multiplying by the first convenient power of ten.

If there are p non-repeating digits after the point and r repeating digits, compare 10^(p+r)x with 10^p x. Their difference is an integer, and the coefficient of x is 10^(p+r)−10^p. For x=0.23(45), compare 10000x=2345.(45) with 100x=23.(45), so 9900x=2322. This method also handles integer parts, provided the entire number is multiplied consistently.

A reduced fraction has a terminating decimal precisely when its denominator contains only prime factors 2 and 5. Such a denominator can be multiplied into a power of ten. A denominator with another prime factor produces a recurring expansion. A denominator containing both factors 2 or 5 and other primes can produce a non-repeating prefix before the recurring block. Always reduce a fraction before examining its denominator; 3/6 simplifies to 1/2 and terminates.

Long division checks a conversion: each step multiplies the current remainder by ten. Repeating a remainder repeats all subsequent digits. A terminating approximation should not be confused with the exact recurring value; 0.167 is close to 1/6 but is not equal. Retain a fraction for exact calculation and round only when the task requests an approximation. The identity 0.(9)=1 follows from the same exact subtraction method and does not assert that a finite string of nines equals one.
examples: Let x=0.2(7). Then 10x=2.(7) and 100x=27.(7). Subtract to obtain 90x=25, so x=25/90=5/18. A quick check gives 5÷18=0.2777… .

Let x=0.04(12). Then 100x=4.(12) and 10000x=412.(12). Subtract: 9900x=408, hence x=408/9900=34/825. The two prefix digits include the initial zero, so multiplying by only ten would not correctly align the repeating part.
lessons.summary: Write recurring decimals so the repeating block is unambiguous.

lessons.title: Standard-form calculations and reported precision
objectives: Calculate with normalised powers of ten
Align exponents before adding or subtracting
Report significant figures without inventing precision
paragraphs: For a positive number in standard form A×10^n, the coefficient satisfies 1≤A<10 and n is an integer. A negative value is written with a separate minus sign, for example −3.2×10⁴. Standard form preserves place value while making scale visible. The expressions 0.72×10⁵ and 72×10³ represent the same quantity, but neither is normalised; both become 7.2×10⁴.

For multiplication, multiply coefficients and add exponents. For division, divide coefficients and subtract the denominator exponent, using brackets around a negative exponent. Renormalise the coefficient afterwards. A result 24×10⁷ becomes 2.4×10⁸ because reducing the coefficient by a factor ten requires increasing the power by one. For a power of a standard-form expression, raise the coefficient and multiply the exponent by the outside power.

Addition and subtraction require matching powers of ten. Rewrite one or both quantities with a common exponent, combine the coefficients and then normalise the result. Exponents do not add during addition of numbers.
