This distinction is particularly important when subtracting nearly equal large quantities, where a small difference can be hidden by premature rounding.

Significant figures communicate which digits have been retained. Leading zeros locate a decimal point and do not count; zeros between significant digits count, and a final zero after a decimal point can indicate retained precision. Thus 4.50×10³ states three significant figures more clearly than the ambiguous integer 4500. A change from 9.96×10⁴ to two significant figures gives 1.0×10⁵: the zero in 1.0 is necessary to retain the stated two figures.

Keep extra digits during calculations and round the final result to the precision requested. For school measurement calculations, multiplication or division is commonly reported to the fewest significant figures among measured inputs, while addition or subtraction follows the least precise decimal place after units are aligned; follow the stated task convention. Exact counts and exact unit conversions do not limit precision. Standard form alone does not guarantee accuracy, and converting a rounded measurement to another unit creates no new measured information.
examples: Calculate (6×10⁵)(4×10^(−3)). Coefficients give 24 and exponents give 5+(−3)=2, hence 24×10²=2.4×10³. The exponent is adjusted during normalisation.

Calculate (8.4×10^(−5))/(2.0×10³). The coefficient is 8.4/2.0=4.2 and exponent is −5−3=−8, giving 4.2×10^(−8). Both measured inputs have two significant figures, so this is an appropriate two-figure result.

Find (5.72×10⁶)−(8.6×10⁵). Rewrite 8.6×10⁵ as 0.86×10⁶; subtract to get 4.86×10⁶. Both inputs were given to the nearest 10000, so the result also ends at that place. Rounding the inputs to one significant figure first would lose important information.
lessons.summary: For a positive number in standard form A×10^n, the coefficient satisfies 1≤A<10 and n is an integer.

lessons.title: Current-electricity graphs and low-voltage evidence
objectives: Design a controlled low-voltage resistor investigation
Extract resistance from correctly labelled graphs
Process repeated readings and report qualified conclusions
paragraphs: Testing whether a component is ohmic requires a range of measured potential differences and currents while its temperature is approximately constant. A single V/I value describes one operating point but cannot establish a proportional relationship. Use several settings within teacher-approved ratings, take repeats and look for a stable ratio together with a straight graph approximately through the origin. A changing ratio may reflect heating, a non-ohmic component or measurement problems.

In a supervised low-voltage circuit, connect an ammeter in series with the test resistor and a voltmeter across it. Include a switch and a teacher-approved current-limiting resistor or supply limit. Start with the supply off, choose suitable meter ranges and ask the teacher to check connections before energising. Never place an ammeter directly across a supply: its low resistance can permit excessive current. Use only the specified low-voltage classroom source, keep hands dry and disconnect power before changing connections.

Change the supply setting or approved variable resistance in small steps. Record voltage in volts and current in amperes, converting milliamperes by dividing by 1000 before calculating R=V/I. Switch off between readings to reduce heating and stop if a component becomes hot or exceeds its rating. Record unexpected observations rather than replacing them. Keep the same component, meter setup and procedure when testing a constant-temperature relationship.

Choose graph axes deliberately. With V on the vertical axis and I horizontally, a straight-line gradient ΔV/ΔI has units V/A=Ω and represents resistance. With I vertically and V horizontally, the gradient is conductance, 1/R, in A/V. Use well-separated points on a best-fit line to estimate the gradient, rather than joining noisy adjacent points. An intercept significantly different from zero is a reason to investigate meter offsets or the circuit; it should not be erased by forcing a line through the origin.

A spreadsheet can store supply setting, V, I₁, I₂, mean I and calculated resistance. Use =AVERAGE(C2:D2) for repeats in those columns, and =B2/E2 for resistance if B contains V and E contains mean current in amperes; omit the ratio at zero current because division by zero is undefined. Use an XY chart and show units. A report should distinguish supplied practice data from real observations, describe controls and repeats, and explain what the graph supports within the tested range. Do not extrapolate to mains voltages or assume that every component has constant resistance.
examples: Practice data for a resistor are V=1,2,3 V and I=0.020,0.040,0.060 A. Each ratio V/I=50 Ω. The V-against-I gradient using the endpoints is (3−1)/(0.060−0.020)=2/0.040=50 Ω, supporting ohmic behaviour over this range if temperature was controlled.

At 2.0 V, repeated currents are 38,40,42 mA. Mean=(38+40+42)/3=40 mA=0.040 A and range=42−38=4 mA. Resistance from the mean is 2.0/0.040=50 Ω. Repeating readings reveals spread but does not remove a meter's systematic offset.

Practice lamp data are (1 V,0.10 A),(2 V,0.16 A),(3 V,0.20 A). Ratios are 10,12.5,15 Ω. Resistance increases as the lamp heats, so these points do not support a constant-resistance model. At the final setting P=VI=3×0.20=0.60 W.
lessons.summary: Testing whether a component is ohmic requires a range of measured potential differences and currents while its temperature is approximately constant.

lessons.title: Solar energy, Earth movements and geographical time
objectives: Distinguish rotation from revolution and explain their effects.
Use latitude, longitude and time differences with stated assumptions.
Explain seasonal changes without confusing distance and tilt.
paragraphs: The Sun supplies most of the energy that drives surface weather and plant growth. Earth is the third planet from the Sun, orbiting between Venus and Mars. Gravity keeps planets in orbit while their existing motion carries them forward. The solar system formed from a rotating cloud of gas and dust; scientific explanations draw on observations and physical evidence rather than direct observation of its formation.

Rotation is Earth’s turning on its axis, taking approximately 24 hours relative to the Sun. A place faces daylight while turned towards the Sun and night while turned away. Because rotation is eastward, the Sun appears to move westward across the sky. A moving shadow can therefore provide evidence of apparent solar movement, but its exact direction depends on place and season.

Revolution is Earth’s movement around the Sun in about 365¼ days. Earth’s axis is tilted about 23½ degrees relative to a line perpendicular to the orbital plane. As Earth revolves, the hemisphere tilted towards the Sun generally receives higher solar angles and longer days. Seasons follow this changing angle and duration, not simply the varying Earth–Sun distance. Near the Equator, rainfall seasons can be more noticeable than temperature seasons.

Latitude measures angular distance north or south of the Equator; longitude measures angular distance east or west of the prime meridian. Parallels are circles of latitude; meridians meet at the poles. Earth turns through 360 degrees in 24 hours, giving 15 degrees per hour or four minutes per degree. Longitude calculations give local solar time differences; actual civil time follows agreed time zones and may differ.
examples: Local solar time at 30°E is 12:00. A place at 45°E lies 15° farther east: 15 ÷ 15 = 1 hour ahead, so its local solar time is 13:00. This is a solar-time model, not a claim about legal time zones.
At 20°W it is 09:20 local solar time. At 10°E the difference is 30°: 30 × 4 = 120 minutes. Move east and add two hours: 11:20.

In a classroom model, hold a tilted globe with its axis pointing in the same direction while moving it around a lamp. The hemisphere tilted towards the lamp receives more direct light and longer exposure. Rotating the globe explains day and night; carrying it around the lamp explains the annual pattern.
lessons.summary: The Sun supplies most of the energy that drives surface weather and plant growth.

lessons.title: Comparing landforms, drainage and inland waters
objectives: Recognise major relief forms using height and shape.
Explain drainage links between land and water bodies.
Use comparative geographical evidence.
paragraphs: Relief describes differences in surface elevation and land shape. A mountain rises prominently above its surroundings, a plateau is an extensive elevated surface with relatively level parts, and a plain has gentle relief. Height alone does not decide the name: a high plateau can contain mountains and valleys. Describe both elevation and local shape before assigning a label to a landscape.

A river flows down a gradient through a channel. Tributaries join a main stream; the land drained by the connected streams forms a drainage basin. A watershed is the higher boundary separating neighbouring basins. Water on opposite sides of a divide can enter different rivers. Weathering, erosion, transport and deposition change a basin over time, while vegetation and settlement affect runoff.

Lakes occupy inland depressions filled with water. Some have river outlets; others lose much of their water through evaporation and seepage. A lake without an outlet may accumulate dissolved salts, but the actual salinity depends on its water and mineral balance. Wetlands have water at or near the surface for significant periods and can store floodwater, support habitats and filter some pollutants.

Continents are major land masses and oceans are connected bodies of salt water. Africa contains varied relief and important inland waters, including Lakes Victoria, Tanganyika and Nyasa/Malawi. A location description should combine a named feature, its position and a relevant characteristic. Claims about flooding or water use need evidence such as river levels, rainfall records, field observations and mapped settlement, because one photograph cannot describe every season.
examples: Site A: elevation 1,500 m, broad rolling surface; Site B: summit 1,450 m, steep sides rising 700 m above nearby land. A may be a plateau and B a mountain: relative relief and shape matter alongside absolute elevation.

A basin receives 100 units of rain. If 35 evaporate, 20 infiltrate into storage and 45 run off, the simplified balance is 100 = 35 + 20 + 45. Real basins also have changing stores and flows across boundaries.

River U joins River V before V enters a lake. U is a tributary, the meeting point is a confluence, and their combined catchment belongs to the drainage basin. A ridge between them and River W can form a watershed.
lessons.summary: Relief describes differences in surface elevation and land shape.

lessons.title: Vegetation zones, adaptation and field evidence
objectives: Compare forest, savanna and arid vegetation.
Connect plant adaptations to environmental conditions.
Collect vegetation evidence responsibly.
paragraphs: Natural vegetation is plant cover developing under local environmental conditions, although human activity modifies most inhabited landscapes. Vegetation zones describe broad patterns, not sharp boundaries. Temperature, rainfall amount and seasonality, soil, altitude, drainage, fire and grazing interact. Two places with similar annual rainfall may support different plants if one has a much longer dry season or poorly drained soil.

Humid tropical forest commonly has many broad-leaved trees and a layered canopy where moisture and warmth support growth. Dense upper foliage reduces light reaching the forest floor, favouring shade-tolerant plants. Savanna commonly combines grasses with scattered trees or shrubs and has a marked wet and dry season. Tree spacing varies with soils, water, fire and land use, so a single tree does not identify an entire vegetation zone.

Arid and semi-arid vegetation is often sparse and includes plants with features that reduce water loss or improve water access. Small leaves or thorns reduce exposed leaf area, thick cuticles limit water loss, succulent tissues store water and some roots spread widely or reach deeply. No single adaptation belongs to every dryland plant. Highland vegetation can change with altitude because temperature and moisture conditions change.

Vegetation investigation should link a claim to a measured observation. Use a small quadrat or a line transect, record the same categories at each site and note soil moisture, shade and signs of disturbance. Avoid damaging plants or entering unsafe areas. A table showing several samples is stronger than a selected photograph, but a small school survey cannot justify a claim about an entire region. Distinguish observed plant cover from your explanation of why it occurs.
examples: Five equal quadrats have grass cover 40%, 50%, 60%, 30% and 70%. Mean cover = 250 ÷ 5 = 50%. The range is 70 − 30 = 40 percentage points, showing considerable local variation.

On a transect, shaded sites have fewer grasses and deeper leaf litter. A reasonable explanation is reduced light beneath trees. Soil moisture and trampling may also differ; measure these before attributing everything to shade.
A shrub has tiny leaves and a thick waxy surface. These features can reduce water loss. They support an adaptation hypothesis, but identifying its species or exact climate requires further evidence.
lessons.summary: Natural vegetation is plant cover developing under local environmental conditions, although human activity modifies most inhabited landscapes.

lessons.title: Topographic maps: contours, slopes and route decisions
objectives: Read contour heights and slope patterns.
Calculate gradient and construct a simple profile.
Justify route choices with map evidence.
paragraphs: A topographic map represents surface features with symbols, scale and relief information. Begin with the title, key, north arrow and scale, then read the contour interval before interpreting heights. A contour joins points at equal elevation above a reference level. Adjacent contours usually differ by a constant vertical interval; the space between them on paper shows horizontal distance, not another height measurement.

Closely spaced contours indicate a steep slope because a given height change occurs over a short horizontal distance. Widely spaced contours indicate gentler slopes. Concentric closed contours with increasing values inward commonly represent a hill. A valley usually makes contours bend upstream into a V; confirm the direction using height values and any river symbol. A closed contour alone does not prove a hill if heights or depression markings indicate otherwise.

Gradient compares vertical rise with horizontal distance measured in the same units. A 40 m rise over 800 m gives 40:800 = 1:20. This is different from the slope distance actually walked. To draw a profile, place a paper strip along a line, mark contour crossings and heights, transfer their horizontal positions to graph paper, then plot and connect heights. A steep-looking profile may result from vertical exaggeration, so label both scales.

Route selection combines relief with other mapped evidence. A short straight route can cross a steep slope, river or wet ground; a longer route may be safer or easier to build. A map cannot establish current bridge condition, path access or seasonal flooding by itself. Explain a proposed route by citing the contour spacing, crossings and distance, then identify what must be checked on the ground.
examples: Contours labelled 100, 120, 140 and 160 m have a 20 m interval. A point exactly on the 140 m line is 140 m high. A point between 140 and 160 m is within that interval; do not report an exact height without further evidence.
A route rises from 200 to 260 m across 1.5 km horizontally. Rise = 60 m; run = 1,500 m; gradient = 60:1,500 = 1:25. Every 25 m horizontally corresponds to an average 1 m rise.

Profile table: distance from A (m): 0 | 100 | 200 | 300 | 400; height (m): 100 | 120 | 160 | 180 | 180. The steepest sampled section is 100–200 m, rising 40 m in 100 m. The final segment is level in this simplified sample.
lessons.diagramAlt: Topographic maps: contours, slopes and route decisions — original labelled teaching diagram; explanatory values are illustrative.
lessons.summary: A topographic map represents surface features with symbols, scale and relief information.

lessons.title: Statistical maps, rates and honest comparisons
objectives: Choose maps suitable for counts, rates and movement.
Interpret a data table alongside a statistical map.
Recognise misleading map comparisons.
paragraphs: Statistical maps show the spatial distribution of numerical information. A choropleth map shades defined areas according to a value or class; a dot map uses repeated dots to represent quantities; proportional symbols vary symbol size with quantity. Flow maps show movement using lines or arrows whose widths may represent volume. Every map needs a title, time period, key and source so readers know what is being compared.

For a choropleth map, a rate or density is often more useful than a raw total when areas differ in population or size. Population density equals population divided by land area. The average describes the whole mapped area and does not show each settlement. Shading an entire district with one class must not be interpreted as proof that every part has the same density.

Class intervals change the map’s visual pattern. Non-overlapping classes such as 0–49, 50–99 and 100–149 people per km² place each integer value in one class. Equal intervals are easy to compare, while other classifications may emphasise different patterns. A dot represents a stated quantity and an approximate distribution; it does not automatically identify a real household at the exact dot position.

Read the table before explaining the map. Check units, dates, missing values and whether geographical boundaries match. Correlation between two mapped variables can suggest a question but does not establish cause. A district with many shops might also have a large population; shops per thousand residents can answer a different question from total shops. Use both absolute totals and suitable rates when the decision requires them.
examples: Teaching table: Area A: 12,000 people, 200 km², 24 shops; B: 9,000 people, 50 km², 27 shops; C: 20,000 people, 400 km², 20 shops. Densities are 60, 180 and 50 people/km² respectively. C has the largest population, while B has the greatest density.
Using the same table, shops per 1,000 people are A: 24/12,000 × 1,000 = 2; B: 3; C: 1. A total-shop map and a shop-rate map answer different questions.
If one dot represents 500 people, A needs 12,000 ÷ 500 = 24 dots. An exactly divisible teaching total is convenient; real data may require rounding that must be stated in the legend.
lessons.diagramAlt: Statistical maps, rates and honest comparisons — original labelled teaching diagram; explanatory values are illustrative.
lessons.summary: Statistical maps show the spatial distribution of numerical information.

lessons.title: Earth-system connections and photographic field investigation
objectives: Trace exchanges among Earth systems.
Use photographs as evidence with explicit limits.
Plan a safe repeatable field investigation.
paragraphs: The crust is Earth’s thin outer rocky layer, generally about 5–70 km thick; oceanic crust is usually thinner than continental crust. The mantle extends down to roughly 2,900 km and is mainly solid rock that can flow very slowly over geological time. The core contains an outer liquid part and an inner solid part, composed largely of iron with other elements. Increasing pressure helps explain why the inner core remains solid despite high temperature.

The atmosphere contains gases surrounding Earth, the hydrosphere includes water in liquid, solid and gaseous forms, and the biosphere includes living organisms and their zones of life. These systems overlap rather than forming completely separate boxes. Soil contains minerals, water, air and organisms. A tree takes water from soil, exchanges gases with air and returns moisture through transpiration, connecting several systems.

A photograph records visible features from one position at one moment. Ground photographs can be divided into foreground, middle ground and background; oblique photographs look down at an angle, while vertical aerial photographs look approximately straight down. A title, date, location and viewing direction improve interpretation. Relative position in a photograph does not provide a uniform distance scale because perspective makes distant objects appear smaller.

Interpretation begins with observations: bare soil, tree cover, channel shape or visible buildings. Then propose explanations and identify evidence needed to test them. Muddy stream water after rain may be consistent with erosion, but a photograph cannot measure sediment concentration or prove its source. Repeat photographs from a fixed safe point, combine them with rainfall and stream observations, and protect people’s privacy. Never enter fast water or unstable slopes to obtain evidence.
examples: Rain falls on a wooded slope: atmosphere to hydrosphere; some water infiltrates soil; roots absorb it; plants transpire moisture into air. Clearing trees may alter these flows, but the size of the change depends on soil, slope and land management.

Photo log table: image P1 | 10:00 | fixed bridge viewpoint | after rain | brown stream, bare bank. P2 | 10:00 two dry days later | same viewpoint | clearer stream. The pair shows visible change; measured turbidity and upstream observations would test the proposed sediment explanation.

A ground image shows a large tree in the foreground and small buildings behind. The image alone cannot establish that the tree is taller than the buildings: different distances affect apparent size. Use known dimensions or a measured map for reliable comparisons.
lessons.diagramAlt: Earth-system connections and photographic field investigation — original labelled teaching diagram; explanatory values are illustrative.
lessons.summary: The crust is Earth’s thin outer rocky layer, generally about 5–70 km thick; oceanic crust is usually thinner than continental crust.

lessons.title: Entrepreneurship theories: innovation, opportunity and uncertainty
objectives: Compare explanations of entrepreneurial action.
Apply theories to a local business scenario.
Distinguish evidence from entrepreneurial assumptions.
paragraphs: An entrepreneur organises resources to pursue an opportunity and accepts uncertainty about the result. Entrepreneurship is a process of identifying needs, developing an offer, arranging resources and learning from customers. Owning a business does not guarantee innovation or profit. A useful explanation identifies what a person does and why it creates value, rather than relying on a list of personality traits.

An innovation explanation emphasises new combinations: a new product, improved process, new market or different way of organising work. Innovation need not be a completely new invention. A food seller who introduces pre-orders to reduce waiting and waste changes the service process. The change becomes commercially useful only if customers value it and its benefits justify its costs.

An opportunity or alertness explanation emphasises noticing an unmet need, an overlooked resource or a mismatch between supply and demand. A learner may notice that nearby workers cannot buy affordable lunch during a short break. This observation suggests an opportunity, but demand must be tested. Interviews, small trials and observation of existing sellers provide stronger evidence than simply assuming every worker will buy.

An uncertainty explanation emphasises decisions whose outcomes cannot be known fully in advance. A trader may estimate demand but cannot know the exact number of buyers next month. Calculated risk involves gathering information, limiting potential loss and preparing alternatives; it does not mean ignoring danger. These explanations complement one another: one enterprise can notice a need, innovate in delivery and manage uncertainty at the same time.
examples: A tailor introduces appointments by message and groups similar jobs. Innovation lies in the scheduling process; evidence of value would include reduced waiting, fewer missed deadlines and repeat orders. A new label alone would not demonstrate improved value.

A fruit seller observes unsold ripe fruit and interviews ten nearby workers. Six express interest in small fruit portions. A limited paid trial tests actual purchases; six interested interviewees do not prove that six people will buy every day.

Two production choices have different possible losses: making 100 units may leave 40 unsold, while a 20-unit trial limits initial exposure. The smaller trial sacrifices some potential sales but provides information before expansion.
lessons.summary: An entrepreneur organises resources to pursue an opportunity and accepts uncertainty about the result.

lessons.title: Enterprise skills: customer research, communication and negotiation
objectives: Collect usable customer evidence.
Communicate an offer clearly and ethically.
Negotiate while checking costs and promises.
paragraphs: Enterprise skills are learned abilities used to turn an idea into dependable action. Communication, numeracy, planning, problem-solving and teamwork support one another. A seller who understands customer needs but cannot calculate costs may price badly; a skilled producer who misses deadlines may lose trust. Skills improve through practice, feedback and records rather than through confidence alone.

Customer research begins with a focused decision, such as choosing package size or delivery time. Ask neutral questions about existing behaviour: what people currently buy, how often, at what price and what problems occur. A leading question such as “Would you buy our excellent cheap product?” encourages favourable answers. Include people beyond friends and record refusals or negative responses, because selective evidence creates false confidence.

A clear offer states what is supplied, the quantity or quality, price, delivery timing and any conditions. Listening matters as much as speaking: repeat the customer’s requirement and check ambiguities before accepting an order. Keep a simple order record with agreed details. Protect customer contact information, avoid false claims and do not promise delivery that the available materials or time cannot support.

Negotiation seeks an agreement acceptable to both sides. Prepare by estimating costs, deciding a minimum acceptable outcome and considering alternatives. A lower unit price may be workable for a large order if production savings cover the discount, but extra packaging or transport can erase the benefit. Confirm the final quantity, total charge, deadline and payment arrangement in a clear record; disagreement often follows assumptions that were never checked.
examples: Neutral survey question: “How many notebooks did you buy last month, and what size?” This gathers behaviour. “You want our better notebooks, don’t you?” is leading and gives weak evidence.

An order is 12 bags at 2,500 currency units each. Total = 12 × 2,500 = 30,000. Record bag size, collection date and whether payment is due at collection; the price calculation alone does not define the full agreement.

Unit cost is 1,600 and usual price is 2,000. A buyer requests 1,700 for 20 units. Contribution before other fixed costs is (1,700 − 1,600) × 20 = 2,000. An extra delivery cost of 2,500 would make that offer unattractive on these assumptions.
lessons.summary: Enterprise skills are learned abilities used to turn an idea into dependable action.

lessons.title: Sole-trader launch: feasibility, liability and a first-month plan
objectives: Assess whether a small sole-trader idea is feasible.
Explain ownership, control and personal exposure.
Prepare a practical launch plan and review criteria.
paragraphs: A sole proprietorship has one owner who makes decisions and receives the business’s profit or bears its loss. The owner can employ other people; one owner does not mean one worker. Direct control and simple decision-making can help a small business respond quickly, while limited finance, workload and dependence on the owner can restrict growth. The business may struggle if the owner becomes unavailable.

Unlimited liability means the owner may be personally responsible for business debts; business losses are not automatically limited to the amount initially invested. Keep business and personal records separate to understand performance, even where ownership is not legally separate. Avoid treating sales receipts as money freely available for household use: stock replacement, unpaid bills and other obligations must be considered.

A feasibility check asks whether the enterprise can obtain customers, resources and enough income to cover its costs. List start-up assets separately from recurring expenses and stock. Confirm access to workspace, equipment, inputs and suitable skills. Check applicable requirements with reliable local authorities before opening; requirements differ by location and activity, so a textbook should not invent a universal permit rule.

A first-month plan should state the target customer, offer, starting quantity, price, spending limit and daily records. Assign dates to purchasing, production and customer testing. Set review criteria before launch, such as repeat purchases, delivery reliability and adequate cash for restocking. If results are weak, identify whether demand, price, quality or costs need adjustment rather than borrowing automatically to continue an untested idea.
examples: Teaching start-up table: equipment 60,000; opening stock 40,000; packaging 10,000; reserve cash 20,000. Total required = 130,000 currency units. Equipment is a longer-use asset; opening stock is intended for sale; reserve remains cash until used.

An owner receives 50,000 in sales but owes 25,000 for stock and 10,000 for transport. Only looking at the cash received exaggerates available resources. Record obligations before deciding whether a withdrawal is affordable.

A one-week trial sells 16 of 20 planned items and delivers 14 on time. Sales completion = 16/20 = 80%; on-time rate among actual orders = 14/16 = 87.5%. Different denominators answer different questions.
lessons.summary: A sole proprietorship has one owner who makes decisions and receives the business’s profit or bears its loss.

lessons.title: Financing decisions, microfinance and cooperative organisation
objectives: Compare sources of capital using cost, timing and obligations.
Explain how microfinance and cooperatives support enterprise.
Assess a finance proposal without recommending a provider.
paragraphs: Capital for a small business may come from savings, loans, family or friends, and deferred payment to suppliers. Savings avoid contractual interest but reduce the owner’s reserve for other needs. A loan creates repayment obligations even when sales disappoint. Family funds may be a gift, loan or ownership contribution; clarify which arrangement is intended so expectations about repayment and decision-making are explicit.

Deferred payment allows goods to be obtained now and paid for later. It can help match payments with sales, but goods may cost more than under cash terms and a late payment can damage supplier trust. Compare the full amount payable, payment dates, penalties or fees if any, and the realistic cash available at those dates. A low advertised instalment does not establish the lowest total cost.

Microfinance refers broadly to relatively small-scale financial services for people or enterprises that may have limited access to conventional finance. Depending on the organisation, services can include savings, small loans or financial education. Group arrangements may use peer support or shared responsibility, which can create pressure as well as assistance. Read the actual terms and ask how missed payments affect the individual and group; no provider or product is automatically suitable.

A cooperative is an organisation formed by members to meet shared economic or social needs through joint activity and member participation. Members may pool savings, purchase inputs or market produce together. Joint action can improve bargaining power and spread service costs, but weak records, poor participation or misuse of funds can harm members. Sound operation requires transparent accounts, agreed rules, elected accountability and informed decisions; the exact legal structure and obligations must be verified locally.
examples: Compare two hypothetical funding offers: A provides 100,000 with total scheduled repayment 112,000; B provides 100,000 with repayment 108,000 plus a compulsory non-refundable fee of 6,000. Total stated cost is A 12,000 and B 14,000. This comparison excludes unstated charges and does not evaluate timing or suitability.
A supplier charges 40,000 cash or 44,000 after one month for the same goods. Deferred payment adds 4,000, equal to 10% of the cash price for that period. This is not an annual rate calculation.

Ten cooperative members each contribute 8,000 to a shared input purchase. Pool = 80,000. If inputs cost 72,000 and transport 5,000, the balance is 3,000. Record contributions, invoices and the agreed treatment of the remaining balance.
lessons.summary: Capital for a small business may come from savings, loans, family or friends, and deferred payment to suppliers.

lessons.title: Managing cash, budgets, profit and corrective action
objectives: Distinguish profit from cash availability.
Prepare and interpret a cash budget.
Use records and management functions to correct problems.
paragraphs: Management coordinates people and resources to achieve business objectives. Planning decides targets and actions; organising assigns work and resources; leading communicates and supports action; control compares actual results with plans and makes corrections. These functions interact: a missed delivery can reveal an unrealistic plan, unclear responsibility or a resource shortage. Blaming a worker without checking the system may leave the cause unresolved.

Records provide evidence for decisions. Keep dated source documents such as receipts and invoices, then record cash received, cash paid, sales, purchases, inventory and amounts owed where relevant. Credit sales create revenue and a customer debt but no immediate cash receipt. Buying equipment uses cash, yet its full cost is not necessarily treated as one period’s operating expense in a developed accounting system. State the simplifying assumptions used in classroom calculations.

For a simple trading period, gross profit equals sales revenue minus cost of goods sold. Operating profit in a simplified exercise subtracts other operating expenses. Cost of goods sold equals opening inventory plus purchases minus closing inventory, assuming the figures cover comparable goods and no other adjustments. Unsold stock is not automatically all charged as goods sold. Personal withdrawals are not an operating expense, although they reduce cash.

A cash budget estimates opening cash, expected receipts and expected payments for each period. Closing cash equals opening cash plus receipts minus payments. A profitable enterprise can face a cash shortage when customers pay late or money is tied up in inventory. Compare actual and budgeted figures, investigate the reason for variances, and take proportionate action such as improving collection, revising purchase timing or addressing waste. Cutting essential quality or safety to meet a budget can create larger losses.
examples: Opening inventory 20,000 + purchases 70,000 − closing inventory 15,000 gives cost of goods sold 75,000. Sales 110,000 − 75,000 = gross profit 35,000. Other operating expenses 18,000 give simplified operating profit 17,000.

Cash budget table: opening cash 12,000; receipts 40,000; supplier payments 28,000; transport 6,000; owner withdrawal 5,000. Closing cash = 12,000 + 40,000 − 28,000 − 6,000 − 5,000 = 13,000. The withdrawal affects cash but is not an operating expense.

Budgeted material cost is 30,000 and actual cost 36,000. Variance is 6,000 over budget. Investigate price changes, extra output and wastage before concluding poor performance; extra output may explain part of the difference.
lessons.summary: Management coordinates people and resources to achieve business objectives.

lessons.title: Warehousing, stock control and a practical enterprise project
objectives: Explain warehouse functions and inventory records.
Calculate stock balances and reorder needs.
Test a local enterprise using operational evidence.
paragraphs: Warehousing is the organised storage and handling of goods until they are needed. It helps bridge time between production and consumption, protects stock and supports reliable supply. A warehouse may be a simple secure storeroom rather than a large specialised building. Suitable storage depends on the product: moisture, heat, pests, theft and contamination create different risks. Follow verified product-specific storage instructions where required.

Inventory includes goods for sale, raw materials and partly completed products where relevant. Stock control records receipts, issues and balances so the business knows what should be available. A stock card records one item consistently by unit, with date, reference, quantities received, quantities issued and balance. Physical counts test whether records match reality; differences can arise from errors, damage, spoilage or theft and should be investigated rather than silently altered.

Stock rotation reduces avoidable loss. First-in, first-out issues older receipts before newer ones; first-expiry, first-out prioritises goods with the earliest expiry date. The two methods can give different orders when a later delivery expires sooner. Keep aisles clear, stack safely, separate incompatible goods and mark damaged stock for assessment. A high stock balance is not always beneficial because it ties up cash and may increase deterioration.

A reorder decision considers average demand during supplier lead time plus a safety buffer. The calculation is only a planning aid: demand and delivery times can change. Apply these ideas in a small enterprise project by identifying a local need, surveying customers, budgeting a limited trial, recording stock and sales, and reviewing profit, cash and customer feedback. Use locally observed evidence rather than assuming an opportunity exists simply because a product is common elsewhere.
examples: Stock-card table for exercise books: opening 50; receive 30 → balance 80; issue 45 → 35; receive 20 → 55; damaged 3 removed after authorisation → 52. Record damage separately from sales so revenue is not overstated.
Average demand is 8 units/day, lead time 4 days and safety stock 10 units. Simplified reorder point = 8 × 4 + 10 = 42 units. Review the assumptions if demand or lead time changes.

Batch A arrived first but expires in August; Batch B arrived later but expires in June. FIFO would issue A first by arrival; FEFO issues B first because June expiry is earlier. Inspect actual product condition as well as dates.
lessons.summary: Warehousing is the organised storage and handling of goods until they are needed.

lessons.title: Chemistry, other sciences and decisions in society
objectives: Distinguish major branches of chemistry using concrete questions.
Explain links between chemistry, health, farming and other disciplines.
Evaluate a chemical technology using evidence about benefits and costs.
paragraphs: Chemistry investigates what substances contain, how their particles are arranged, the properties they show and how they change into other substances. A chemist may identify a powder, measure the amount of a dissolved substance or design a material with a useful property. Observation comes before explanation: “a colourless gas formed” records evidence, while “carbon dioxide formed” is an identification that needs a suitable test. Reliable chemical work combines practical observations with models and numerical measurements.

Branches describe overlapping kinds of questions. Analytical chemistry identifies substances and measures their amounts; testing drinking water for dissolved contaminants is an example. Organic chemistry studies carbon compounds, including fuels and many medicines. Inorganic chemistry includes metals, minerals and many salts. Physical chemistry relates changes and properties to energy, rates and particle behaviour. Biochemistry studies chemical processes in living things, such as enzymes breaking down food. A single project may use several branches, so a branch name is a useful focus rather than a barrier.

Chemistry connects sciences through shared problems. A farmer investigating poor crop growth may combine soil chemistry, plant biology and measurements of rainfall. A pharmacist needs chemical knowledge of a medicine and biological knowledge of its effects. Physics helps explain the electricity used in electrolysis and the energy transferred during heating. Mathematics supports concentration calculations and comparisons between samples. Engineering turns a small laboratory process into controlled production, while geography helps explain where raw materials and water are available.

Chemical technologies can improve health, food supply and living conditions. Water-treatment chemicals help reduce disease when used correctly; fertilisers replace nutrients removed by harvests; alloys and polymers provide useful construction materials. Evaluation must consider the whole process: raw-material extraction, manufacturing energy, product use and disposal. Excess fertiliser entering water can encourage excessive algal growth. A useful decision therefore identifies the need, compares workable alternatives and checks evidence about benefits and unwanted effects instead of assuming that every chemical product is either harmless or harmful.
examples: A water supplier asks two questions: “Which dissolved substances are present?” and “How much is present?” Both are analytical chemistry questions. Deciding how a disinfectant affects microbes also brings in biology.

A plant makes steel cooking pots. Investigating how a changed alloy composition affects corrosion links inorganic chemistry to materials engineering. Measuring masses and comparing service lifetimes provides evidence for the decision.

A village compares two fertiliser practices. Practice A gives 300 kg of extra crop and practice B gives 270 kg, but B uses half as much fertiliser. Yield alone favours A; deciding overall value also requires cost, soil and water evidence. The numbers do not establish that either practice is best in every field.
lessons.summary: Chemistry investigates what substances contain, how their particles are arranged, the properties they show and how they change into other substances.

lessons.title: Recognising physical and chemical changes
objectives: Use substance identity to distinguish physical and chemical changes.
Assess observations as evidence rather than automatic proof of reaction.
Explain why compounds can differ from their starting elements.
paragraphs: A physical change alters a state, shape, size or distribution without producing a different chemical substance. Cutting copper wire changes its length but leaves copper. Melting pure ice gives liquid water, so the particles have a different arrangement and movement while retaining their chemical identity. Dissolving can also be physical: when ordinary salt dissolves in water, its ions spread through the water and salt can be recovered by removing the water. This example does not mean that every process involving a liquid is a physical change.

A chemical change forms one or more different substances. When iron rusts in suitable conditions, iron-containing substances with different properties develop. When a fuel burns completely in enough oxygen, new products form; the atoms have been rearranged rather than destroyed. “Easy to reverse” is only a useful clue, not a definition. A broken glass is difficult to restore but breaking is physical. Some chemical reactions can be reversed by a different reaction, so reversibility alone cannot settle the classification.

Colour change, gas formation, a new solid and energy transfer can suggest a chemical reaction, but each observation needs context. Bubbles in boiling water are water vapour, whereas gas from a carbonate reacting with acid is a reaction product. A solid forming when a hot salt solution cools may be unchanged salt crystallising; a solid appearing when two solutions react may be a new insoluble compound. Compare starting materials and products, and use appropriate tests rather than relying on one visible sign.

Compounds may behave very differently from their elements because atoms are joined in new structures and ratios. Metallic iron and yellow sulfur are separate substances in an unreacted mixture; after a suitable teacher-led reaction they form iron sulfide with different properties. This comparison needs controlled preparation and is not an invitation to heat unknown mixtures. Chemical reactions conserve atoms. In a closed system the total mass is conserved, but an open container may appear to lose mass if gas escapes or gain mass if oxygen enters from the air.
examples: Wax first melts near a candle flame: this is physical because wax remains wax. Wax vapour then burns and makes other substances: this is chemical. A single everyday event can include both kinds of change.
A beaker of water bubbles when heated. Cooling the collected vapour returns liquid water, supporting a state-change explanation. Bubbles alone did not prove a new gas substance had been made.

A closed reaction vessel has mass 145.6 g before mixing and 145.6 g afterward. A gas forms inside it, but all material stays in the vessel. Gas formation and unchanged total mass are compatible because atoms have rearranged without leaving the system.
lessons.summary: A physical change alters a state, shape, size or distribution without producing a different chemical substance.

lessons.title: Investigating heating, cooling and changes of state
objectives: Plan a supervised investigation of a state change.
Read heating and cooling records with correct units.
Explain plateaus and distinguish boiling from evaporation.
paragraphs: A heating record relates temperature to time while energy is transferred to a substance. Before collecting data, identify the material, the amount used, the heating method and the measuring interval. A fair comparison between two samples keeps these conditions similar. A thermometer measures its own temperature after approaching thermal equilibrium with its surroundings, so placement matters: the bulb should be in the sample as instructed, without touching the vessel wall or base. Read the scale at eye level and record units.

For a pure substance at constant pressure, melting or boiling can occur while the temperature stays approximately constant even though heating continues. The transferred energy changes the arrangement and separation of particles rather than increasing their average motion. On an ideal heating graph, these intervals appear as plateaus. Real school graphs may be less flat because of impurities, heat loss, uneven heating or measurement limits. A temperature plateau supports an explanation only alongside observations of the state change.

Cooling reverses energy transfer. A liquid may cool, freeze over a nearly steady-temperature interval and then cool further as a solid. The particles do not disappear when a liquid evaporates or a vapour condenses. Evaporation occurs at the liquid surface at temperatures below boiling as some particles escape; boiling produces vapour throughout the liquid at the boiling temperature for the prevailing pressure. Condensation on a cool surface provides evidence that water vapour is present even when the vapour itself cannot be seen.

Practical state-change work needs teacher supervision, stable apparatus and protection against hot surfaces and splashes. Use the school-approved heating arrangement; never heat a sealed container. Steam and hot water can burn even when no flame is visible. Record observations separately from temperature readings: “solid and liquid both present” is more informative than writing only “melting happened”. Repeat measurements where feasible, plot time on the horizontal axis, and explain limitations rather than adjusting unexpected data to match a textbook graph.
examples: A sample reads 22, 31 and 40 °C at 0, 1 and 2 minutes. From 0 to 2 minutes the mean temperature rise is (40 − 22)/2 = 9 °C per minute. This average need not describe every instant.

A pure sample rises to 64 °C, stays near 64 °C while solid and liquid coexist, then rises again after all solid disappears. The likely melting temperature under those conditions is about 64 °C; the plateau does not mean heating stopped.

Water on the outside of a cold closed bottle is not evidence that water passed through the glass. Water vapour in surrounding air loses energy at the cold surface and condenses. Drying the bottle first and comparing a room-temperature bottle helps test this explanation.
lessons.summary: A heating record relates temperature to time while energy is transferred to a substance.

lessons.title: Valency, oxidation states and naming compounds
objectives: Write neutral ionic formulae from ion charges.
Name binary compounds and distinguish valency from oxidation state.
Use brackets correctly for repeated polyatomic ions.
paragraphs: A chemical name and formula describe composition precisely. For a binary compound, only two different elements are present, although there may be more than two atoms. Magnesium oxide contains magnesium and oxygen; magnesium hydroxide contains three elements and is therefore not binary. In common binary ionic names, name the positive ion first and change the non-metal ending to -ide: calcium chloride, aluminium oxide and sodium sulfide. Accurate spelling distinguishes sulfide, which contains sulfur without oxygen, from sulfate, a different ion containing sulfur and oxygen.

Valency describes combining capacity and is commonly written without a sign. Oxidation state is a formal electron-accounting number written with a positive or negative sign. In introductory ionic compounds it often matches the monatomic ion charge: sodium is +1 and oxide oxygen is −2. The sum of oxidation states is zero in a neutral compound. An element in its uncombined form has oxidation state zero. These rules are useful bookkeeping; they do not mean every compound contains separate ions or that a covalent atom has a whole electrical charge.

Some metals form more than one positive ion. The Roman numeral in iron(II) chloride identifies iron in oxidation state +2, while iron(III) chloride identifies +3. It does not count the number of iron atoms. Chloride has charge −1, so charge balance gives FeCl₂ and FeCl₃ respectively. Use the smallest whole-number ratio that makes the total positive and negative charges cancel. The same reasoning gives Mg₃N₂ from Mg²⁺ and N³⁻; writing subscripts mechanically without checking charges can produce an incorrect formula.

A polyatomic ion is a bonded group of atoms with an overall charge; some school texts call it a radical. Examples include hydroxide OH⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻, sulfate SO₄²⁻, carbonate CO₃²⁻ and ammonium NH₄⁺. Keep the internal formula intact when combining ions. Calcium nitrate requires two nitrate ions to balance Ca²⁺, giving Ca(NO₃)₂. Brackets mean that the subscript multiplies every atom inside, so it contains two nitrogen and six oxygen atoms per formula unit. Ammonium is a positive polyatomic ion, showing that positive ions need not be metals.
examples: For aluminium sulfide, combine Al³⁺ and S²⁻. Two aluminium ions give +6 and three sulfide ions give −6, so the formula is Al₂S₃. The subscripts express a ratio, not the ion charges themselves.
For CuO, oxide contributes −2. The copper must contribute +2 to make zero overall, so the name is copper(II) oxide. Cu₂O instead requires two +1 copper ions and is copper(I) oxide.
For ammonium sulfate, two NH₄⁺ ions balance one SO₄²⁻ ion, giving (NH₄)₂SO₄. Count atoms: N = 2, H = 8, S = 1, O = 4. Omitting the brackets would change the meaning of the formula.
lessons.summary: A chemical name and formula describe composition precisely.

lessons.title: Calculating empirical and molecular formulae
objectives: Convert masses to relative amounts of atoms.
Derive empirical formulae from mass and percentage data.
Use relative molecular mass to obtain a molecular formula.
paragraphs: An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of the different elements in a compound. A molecular formula gives the actual number of each kind of atom in a molecule. Ethene has molecular formula C₂H₄ and empirical formula CH₂. Water has both empirical and molecular formula H₂O because its ratio is already simplest. Ionic solids are usually represented by formula-unit ratios rather than molecular formulae, since an ionic lattice is not made from separate molecules.

Masses cannot be used directly as atom ratios because different atoms have different masses. Divide each elemental mass by the corresponding relative atomic mass to obtain proportional amounts of atoms. Then divide all these results by the smallest result. If the ratios are close to whole numbers within the precision of the data, use those integers as subscripts. Record your intermediate values so that a mistake can be located. Unless specified otherwise, the examples here use H = 1, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16 and Mg = 24.

Percentage-composition problems can be treated as a hypothetical 100 g sample: 40.0% carbon becomes 40.0 g carbon. The procedure is then the same as for masses. A ratio such as 1:1.5 should not be rounded to 1:2. Multiply every ratio by 2 to obtain 2:3; similarly, thirds may require multiplication by 3. The final ratio must be consistent with the accuracy of the data, not forced to a convenient formula. If percentages do not total approximately 100%, check whether an element or other information is missing.

To obtain a molecular formula, first calculate the relative formula mass of the empirical unit by adding its relative atomic masses. Divide the supplied relative molecular mass by that empirical formula mass. The result should be a positive whole-number multiplier, allowing for rounding. Multiply every empirical subscript by the same factor. This extra information is essential: composition alone cannot distinguish CH₂O, C₂H₄O₂ and C₆H₁₂O₆ because all have the same simplest atomic ratio.
examples: A compound contains 12 g carbon and 4 g hydrogen. Relative amounts are 12/12 = 1 and 4/1 = 4. The ratio is 1:4, so its empirical formula is CH₄. Using the mass ratio 3:1 would have given the wrong answer.
A sample contains 2.4 g magnesium and 1.6 g oxygen. Relative amounts are 2.4/24 = 0.10 and 1.6/16 = 0.10. Dividing by 0.10 gives 1:1, hence MgO.

A compound is 40.0% C, 6.7% H and 53.3% O. For 100 g, relative amounts are about 3.33, 6.7 and 3.33, giving about 1:2:1 and CH₂O. Its empirical mass is 30. If its relative molecular mass is 180, the multiplier is 180/30 = 6, giving C₆H₁₂O₆.
lessons.summary: An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of the different elements in a compound.

lessons.title: Acids, bases, salts and useful reactions
objectives: Distinguish acids, bases and alkalis using aqueous behaviour.
Predict products of common acid reactions.
Choose safe salt-preparation and neutralisation applications.
paragraphs: In introductory aqueous chemistry, an acid produces hydrogen ions in water and a base neutralises an acid. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water and produces hydroxide ions. All alkalis are bases, but insoluble copper(II) oxide is a base without being an alkali. The pH scale indicates acidity and alkalinity: at ordinary classroom temperature, solutions below pH 7 are acidic, pH 7 is neutral and above pH 7 are alkaline. “Strong” describes the extent of ionisation, while “concentrated” describes the amount dissolved per volume; these words are not interchangeable.

Neutralisation commonly involves acid reacting with base to form a salt and water. A salt contains the positive ion from a base or metal and the negative ion associated with the acid. Hydrochloric acid forms chlorides, sulfuric acid sulfates and nitric acid nitrates. For example, hydrochloric acid plus sodium hydroxide gives sodium chloride and water. Neutralisation can release heat. It is not safe to improvise mixing concentrated acids and alkalis: laboratory work uses approved concentrations, eye protection and teacher supervision.

Acids also react with many carbonates to give a salt, water and carbon dioxide. A suitable test for carbon dioxide is that it turns limewater milky under the prescribed school procedure. Many reactive metals produce a salt and hydrogen with suitable dilute acids, but not every metal reacts this way. Copper does not release hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid under ordinary school conditions. Hydrogen is flammable, so gas tests and metal–acid reactions require supervised small-scale procedures and ignition control.

Salt preparation depends on reactant solubility. A teacher may prepare a soluble salt from an acid and an insoluble base by adding excess base, filtering off what remains and concentrating the solution to crystallise the salt. If both reactants are soluble, controlled titration is needed to find neutralising amounts without leaving excess acid or alkali; these methods are not interchangeable. Everyday applications include suitable treatment of acidic soils and the use of approved antacid medicines. These applications require appropriate quantities and context: a classroom equation alone cannot set an agricultural or medical dose.
examples: Hydrochloric acid and magnesium oxide form magnesium chloride and water: MgO + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O. Counting atoms gives Mg 1, O 1, H 2 and Cl 2 on each side.
Calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid: CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. The carbonate pattern predicts the gas; an appropriate test is needed to confirm its identity.

To obtain copper(II) sulfate crystals, a teacher can add excess copper(II) oxide to warm dilute sulfuric acid, filter away unreacted oxide and crystallise the filtrate. Filtering removes excess solid base, but it could not remove dissolved excess sodium hydroxide in an alternative mixture.
lessons.summary: In introductory aqueous chemistry, an acid produces hydrogen ions in water and a base neutralises an acid.

lessons.title: Explaining patterns across periods and down groups
objectives: Locate first-twenty elements using electron arrangements.
Explain selected group and period trends with particle ideas.
State limits of introductory periodic trends.
paragraphs: The periodic table arranges elements by increasing atomic number, so its patterns connect to proton and electron numbers. For the first twenty elements, the number of occupied electron shells gives the period. In the main groups, outer-electron counts connect to group membership: one outer electron for group 1, two for group 2, then three to eight for groups 13 to 18. Helium has two electrons in its only shell and is placed with the noble gases because that shell is full. State the numbering convention because some older tables label the main groups differently.

Across period 3, atomic number increases while electrons are added to the same main shell. Increasing positive nuclear charge generally attracts these electrons more strongly, so atomic radius generally decreases from sodium towards chlorine. Metallic character declines across the period: sodium, magnesium and aluminium are metals, silicon is commonly described as a metalloid, and phosphorus, sulfur and chlorine are non-metals. Not every physical property varies smoothly: melting points depend on structure and bonding, so they do not simply rise or fall across the whole period.

Down a group, additional occupied shells make atoms generally larger. Outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded by inner electrons. Group 1 elements readily lose one outer electron; this becomes easier down the group, so their reactions with water generally become more vigorous. These reactions are demonstrations for a trained teacher, not learner experiments. Group 17 halogens react by gaining an electron in many reactions; their reactivity generally decreases down the group because attraction for an incoming electron is less effective farther from the nucleus.

Chemical patterns support predictions when the kind of reaction is specified. Group 1 metals form +1 ions, group 2 metals form +2 ions, and halogens commonly form −1 ions. Noble gases are much less reactive in ordinary conditions because their outer shell is full, though “unreactive” should not be interpreted as impossible to react under all conditions. A trend is a general relationship drawn from evidence. Distinguish a structural explanation from an observation, and do not extend the first-twenty shell model to all elements without further rules.
examples: An atom has arrangement 2,8,2. It has three occupied shells, placing it in period 3, and two outer electrons, placing it in group 2. Its 12 electrons identify the neutral atom as magnesium.

Compare lithium, 2,1, with sodium, 2,8,1. Both have one outer electron, but sodium has an additional occupied shell. Its outer electron is farther out and more shielded, helping explain its greater reactivity with water.
An atom with 2,8,7 is in period 3 and group 17. Gaining one electron gives a full outer shell and a −1 ion. With Mg²⁺, two such chloride ions are needed, so magnesium chloride is MgCl₂.
lessons.summary: The periodic table arranges elements by increasing atomic number, so its patterns connect to proton and electron numbers.

lessons.title: Preparing and evaluating local acid–base indicators
objectives: Plan preparation of a plant-pigment indicator under supervision.
Use reference samples and controls to interpret colour changes.
Report limitations of a natural indicator.
paragraphs: An acid–base indicator is a substance whose colour changes over a particular pH range. Some leaves, flowers and fruit skins contain pigments that can serve as indicators, but not every coloured extract responds usefully to pH. A locally available purple leaf or flower can be investigated with teacher approval. Identify the plant reliably and avoid unknown, poisonous or irritating material. A plant extract is a laboratory reagent after preparation; it must not be tasted even if the original plant is normally eaten.

For a school preparation, wash the approved plant material, break it into small pieces and extract the pigment using a small measured volume of warm water under teacher direction. Filter to obtain a clearer coloured solution. Record the plant part, mass or approximate amount, solvent volume and extraction time, because changing these can change colour strength. Water extraction avoids introducing a flammable solvent, though heating and glassware still require supervision. Label the extract and prepare it freshly if storage causes fading or contamination.

Calibrate before testing unknowns. Add the same volume of indicator to equal volumes of a known dilute acidic reference, water and a known dilute alkaline reference supplied by the teacher. Record observed colours rather than assuming universal names: a given extract might be red in acid and green in alkali, but another plant may behave differently. A water sample establishes a comparison near neutral conditions, and a sample without indicator helps reveal the liquid’s own colour. Use clean droppers so that one sample does not contaminate another.

Test approved local samples in separate labelled containers and compare their colours with the references. A matching colour supports a broad classification such as acidic or alkaline; it does not give an exact pH without further calibration. Strongly coloured or cloudy samples can mask an indicator. Adding too much extract can also alter the test mixture or obscure differences. Never mix household cleaners, test unknown chemicals or infer drinking safety from indicator colour. Report ambiguous observations honestly and suggest a pH meter or a suitable standard indicator as a follow-up.
examples: A purple extract turns pink in an approved acidic reference, purple in water and green in an alkaline reference. An uncoloured sample turns pink after the same indicator volume is added. It is reasonable to classify it as acidic within the tested range, but not to assign pH 2 from colour alone.

Tube A contains 5 mL of reference acid and 1 mL of extract; tube B contains 5 mL of an unknown and 5 mL of extract. Their colours are not a fair comparison because the indicator proportion differs. Repeat using equal sample and indicator volumes.

A dark brown drink still looks brown after indicator is added. This is inconclusive, not evidence of neutrality. Compare with a no-indicator sample and use a different suitable measurement method if the original colour masks the response.
lessons.summary: An acid–base indicator is a substance whose colour changes over a particular pH range.

lessons.title: Observation, measurement and biological reports
objectives: Distinguish observations from explanations in biology.
Measure biological quantities with suitable units and sampling.
Prepare a clear report containing evidence and limitations.
paragraphs: Biology studies living organisms and their processes. Its branches include botany for plants, zoology for animals, microbiology for microscopic organisms and ecology for relationships with surroundings. These connect to chemistry through substances and reactions in cells, to physics through light and movement, and to mathematics through measurement and data analysis. Scientific terms make descriptions precise: an organism is an individual living thing, a tissue is a group of cooperating similar specialised cells, and a habitat is the place where an organism lives.

Observation records what is detected with the senses or suitable instruments; an inference proposes what it means. “The seedling leans towards the window” is an observation, while “unequal light caused its growth direction” is an explanation to test. Use counts, drawings and measurements instead of vague words where possible. Length may be measured in millimetres or centimetres, mass in grams, and temperature in degrees Celsius. Start a ruler at its zero mark, read scales consistently and report a precision supported by the instrument rather than inventing extra decimal places.

A biological investigation begins with a focused question and a testable prediction. Identify the independent variable to change, the dependent variable to measure and important conditions to control. Living samples vary, so use multiple organisms where appropriate and record a range or mean rather than treating one individual as typical. Repeated readings of the same plant can check measurement consistency, but they are not the same as testing several independent plants. Obtain permission for specimen collection, avoid damaging habitats and follow supervised handling rules for slides and biological material.

A useful report contains a title or question, purpose, prediction, materials, method, results, interpretation, conclusion and limitations. A results table gives labelled quantities and units; the discussion explains patterns without rewriting every number. A drawing from a microscope records structures actually observed, with clear outlines and labelled lines. In the conclusion, answer the original question using the evidence, then state how measurement limits, sample size or uncontrolled conditions affect confidence. A claim that no effect was detected is different from proving that an effect can never occur.
examples: Five seedling lengths are 4, 5, 5, 6 and 10 cm. Their mean is (4 + 5 + 5 + 6 + 10)/5 = 6 cm, while the range is 4–10 cm. Reporting both shows that the mean does not describe every plant.

A learner sees rectangular cell outlines in a leaf slide. The drawing should include these observed outlines, not add a clearly visible nucleus to every cell if nuclei were not resolved. A textbook expectation guides questions but cannot replace observation.

Two pots differ in both watering and light. Their growth difference cannot be attributed confidently to water alone because light is a confounding variable. A stronger design varies watering while keeping light, plant type and starting size comparable.
lessons.summary: Biology studies living organisms and their processes.

lessons.title: Testing photosynthesis requirements and reporting evidence
objectives: Interpret controlled experiments on light, carbon dioxide and chlorophyll.
Explain destarching and the starch test as indirect evidence.
Recognise confounding variables and limits of leaf investigations.
paragraphs: Photosynthesis makes organic food using light energy, carbon dioxide and water in chlorophyll-containing cells. A school starch investigation does not measure every step directly: it tests whether starch accumulated in a leaf under the investigated conditions. Before comparing treatments, a teacher may destarch suitable plants by keeping them in darkness for a prescribed period. Stored starch is used during respiration, reducing the chance that an earlier store will be mistaken for starch made during the experiment. Plant health and the species used affect how well this preparation works.

To investigate light, a teacher covers part of a leaf with an opaque material while leaving another part exposed and then places the plant in suitable light. The covered and exposed areas share much of the same leaf environment. After the approved exposure, both areas undergo the same supervised starch test. If the exposed region stains blue-black with iodine while the covered region does not, the result supports the need for light for starch accumulation in those conditions. The cover should exclude light without crushing the leaf; a damaged or overheated region creates an alternative explanation.

A variegated leaf has green and non-green regions that can be mapped before testing. Comparing their starch results can support the role of chlorophyll, provided the plant was prepared appropriately and the original colour map is retained. Carbon-dioxide investigations require a comparison between otherwise similar plants with and without an effective carbon-dioxide supply. Any absorbent chemicals and sealed chambers are managed by the teacher. Temperature, water availability, plant type and exposure duration should remain comparable; a hot sealed chamber would introduce a confounding stress.

In the starch test, a teacher first treats the leaf with hot water, removes chlorophyll using ethanol heated indirectly in a water bath, rinses the leaf as instructed and applies iodine solution. Removing green pigment makes the final colour easier to see. Ethanol is flammable and must not be heated directly over a flame. Students working independently should interpret supplied observations or prepare reports rather than perform this procedure alone. A conclusion must match the result: absence of detectable starch may reflect insufficient photosynthesis, preparation problems or rapid use of sugars, not proof that the plant never photosynthesises.
examples: A destarched leaf is half covered and exposed to light. The exposed half becomes blue-black with iodine and the covered half remains yellow-brown. Since light access differs while much of the leaf is shared, the results support light being required for starch accumulation.

Before testing a variegated leaf, a learner draws the green areas. After decolourisation and iodine, blue-black regions align with that map. This correspondence supports chlorophyll’s role; without the original map the learner could not reliably compare green and non-green tissue.

Both a carbon-dioxide-deprived plant and its control fail to show starch. The treatment effect cannot be established because the control did not demonstrate starch accumulation. Check light, preparation, leaf health and test procedure before attributing the result to carbon dioxide.
lessons.summary: Photosynthesis makes organic food using light energy, carbon dioxide and water in chlorophyll-containing cells.

lessons.title: Ruminant digestion and microbial partnerships
objectives: Trace food through the four compartments of a ruminant stomach.
Explain rumination and microbial cellulose digestion.
Compare ruminant and human digestion without confusing absorption with egestion.
paragraphs: A ruminant such as a cow, goat or sheep feeds on plant material containing much cellulose in cell walls. Mammals do not produce their own cellulase enzymes in sufficient form to digest this cellulose directly. Ruminants gain access to its energy through a partnership with microorganisms in a specialised digestive system. Their stomach has four compartments called the rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum; this is one multi-compartment stomach rather than four independent stomachs. Teeth, jaws, saliva and gut movements also contribute to processing the food.

After initial chewing and swallowing, food enters the fore-stomach compartments, especially the rumen and reticulum. The rumen provides a warm, moist environment where microbes ferment plant material without free oxygen. They produce substances, including volatile fatty acids, that can be absorbed and used by the animal. The microbes obtain habitat and food in return. Gas is also produced during fermentation and normally leaves by eructation. This explanation concerns normal digestion and should not be used to diagnose or treat an animal with abdominal swelling.

Rumination returns a portion of partly processed food, called cud, to the mouth. The animal chews it again and swallows it, reducing particle size and exposing more surface for microbial action. Material subsequently passes through the omasum, where further handling and absorption of water and some dissolved substances occur, to the abomasum, which secretes acid and digestive enzymes. Microbial cells can themselves become a source of nutrients after they pass onward and are digested. Much further digestion and nutrient absorption takes place in the small intestine.

Human and ruminant systems share ingestion, muscular movement, chemical digestion, absorption and egestion, but differ in their treatment of fibrous food. Humans have a single-chambered stomach and cannot obtain energy from grass in the same way as a cow. Dietary fibre still supports normal bowel function in humans. Absorption transfers digested nutrients across the intestinal wall into internal transport systems; egestion expels undigested material as faeces. Excretion instead removes metabolic wastes such as urea, so these processes should not be treated as synonyms.
examples: A cow swallows grass, later brings cud to the mouth and chews again. This second chewing is rumination, not vomiting caused by illness in the normal description. It makes particles smaller and increases access for microbial enzymes.

In a comparison, both a person and a goat eat a cellulose-rich plant. The goat’s fore-stomach microbes ferment much of the cellulose; the human lacks this extensive fore-stomach system. The same plant material therefore need not provide the same usable energy to both.

An arrow sequence for a simplified account is mouth → oesophagus → rumen/reticulum → omasum → abomasum → small intestine → large intestine. A return arrow from rumen/reticulum to mouth represents cud chewing, not a separate route for absorbed nutrients.
lessons.summary: A ruminant such as a cow, goat or sheep feeds on plant material containing much cellulose in cell walls.

lessons.title: Breathing and gaseous exchange in mammals
objectives: Trace air through the respiratory system.
Explain ventilation using volume and pressure changes.
Relate alveolar features to diffusion into and out of blood.
paragraphs: Air enters the mammalian respiratory system through the nose or mouth and passes through the pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and smaller bronchioles to the alveoli. Nasal passages help warm, moisten and filter incoming air. Rings of cartilage help keep the trachea and major bronchi open. Mucus traps many particles and cilia move the mucus towards the throat for removal. These defences reduce exposure of delicate exchange surfaces, but they do not make inhaled smoke or dust harmless.

Ventilation is the bulk movement of air into and out of the lungs. During normal inspiration the diaphragm contracts and flattens, while external intercostal muscles help raise the ribs. The thoracic volume increases and pressure within the lungs falls slightly below atmospheric pressure, so air moves inward. The lungs expand with the chest through their mechanical connection to the chest wall via the pleural arrangement. They do not actively pull air in by contracting their own muscles.

During quiet expiration the inspiratory muscles relax, the diaphragm returns towards its domed shape and elastic recoil reduces lung volume. Pressure within the lungs rises slightly above atmospheric pressure and air moves out. Forceful expiration can involve additional muscles, so the description of quiet breathing does not cover every breathing situation. Airflow responds to pressure differences. The amount and rate of ventilation can change with activity, but neither a fast breathing rate nor a large breath alone specifies exactly how much oxygen reaches body tissues.

Gaseous exchange occurs mainly across alveolar and capillary walls by diffusion. Oxygen has a higher partial pressure in alveolar air than in arriving blood and moves into the blood; carbon dioxide moves in the opposite direction. Numerous alveoli provide a large area, thin walls give a short diffusion path, moisture allows gases to dissolve, and blood flow plus ventilation maintain the gradients. Ventilation supplies fresh air, gaseous exchange transfers gases across surfaces, and cellular respiration releases usable energy in cells. These related processes should be distinguished.
examples: On inspiration, an increase in chest volume lowers lung air pressure relative to outside air. Air therefore flows down the pressure difference into the lungs. “The lungs suck because oxygen is needed” gives a purpose without the physical mechanism.

A model with two balloons inside a bottle and a rubber sheet at its base can show that moving the sheet down increases enclosed volume and inflates the balloons. Its limitations include a rigid bottle instead of moving ribs and a flat sheet instead of a domed diaphragm.

If the alveolar surface becomes thicker, diffusion has a longer path. Even with air entering the lungs, gas transfer can become less effective. This shows why ventilation and exchange are separate steps; the explanation is educational rather than a diagnosis.
lessons.summary: Air enters the mammalian respiratory system through the nose or mouth and passes through the pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and smaller bronchioles to the alveoli.

lessons.title: Aerobic and anaerobic respiration: evidence and investigations
