questions.content: A compound has empirical formula HO and relative molecular mass 34. Find its molecular formula.
questions.markingGuide: Empirical mass = 17; multiplier = 2; H₂O₂.

questions.content: Explain why percentage composition alone cannot give a unique molecular formula.
questions.answerKey: Different whole-number multiples of the empirical formula have the same composition percentages.
questions.markingGuide: Different whole-number multiples of the empirical formula have the same composition percentages.

questions.content: For a 100 g sample, convert 75% carbon and 25% hydrogen into masses.
questions.markingGuide: 75 g C and 25 g H.

questions.content: Find the empirical formula of a substance with 75% C and 25% H. Use C = 12, H = 1.
Is C₂H₂ the simplest formula for acetylene? Give its empirical formula.
questions.answerKey: No. Both subscripts divide by 2, so CH.
questions.markingGuide: No. Both subscripts divide by 2, so CH.

questions.content: A calculated multiplier is 3.99. What whole number is likely, assuming rounded input data?
questions.answerKey: 4, provided the discrepancy is consistent with the precision of the supplied data.
questions.markingGuide: 4, provided the discrepancy is consistent with the precision of the supplied data.

questions.content: Why would a molecular-formula multiplier of exactly 0.5 indicate an error?
questions.answerKey: A molecular formula contains a whole-number multiple of its empirical unit, so the multiplier cannot be less than 1.
questions.markingGuide: A molecular formula contains a whole-number multiple of its empirical unit, so the multiplier cannot be less than 1.

questions.content: Work through a full calculation for 4.8 g Mg combined with 3.2 g O, using Mg = 24 and O = 16. Present masses, divisions, simplest ratio and formula in a table.
Diagnose this solution: “A compound is 27.3% C and 72.7% O, so its atom ratio is 27.3:72.7.” Use C = 12 and O = 16 to correct it.
questions.answerKey: Mass percentages are not atom ratios. 27.3/12 = 2.275 and 72.7/16 = 4.54375; dividing by 2.275 gives approximately 1:2, so the empirical formula is CO₂ within the precision of the data.
questions.markingGuide: Mass percentages are not atom ratios. 27.3/12 = 2.275 and 72.7/16 = 4.54375; dividing by 2.275 gives approximately 1:2, so the empirical formula is CO₂ within the precision of the data.

questions.content: A fictional molecular compound has empirical formula CH, relative molecular mass 78, and C = 12, H = 1. Calculate its molecular formula and verify its relative molecular mass.
questions.answerKey: Empirical mass = 13; 78/13 = 6; molecular formula C₆H₆. Check: 6(12) + 6(1) = 78.
questions.markingGuide: Empirical mass = 13; 78/13 = 6; molecular formula C₆H₆. Check: 6(12) + 6(1) = 78.

questions.content: Explain the difference between a base and an alkali.
questions.answerKey: A base neutralises acid; an alkali is a base soluble in water that produces hydroxide ions.
questions.markingGuide: A base neutralises acid; an alkali is a base soluble in water that produces hydroxide ions.

questions.content: Classify solutions at pH 3, 7 and 11 at ordinary classroom temperature.
questions.markingGuide: Acidic, neutral and alkaline respectively.

questions.content: Name the salt formed by hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide.
questions.markingGuide: Sodium chloride.

questions.content: Give the general word products of acid plus carbonate.
questions.markingGuide: Salt, water and carbon dioxide.

questions.content: Give the general products of a suitable reactive metal with dilute hydrochloric acid.
questions.markingGuide: A metal chloride and hydrogen.

questions.content: Complete and balance: Mg + HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂.
questions.markingGuide: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂.

questions.content: Name the salt formed from sulfuric acid and magnesium oxide.
questions.markingGuide: Magnesium sulfate.

questions.content: Why is insoluble copper(II) oxide called a base but not an alkali?
questions.answerKey: It neutralises acid but is not water-soluble.
questions.markingGuide: It neutralises acid but is not water-soluble.

questions.content: State a school test for carbon dioxide.
questions.answerKey: It turns limewater milky when passed through it in a supervised test.
questions.markingGuide: It turns limewater milky when passed through it in a supervised test.

questions.content: Why must hydrogen-producing reactions be kept away from uncontrolled ignition sources?
questions.answerKey: Hydrogen is flammable and can form an explosive mixture with air.
questions.markingGuide: Hydrogen is flammable and can form an explosive mixture with air.

questions.content: Does a concentrated acid have to be a strong acid? Explain.
questions.answerKey: No. Concentration concerns amount per volume; strength concerns extent of ionisation.
questions.markingGuide: No. Concentration concerns amount per volume; strength concerns extent of ionisation.

questions.content: Why add excess insoluble base during some salt preparations?
questions.answerKey: To use up the acid; unreacted solid base can then be removed by filtration.
questions.markingGuide: To use up the acid; unreacted solid base can then be removed by filtration.

questions.content: Why cannot filtration remove excess dissolved alkali?
questions.answerKey: Dissolved ions pass through the filter with the solution.
questions.markingGuide: Dissolved ions pass through the filter with the solution.

questions.content: Balance NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + H₂O.
questions.markingGuide: 2NaOH + H₂SO₄ → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O.

questions.content: Explain why “neutralise acidic soil” is not enough information to choose a lime quantity.
questions.answerKey: The soil condition, suitable material and required amount need measurement and agricultural guidance.
questions.markingGuide: The soil condition, suitable material and required amount need measurement and agricultural guidance.

questions.content: Make a reaction-pattern table for acid + oxide base, acid + carbonate and acid + suitable reactive metal. Include products and one balanced example for each.
questions.answerKey: Base: salt + water, MgO + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O. Carbonate: salt + water + CO₂, CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. Metal: salt + H₂, Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂.
questions.markingGuide: Base: salt + water, MgO + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O. Carbonate: salt + water + CO₂, CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. Metal: salt + H₂, Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂.

questions.content: Write a teacher-supervised plan to obtain a soluble salt from an acid and an insoluble base. Explain the purpose of excess base, filtration and crystallisation.
questions.answerKey: Use approved dilute reactants; add insoluble base until some remains, showing acid has been consumed; filter to remove excess solid; concentrate gently and cool to form crystals; separate and dry as instructed. Protect eyes and avoid heating to dryness.
questions.markingGuide: Use approved dilute reactants; add insoluble base until some remains, showing acid has been consumed; filter to remove excess solid; concentrate gently and cool to form crystals; separate and dry as instructed. Protect eyes and avoid heating to dryness.

questions.content: Evaluate the claim “All acids react with all metals to release hydrogen.” Use a counterexample and explain why prediction needs conditions.
questions.answerKey: The claim is too broad. Copper does not release hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid under ordinary school conditions. Metal reactivity, acid identity and concentration affect behaviour, so the restricted reactive-metal pattern must be stated.
questions.markingGuide: The claim is too broad. Copper does not release hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid under ordinary school conditions. Metal reactivity, acid identity and concentration affect behaviour, so the restricted reactive-metal pattern must be stated.

questions.content: Locate an element with electron arrangement 2,8,1 by period and group.
questions.markingGuide: Period 3, group 1.

questions.content: Locate an element with arrangement 2,6.
questions.markingGuide: Period 2, group 16.

questions.content: Which of 2,1 and 2,8,1 has more occupied shells?
Explain the general increase in atomic size down a group.
questions.answerKey: Additional occupied shells place outer electrons farther from the nucleus.
questions.markingGuide: Additional occupied shells place outer electrons farther from the nucleus.

questions.content: State the general trend in group 1 reactivity down the group.
questions.markingGuide: It increases.

questions.content: Explain the group 1 trend using outer electrons.
questions.answerKey: The outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is more easily lost.
questions.markingGuide: The outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is more easily lost.

questions.content: State the general trend in halogen reactivity down group 17.
questions.markingGuide: It decreases.

questions.content: Explain why chlorine commonly forms Cl⁻ rather than Cl²⁻ in introductory reactions.
questions.answerKey: It needs one electron to complete its outer shell.
questions.markingGuide: It needs one electron to complete its outer shell.

questions.content: Why is helium in group 18 despite having only two electrons?
questions.answerKey: Its first and only shell is full, giving noble-gas-like low reactivity.
questions.markingGuide: Its first and only shell is full, giving noble-gas-like low reactivity.

questions.content: State the general atomic-radius trend across period 3 from sodium to chlorine.
questions.markingGuide: Radius generally decreases.

questions.content: Explain the trend across period 3.
questions.answerKey: Increasing nuclear charge attracts electrons in the same main shell more strongly.
questions.markingGuide: Increasing nuclear charge attracts electrons in the same main shell more strongly.

questions.content: Does melting point decrease smoothly across period 3? Explain.
questions.answerKey: No. Different structures and bonding lead to a non-uniform pattern.
questions.markingGuide: No. Different structures and bonding lead to a non-uniform pattern.

questions.content: Predict the ion formed by a group 2 metal.
questions.answerKey: A 2+ ion, formed by losing two outer electrons.
questions.markingGuide: A 2+ ion, formed by losing two outer electrons.

questions.content: Why must a reactivity comparison name the reaction being compared?
questions.answerKey: Different reactions and conditions can give different behaviours; an undefined reactivity label is insufficient.
questions.markingGuide: Different reactions and conditions can give different behaviours; an undefined reactivity label is insufficient.

questions.content: Compare the metallic character of sodium and chlorine.
questions.answerKey: Sodium is a metal; chlorine is a non-metal, consistent with decreasing metallic character across period 3.
questions.markingGuide: Sodium is a metal; chlorine is a non-metal, consistent with decreasing metallic character across period 3.

questions.content: Create a table giving total electrons, period and modern group number for 2,2; 2,8,3; 2,8,8; and 2,8,8,2.
questions.answerKey: 2,2: 4 electrons, period 2, group 2. 2,8,3: 13, period 3, group 13. 2,8,8: 18, period 3, group 18. 2,8,8,2: 20, period 4, group 2.
questions.markingGuide: 2,2: 4 electrons, period 2, group 2. 2,8,3: 13, period 3, group 13. 2,8,8: 18, period 3, group 18. 2,8,8,2: 20, period 4, group 2.

questions.content: Write two linked explanations: why group 1 atoms get larger down the group and why this helps them lose their outer electron. Include shielding.
questions.answerKey: Added shells increase radius and inner-electron shielding. The outer electron experiences less effective attraction and is more easily removed, contributing to increasing group 1 reactivity in comparable reactions.
questions.markingGuide: Added shells increase radius and inner-electron shielding. The outer electron experiences less effective attraction and is more easily removed, contributing to increasing group 1 reactivity in comparable reactions.

questions.content: A learner predicts that every property decreases steadily from sodium to argon. Critique the prediction and specify one property that approximately follows a trend and one that requires structural evidence.
questions.answerKey: The claim is too broad. Atomic radius generally decreases towards chlorine, but melting point changes non-uniformly because bonding and structure vary. Noble-gas size comparisons also depend on the radius definition used.
questions.markingGuide: The claim is too broad. Atomic radius generally decreases towards chlorine, but melting point changes non-uniformly because bonding and structure vary. Noble-gas size comparisons also depend on the radius definition used.

questions.content: Why must a plant extract be tested on reference solutions first?
questions.answerKey: Its colour response is not known until compared with known acidity or alkalinity.
questions.markingGuide: Its colour response is not known until compared with known acidity or alkalinity.

questions.content: Give two details to record during extraction.
questions.answerKey: Plant part and solvent volume; amount of material, extraction time and temperature are also valid.
questions.markingGuide: Plant part and solvent volume; amount of material, extraction time and temperature are also valid.

questions.content: Why filter the extract?
questions.answerKey: To remove solid plant fragments and make colour observations clearer.
questions.markingGuide: To remove solid plant fragments and make colour observations clearer.

questions.content: State a reason to prepare indicator freshly.
questions.answerKey: Pigments may fade, change or become contaminated during storage.
questions.markingGuide: Pigments may fade, change or become contaminated during storage.

questions.content: Why should all test tubes receive the same indicator volume?
questions.answerKey: To make colour intensity and the indicator’s influence comparable.
questions.markingGuide: To make colour intensity and the indicator’s influence comparable.

questions.content: What does a no-indicator sample reveal?
questions.answerKey: The original colour or cloudiness of the tested liquid.
questions.markingGuide: The original colour or cloudiness of the tested liquid.

questions.content: Can one colour reading give an exact pH without calibration? Explain.
questions.answerKey: No. The colour response must be linked to known pH references and may cover a range.
questions.markingGuide: No. The colour response must be linked to known pH references and may cover a range.

questions.content: A known acid gives red and a known alkali gives blue. An unknown gives red. State a justified conclusion.
questions.answerKey: The unknown is acidic within the indicator’s tested response range; an exact pH is not established.
questions.markingGuide: The unknown is acidic within the indicator’s tested response range; an exact pH is not established.

questions.content: Why are separate clean droppers useful?
questions.answerKey: They reduce cross-contamination that could alter sample pH or colour.
questions.markingGuide: They reduce cross-contamination that could alter sample pH or colour.

questions.content: Explain why a brown sample that stays brown is not proved neutral.
questions.answerKey: Its own colour may mask the indicator response.
questions.markingGuide: Its own colour may mask the indicator response.

questions.content: Name an appropriate follow-up method for an ambiguous natural-indicator result.
questions.answerKey: A suitable calibrated pH meter or standard indicator.
questions.markingGuide: A suitable calibrated pH meter or standard indicator.

questions.content: Why should household cleaners never be mixed during this activity?
questions.answerKey: Mixtures can react dangerously and release harmful gases or heat.
questions.markingGuide: Mixtures can react dangerously and release harmful gases or heat.

questions.content: What is the role of a water comparison tube?
questions.answerKey: It shows the indicator colour in a reference near neutral conditions.
questions.markingGuide: It shows the indicator colour in a reference near neutral conditions.

questions.content: Does an acidic colour establish that a sample is safe to drink?
questions.answerKey: No. Acidity classification does not test pathogens or toxic contaminants.
questions.markingGuide: No. Acidity classification does not test pathogens or toxic contaminants.

questions.content: Identify the independent and dependent variables in comparing approved samples using one extract.
questions.answerKey: Independent: sample identity. Dependent: observed indicator colour.
questions.markingGuide: Independent: sample identity. Dependent: observed indicator colour.

questions.content: Design a results table for three references and four unknown samples. Include columns that allow original sample colour to be distinguished from final indicator colour.
questions.answerKey: Use columns for sample label, reference status, original colour, sample volume, indicator volume, final colour and interpretation. Record actual observations and mark ambiguous results as inconclusive.
questions.markingGuide: Use columns for sample label, reference status, original colour, sample volume, indicator volume, final colour and interpretation. Record actual observations and mark ambiguous results as inconclusive.

questions.content: Critique this method: “Use any flower, add different amounts of extract to each cleaner, mix the cleaners together and decide the safest one by colour.” Write four corrections.
questions.answerKey: Use identified approved non-hazardous plant material; calibrate on known references; use equal measured amounts in separate tubes; never mix cleaners; do not infer overall safety from pH colour. Any four well-explained corrections earn credit.
questions.markingGuide: Use identified approved non-hazardous plant material; calibrate on known references; use equal measured amounts in separate tubes; never mix cleaners; do not infer overall safety from pH colour. Any four well-explained corrections earn credit.

questions.content: Use this supplied calibration: acid = pink, water = purple, alkali = green. Sample P becomes pink, Q green and dark R remains brown. Report conclusions and one limitation.
questions.answerKey: P is acidic and Q alkaline within the tested response range. R is inconclusive because its colour may mask the indicator. No exact pH is justified from these three references alone.
questions.markingGuide: P is acidic and Q alkaline within the tested response range. R is inconclusive because its colour may mask the indicator. No exact pH is justified from these three references alone.

questions.content: Name the branch that studies plants.
questions.markingGuide: Botany.

questions.content: Distinguish an organism from a tissue.
questions.answerKey: An organism is an individual living thing; a tissue is a group of cooperating similar specialised cells.
questions.markingGuide: An organism is an individual living thing; a tissue is a group of cooperating similar specialised cells.

questions.content: Classify “three roots are visible” as observation or inference.
questions.markingGuide: Observation.

questions.content: Classify “the plant grew poorly because it lacked nitrate” as observation or inference.
questions.markingGuide: Inference or proposed explanation.

questions.content: Give an appropriate unit for the length of a small root.
questions.markingGuide: Millimetres or centimetres.

questions.content: Why must a ruler be aligned with its zero mark?
questions.answerKey: Starting elsewhere gives an offset error unless that offset is accounted for.
questions.markingGuide: Starting elsewhere gives an offset error unless that offset is accounted for.

questions.content: Define an independent variable.
questions.answerKey: The factor deliberately changed in an investigation.
questions.markingGuide: The factor deliberately changed in an investigation.

questions.content: Define a dependent variable.
questions.markingGuide: The response measured or observed.

questions.content: State two controls in a test of watering volume on seedling growth.
questions.answerKey: Plant species and light conditions; starting size, soil and duration are also valid.
questions.markingGuide: Plant species and light conditions; starting size, soil and duration are also valid.

questions.content: Calculate the mean of 3, 4, 5 and 8 leaves per plant.
questions.markingGuide: (3 + 4 + 5 + 8)/4 = 5 leaves per plant.

questions.content: Why investigate several plants rather than one?
questions.answerKey: Plants vary naturally, so several independent samples give a better indication of the response and variability.
questions.markingGuide: Plants vary naturally, so several independent samples give a better indication of the response and variability.

questions.content: Why is measuring one plant five times not equivalent to measuring five plants?
questions.answerKey: The repeated readings assess one individual; they do not capture variation between independent plants.
questions.markingGuide: The repeated readings assess one individual; they do not capture variation between independent plants.

questions.content: Name two features of a clear results table.
questions.answerKey: Descriptive column headings and units; consistent recording and sample labels are also suitable.
questions.markingGuide: Descriptive column headings and units; consistent recording and sample labels are also suitable.

questions.content: What should a microscope drawing show when a structure is not resolved?
questions.answerKey: Only structures actually observed; do not invent an unseen structure.
questions.markingGuide: Only structures actually observed; do not invent an unseen structure.

questions.content: Why should a conclusion mention sample size or uncontrolled conditions?
questions.answerKey: They affect how confidently the results can support or generalise the explanation.
questions.markingGuide: They affect how confidently the results can support or generalise the explanation.

questions.content: Draft a report framework for a microscope observation. Include purpose, preparation and viewing method, results, interpretation and limitations without claiming structures not seen.
questions.answerKey: Purpose: observe the cells in the approved specimen. Method: prepare or use a supervised slide, start at low power and focus safely. Results: labelled drawing of visible features with magnification. Interpretation: compare observed structures with suitable references. Limitations: resolution, staining, sample condition or field of view.
questions.markingGuide: Purpose: observe the cells in the approved specimen. Method: prepare or use a supervised slide, start at low power and focus safely. Results: labelled drawing of visible features with magnification. Interpretation: compare observed structures with suitable references. Limitations: resolution, staining, sample condition or field of view.

questions.content: Two seedling groups receive different water volumes but the wetter group also receives more light. Identify the problem and redesign the study with independent samples and a measurable outcome.
questions.answerKey: Water and light are confounded. Use comparable seedlings randomly allocated to watering groups, keep light and other conditions similar, measure height change over the same period, and use multiple independent plants per group.
questions.markingGuide: Water and light are confounded. Use comparable seedlings randomly allocated to watering groups, keep light and other conditions similar, measure height change over the same period, and use multiple independent plants per group.

questions.content: Prepare a numerical results statement from these four root lengths: 12, 14, 13 and 17 mm. Calculate the mean and range, then write a cautious conclusion about typical length.
questions.answerKey: Mean = 56/4 = 14 mm; minimum–maximum range = 12–17 mm, spread = 5 mm. These four roots averaged 14 mm, with observed variation; the small sample does not establish the length of all roots.
questions.markingGuide: Mean = 56/4 = 14 mm; minimum–maximum range = 12–17 mm, spread = 5 mm. These four roots averaged 14 mm, with observed variation; the small sample does not establish the length of all roots.

questions.content: Why destarch a plant before some photosynthesis experiments?
questions.answerKey: To reduce pre-existing starch so newly detected starch is more closely linked to the experiment.
questions.markingGuide: To reduce pre-existing starch so newly detected starch is more closely linked to the experiment.

questions.content: What colour indicates starch in the iodine test?
questions.markingGuide: Blue-black.

questions.content: Why remove chlorophyll before judging the iodine colour?
questions.answerKey: The green pigment can mask the test colour.
questions.markingGuide: The green pigment can mask the test colour.

questions.content: Why must ethanol not be heated over a flame?
questions.answerKey: It is flammable and its vapour can ignite.
questions.markingGuide: It is flammable and its vapour can ignite.

questions.content: What is the changed variable in a half-covered leaf experiment?
questions.markingGuide: Access to light.

questions.content: Name two conditions to keep comparable in a carbon-dioxide experiment.
questions.answerKey: Light and temperature; water supply, species and duration are also valid.
questions.markingGuide: Light and temperature; water supply, species and duration are also valid.

questions.content: Why map the green regions of a variegated leaf before decolourisation?
questions.answerKey: The map preserves the original chlorophyll distribution for comparison with starch results.
questions.markingGuide: The map preserves the original chlorophyll distribution for comparison with starch results.

questions.content: What conclusion is supported if only illuminated leaf regions contain detectable starch?
questions.answerKey: Light was required for starch accumulation in the tested conditions.
questions.markingGuide: Light was required for starch accumulation in the tested conditions.

questions.content: Why should a leaf cover avoid crushing the tissue?
questions.answerKey: Damage could prevent normal activity and confound the effect of excluding light.
questions.markingGuide: Damage could prevent normal activity and confound the effect of excluding light.

questions.content: Does the starch test directly measure the instantaneous photosynthesis rate? Explain.
questions.answerKey: No. It detects accumulated starch after a period and is influenced by storage and use.
questions.markingGuide: No. It detects accumulated starch after a period and is influenced by storage and use.

questions.content: Why is a comparison plant needed in a carbon-dioxide investigation?
questions.answerKey: It shows what happens with normal carbon-dioxide availability under otherwise similar conditions.
questions.markingGuide: It shows what happens with normal carbon-dioxide availability under otherwise similar conditions.

questions.content: Both treatment and control lack starch. Why is the treatment conclusion weak?
questions.answerKey: The control failed to show expected accumulation, so another condition or procedural problem may explain both results.
questions.markingGuide: The control failed to show expected accumulation, so another condition or procedural problem may explain both results.

questions.content: Why can leaving a plant in darkness affect starch stores?
questions.answerKey: Respiration and other uses continue while photosynthesis cannot replenish them.
questions.markingGuide: Respiration and other uses continue while photosynthesis cannot replenish them.

questions.content: Name one way a sealed chamber can confound a photosynthesis investigation.
questions.answerKey: It may raise temperature or alter water conditions as well as carbon dioxide.
questions.markingGuide: It may raise temperature or alter water conditions as well as carbon dioxide.

questions.content: Explain why a negative starch result does not prove a leaf never photosynthesises.
questions.answerKey: Starch may not have accumulated above detection, or preparation and testing may have failed.
questions.markingGuide: Starch may not have accumulated above detection, or preparation and testing may have failed.

questions.content: Draw a paper plan of a half-covered leaf investigation. Annotate independent variable, comparison area, measurements, two controls and supervised starch-test precautions.
questions.answerKey: Independent variable: light access; compare covered and exposed areas. Map the cover and record final iodine colours. Keep leaf identity, exposure time and plant water conditions comparable. Teacher handles hot water and ethanol using an indirect bath away from ignition.
questions.markingGuide: Independent variable: light access; compare covered and exposed areas. Map the cover and record final iodine colours. Keep leaf identity, exposure time and plant water conditions comparable. Teacher handles hot water and ethanol using an indirect bath away from ignition.

questions.content: Analyse this supplied result: green illuminated area blue-black; non-green illuminated area yellow-brown; green covered area yellow-brown. Explain what each comparison supports and identify a limitation.
questions.answerKey: Green illuminated versus green covered supports a light requirement. Green versus non-green illuminated regions supports chlorophyll’s role. Starch accumulation is indirect evidence and tissue differences, preparation or detection limits may affect interpretation.
questions.markingGuide: Green illuminated versus green covered supports a light requirement. Green versus non-green illuminated regions supports chlorophyll’s role. Starch accumulation is indirect evidence and tissue differences, preparation or detection limits may affect interpretation.

questions.content: Write a five-sentence investigation report using these observations: prepared plants A and B were equally watered and illuminated; A had carbon dioxide available, B had it removed by a teacher-controlled method; only A tested positive for starch.
questions.answerKey: Purpose: investigate carbon-dioxide availability. The prepared plants were treated alike except for carbon dioxide. Results: A contained detectable starch and B did not. This supports carbon dioxide being needed for starch accumulation under the tested conditions. Confidence depends on equal plant health, effective carbon-dioxide control and a reliable starch-test method.
questions.markingGuide: Purpose: investigate carbon-dioxide availability. The prepared plants were treated alike except for carbon dioxide. Results: A contained detectable starch and B did not. This supports carbon dioxide being needed for starch accumulation under the tested conditions. Confidence depends on equal plant health, effective carbon-dioxide control and a reliable starch-test method.

questions.content: Name two ruminant animals.
questions.answerKey: Cow and goat; sheep is also acceptable.
questions.markingGuide: Cow and goat; sheep is also acceptable.

questions.content: List the four ruminant stomach compartments.
questions.markingGuide: Rumen, reticulum, omasum and abomasum.

questions.content: What is cud?
questions.answerKey: Partly processed food returned to the mouth for rechewing.
questions.markingGuide: Partly processed food returned to the mouth for rechewing.

questions.content: Explain one benefit of rechewing food.
questions.answerKey: It reduces particle size and increases surface area accessible to microbial action.
questions.markingGuide: It reduces particle size and increases surface area accessible to microbial action.

questions.content: What structural plant substance do rumen microbes help digest?
questions.markingGuide: Cellulose.

questions.content: Why can a cow use grass more effectively than a human?
questions.answerKey: Its specialised fore-stomach microbes ferment cellulose and produce absorbable useful substances.
questions.markingGuide: Its specialised fore-stomach microbes ferment cellulose and produce absorbable useful substances.

questions.content: State one benefit to microbes in the rumen partnership.
questions.answerKey: They obtain a suitable habitat and a supply of food.
questions.markingGuide: They obtain a suitable habitat and a supply of food.

questions.content: State one benefit to the ruminant from microbial fermentation.
questions.answerKey: It gains absorbable products such as volatile fatty acids from fibrous plant material.
questions.markingGuide: It gains absorbable products such as volatile fatty acids from fibrous plant material.

questions.content: Which stomach compartment secretes acid and digestive enzymes?
questions.markingGuide: The abomasum.

questions.content: Give one role of the omasum.
questions.answerKey: Absorption of water and some dissolved substances, or further processing of ingesta.
questions.markingGuide: Absorption of water and some dissolved substances, or further processing of ingesta.

questions.content: Do rumen microbes require free oxygen for their fermentation?
questions.answerKey: No; this fermentation occurs under anaerobic conditions.
questions.markingGuide: No; this fermentation occurs under anaerobic conditions.

questions.content: Distinguish absorption from egestion.
questions.answerKey: Absorption moves nutrients through the gut wall into internal transport; egestion removes undigested material as faeces.
questions.markingGuide: Absorption moves nutrients through the gut wall into internal transport; egestion removes undigested material as faeces.

questions.content: Why is faeces removal not simply called excretion?
questions.answerKey: Excretion concerns metabolic waste, while faeces mainly contain undigested material and other gut contents.
questions.markingGuide: Excretion concerns metabolic waste, while faeces mainly contain undigested material and other gut contents.

questions.content: Where does much nutrient absorption take place after stomach processing?
questions.markingGuide: The small intestine.

questions.content: Why is “a cow has four separate stomachs” an imprecise description?
questions.answerKey: It has one stomach divided into four specialised compartments.
questions.markingGuide: It has one stomach divided into four specialised compartments.

questions.content: Make an annotated flow diagram for ruminant digestion including a cud-return arrow, the four stomach compartments and the small intestine. Add the principal process at each stage.
questions.answerKey: Mouth: chewing; rumen/reticulum: microbial processing and cud formation; return arrow to mouth: rumination; omasum: further processing and water absorption; abomasum: acid and enzyme action; small intestine: further digestion and nutrient absorption.
questions.markingGuide: Mouth: chewing; rumen/reticulum: microbial processing and cud formation; return arrow to mouth: rumination; omasum: further processing and water absorption; abomasum: acid and enzyme action; small intestine: further digestion and nutrient absorption.

questions.content: Construct a comparison table for human and cow digestion using stomach structure, cellulose digestion, role of microbes and nutrient absorption.
questions.answerKey: Human: single-chamber stomach, no extensive fore-stomach cellulose fermentation, gut microbes present but no rumen, much nutrient absorption in small intestine. Cow: four-compartment stomach, extensive microbial cellulose fermentation in rumen, useful fermentation products absorbed there and further nutrients absorbed later.
questions.markingGuide: Human: single-chamber stomach, no extensive fore-stomach cellulose fermentation, gut microbes present but no rumen, much nutrient absorption in small intestine. Cow: four-compartment stomach, extensive microbial cellulose fermentation in rumen, useful fermentation products absorbed there and further nutrients absorbed later.

questions.content: Explain a cause-and-effect chain from repeated chewing to improved use of fibrous food. Include particle size, surface area, microbial enzymes and absorption.
questions.answerKey: Repeated chewing makes smaller particles, increasing accessible surface. Microbial enzymes act on plant material during fermentation, releasing or producing useful substances. Absorbable fermentation products cross the gut wall and can be used by the animal.
questions.markingGuide: Repeated chewing makes smaller particles, increasing accessible surface. Microbial enzymes act on plant material during fermentation, releasing or producing useful substances. Absorbable fermentation products cross the gut wall and can be used by the animal.

questions.content: Put these in air-entry order: bronchioles, trachea, alveoli, bronchi.
questions.markingGuide: Trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli.

questions.content: State one function of nasal passages.
questions.answerKey: Warming, moistening or filtering incoming air.
questions.markingGuide: Warming, moistening or filtering incoming air.

questions.content: Why does the trachea need supportive cartilage?
questions.answerKey: To help keep the airway open during pressure changes.
questions.markingGuide: To help keep the airway open during pressure changes.

questions.content: State how mucus and cilia work together.
questions.answerKey: Mucus traps particles and cilia move the mucus towards the throat.
questions.markingGuide: Mucus traps particles and cilia move the mucus towards the throat.

questions.content: What happens to the diaphragm during normal inspiration?
questions.markingGuide: It contracts and flattens.

questions.content: Explain the pressure change that causes air to enter during inspiration.
questions.answerKey: Increased thoracic and lung volume lowers lung pressure below atmospheric pressure, causing inward airflow.
questions.markingGuide: Increased thoracic and lung volume lowers lung pressure below atmospheric pressure, causing inward airflow.

questions.content: What causes quiet expiration?
questions.answerKey: Relaxation of inspiratory muscles and elastic recoil reduce volume, increasing lung pressure and moving air out.
questions.markingGuide: Relaxation of inspiratory muscles and elastic recoil reduce volume, increasing lung pressure and moving air out.

questions.content: Does a lung inflate because it has its own contracting muscles? Explain.
questions.answerKey: No. Chest movements and the pleural mechanical connection expand the lungs.
questions.markingGuide: No. Chest movements and the pleural mechanical connection expand the lungs.

questions.content: Name the process moving oxygen across the alveolar wall.
questions.markingGuide: Diffusion.

questions.content: State the direction of carbon-dioxide movement at the alveoli.
questions.answerKey: From arriving blood into alveolar air.
questions.markingGuide: From arriving blood into alveolar air.

questions.content: Explain why many alveoli improve exchange.
questions.answerKey: They provide a large total surface area for diffusion.
questions.markingGuide: They provide a large total surface area for diffusion.

questions.content: Explain why thin exchange walls matter.
questions.answerKey: They give a short diffusion distance.
questions.markingGuide: They give a short diffusion distance.

questions.content: How does blood flow help maintain oxygen exchange?
questions.answerKey: It brings lower-oxygen blood and carries oxygenated blood away, maintaining the gradient.
questions.markingGuide: It brings lower-oxygen blood and carries oxygenated blood away, maintaining the gradient.

questions.content: Distinguish ventilation from cellular respiration.
questions.answerKey: Ventilation moves air in and out; cellular respiration releases usable energy from food in cells.
questions.markingGuide: Ventilation moves air in and out; cellular respiration releases usable energy from food in cells.

questions.content: Give one limitation of a bottle-and-balloon breathing model.
questions.answerKey: A rigid bottle does not model rib movement, or the flat sheet does not represent the diaphragm’s domed shape.
questions.markingGuide: A rigid bottle does not model rib movement, or the flat sheet does not represent the diaphragm’s domed shape.

questions.content: Draw an annotated sequence for inspiration linking diaphragm action, rib movement, thoracic volume, lung pressure and airflow.
questions.answerKey: Diaphragm contracts and flattens; ribs move up and out; thoracic and lung volume increase; lung pressure drops below atmospheric; air enters. Arrows must show this causal order.
questions.markingGuide: Diaphragm contracts and flattens; ribs move up and out; thoracic and lung volume increase; lung pressure drops below atmospheric; air enters. Arrows must show this causal order.

questions.content: Make a structure–function table for four alveolar features: large number, thin walls, moisture and capillary supply.
questions.answerKey: Large number gives extensive area; thin walls shorten the diffusion path; moisture allows gases to dissolve; blood flow maintains gradients and carries gases. Credit four correctly linked explanations.
questions.markingGuide: Large number gives extensive area; thin walls shorten the diffusion path; moisture allows gases to dissolve; blood flow maintains gradients and carries gases. Credit four correctly linked explanations.

questions.content: Critique the statement “Breathing, gas exchange and respiration all mean the same thing.” Use a single journey of an oxygen molecule to distinguish the three processes.
questions.answerKey: Ventilation brings oxygen-containing air to alveoli; diffusion transfers oxygen into blood and later tissues; cellular respiration uses oxygen in aerobic energy-releasing reactions. These are connected stages with different locations and mechanisms.
questions.markingGuide: Ventilation brings oxygen-containing air to alveoli; diffusion transfers oxygen into blood and later tissues; cellular respiration uses oxygen in aerobic energy-releasing reactions. These are connected stages with different locations and mechanisms.

questions.content: Write the overall word equation for aerobic respiration.
questions.answerKey: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, with energy transferred.
questions.markingGuide: Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, with energy transferred.

questions.content: Do green plants respire in daylight? Explain.
questions.answerKey: Yes. Living cells require energy continuously, even while photosynthesis is occurring.
questions.markingGuide: Yes. Living cells require energy continuously, even while photosynthesis is occurring.

questions.content: Name the two main products of yeast fermentation of glucose.
questions.markingGuide: Ethanol and carbon dioxide.

questions.content: Name the main product used in the school summary of anaerobic glucose breakdown in human muscle.
questions.markingGuide: Lactate.

questions.content: Which pathway generally transfers more usable energy per glucose: aerobic respiration or fermentation?
questions.markingGuide: Aerobic respiration.

questions.content: Why is it inaccurate to say respiration creates energy?
questions.answerKey: Energy is conserved and transferred from chemical stores into usable forms and heat.
questions.markingGuide: Energy is conserved and transferred from chemical stores into usable forms and heat.

questions.content: Where do many aerobic respiration stages occur in a plant cell?
questions.markingGuide: In mitochondria.

questions.content: Why might germinating seeds be used in a respiration investigation?
questions.answerKey: They are actively metabolising and can produce measurable heat, gas exchange or carbon dioxide.
questions.markingGuide: They are actively metabolising and can produce measurable heat, gas exchange or carbon dioxide.

questions.content: What is the purpose of a suitable non-living comparison sample?
questions.answerKey: It helps identify changes caused by apparatus or surroundings rather than living activity.
questions.markingGuide: It helps identify changes caused by apparatus or surroundings rather than living activity.

questions.content: Calculate a mean gas-production rate for 30 mL in 5 minutes.
questions.markingGuide: 30/5 = 6 mL per minute.

questions.content: Why does carbon-dioxide production not by itself prove anaerobic respiration?
questions.answerKey: Aerobic respiration can also produce carbon dioxide; oxygen conditions must be established.
questions.markingGuide: Aerobic respiration can also produce carbon dioxide; oxygen conditions must be established.

questions.content: State two controls for comparing yeast mixtures at different temperatures.
questions.answerKey: Equal yeast amount and sugar concentration; equal total volume and measurement duration are also valid.
questions.markingGuide: Equal yeast amount and sugar concentration; equal total volume and measurement duration are also valid.

questions.content: How could a gas leak affect the measured rate?
questions.answerKey: It would allow some gas to escape collection, making the measured rate too low.
questions.markingGuide: It would allow some gas to escape collection, making the measured rate too low.

questions.content: Why should a fermenting container not be sealed without safe pressure relief?
questions.answerKey: Gas production can increase pressure and rupture it.
questions.markingGuide: Gas production can increase pressure and rupture it.

questions.content: Why are repeated independent trials useful?
questions.answerKey: They reveal variation and improve confidence that a pattern is reproducible.
questions.markingGuide: They reveal variation and improve confidence that a pattern is reproducible.

questions.content: Prepare a comparison table for aerobic respiration, yeast fermentation and the muscle anaerobic pathway. Include oxygen use, main products and relative usable energy per glucose.
questions.answerKey: Aerobic: oxygen required, carbon dioxide and water, greater usable energy. Yeast fermentation: no oxygen required for the pathway, ethanol and carbon dioxide, smaller usable energy. Muscle anaerobic pathway: no oxygen used in the pathway, lactate, smaller usable energy.
questions.markingGuide: Aerobic: oxygen required, carbon dioxide and water, greater usable energy. Yeast fermentation: no oxygen required for the pathway, ethanol and carbon dioxide, smaller usable energy. Muscle anaerobic pathway: no oxygen used in the pathway, lactate, smaller usable energy.

questions.content: Interpret these supplied gas volumes after 5 minutes: yeast + sugar, 20 mL; yeast without added sugar, 3 mL; heat-killed yeast + sugar, 1 mL. State a supported conclusion and two limitations.
questions.answerKey: Living yeast with added sugar produced more collected gas. This supports sugar-dependent metabolism. Gas identity and oxygen availability are not established, and background gas, surviving reserves or collection effects may contribute. Replication is needed to assess variability.
questions.markingGuide: Living yeast with added sugar produced more collected gas. This supports sugar-dependent metabolism. Gas identity and oxygen availability are not established, and background gas, surviving reserves or collection effects may contribute. Replication is needed to assess variability.

questions.content: Write a report calculation from cumulative gas volumes of 0, 8, 18 and 24 mL at 0, 2, 4 and 6 minutes. Find each interval rate and explain why one overall average hides information.
questions.answerKey: 0–2 min: 8/2 = 4 mL/min; 2–4: (18−8)/2 = 5 mL/min; 4–6: (24−18)/2 = 3 mL/min. Overall average = 24/6 = 4 mL/min, hiding the rise then fall in measured interval rates.
questions.markingGuide: 0–2 min: 8/2 = 4 mL/min; 2–4: (18−8)/2 = 5 mL/min; 4–6: (24−18)/2 = 3 mL/min. Overall average = 24/6 = 4 mL/min, hiding the rise then fall in measured interval rates.

questions.content: What process moves gases between a leaf and surrounding air?
questions.markingGuide: Diffusion down appropriate gradients.

questions.content: Name the pores important for gas exchange in many leaves.
questions.markingGuide: Stomata.

questions.content: What do guard cells regulate?
questions.answerKey: The opening and closing of stomata.
questions.markingGuide: The opening and closing of stomata.

questions.content: Why are leaf internal air spaces useful?
questions.answerKey: They allow gases to reach many mesophyll surfaces over short diffusion paths.
questions.markingGuide: They allow gases to reach many mesophyll surfaces over short diffusion paths.

questions.content: Name a gas-exchange structure in many woody stems.
questions.markingGuide: A lenticel.

questions.content: From where do well-aerated roots obtain most of their oxygen?
questions.markingGuide: Air spaces in the soil.

questions.content: Why can waterlogging reduce oxygen supply to roots?
questions.answerKey: It replaces air spaces with water, through which oxygen diffuses much more slowly.
questions.markingGuide: It replaces air spaces with water, through which oxygen diffuses much more slowly.

questions.content: Do non-green root cells need oxygen for aerobic respiration?
questions.answerKey: Yes; living root cells respire even though they do not normally photosynthesise.
questions.markingGuide: Yes; living root cells respire even though they do not normally photosynthesise.

questions.content: State the net gas exchange expected in a healthy green leaf in darkness.
questions.answerKey: Net oxygen uptake and carbon-dioxide release.
questions.markingGuide: Net oxygen uptake and carbon-dioxide release.

questions.content: Explain why net oxygen release in daylight does not show respiration has stopped.
questions.answerKey: Photosynthesis can produce more oxygen than respiration consumes while both continue.
questions.markingGuide: Photosynthesis can produce more oxygen than respiration consumes while both continue.

questions.content: A leaf produces 15 units of oxygen and uses 6 units in the same interval. Find its net oxygen release.
questions.markingGuide: 15 − 6 = 9 units.

questions.content: Explain a compensation condition for carbon dioxide.
questions.answerKey: Photosynthetic uptake equals respiratory release, giving approximately zero net exchange.
questions.markingGuide: Photosynthetic uptake equals respiratory release, giving approximately zero net exchange.

questions.content: Why does zero net carbon-dioxide exchange not mean the leaf is inactive?
questions.answerKey: Opposing active processes may balance each other.
questions.markingGuide: Opposing active processes may balance each other.

questions.content: Give one effect of stomatal closure on photosynthesis and one on water loss.
questions.answerKey: It can restrict carbon-dioxide entry and reduce water-vapour loss.
questions.markingGuide: It can restrict carbon-dioxide entry and reduce water-vapour loss.

questions.content: Why must predictions about net plant gas exchange state light and plant condition?
questions.answerKey: Photosynthesis and respiration depend on conditions, so their balance and net direction can vary.
questions.markingGuide: Photosynthesis and respiration depend on conditions, so their balance and net direction can vary.

questions.content: Make a day-and-night concept diagram showing photosynthesis, respiration and net gas exchange in a healthy leaf. State assumptions for the daytime prediction.
questions.answerKey: Day: photosynthesis and respiration both occur; if photosynthesis exceeds respiration, net CO₂ enters and O₂ leaves. Night: photosynthesis stops, respiration continues, net O₂ enters and CO₂ leaves. Assume adequate water, suitable temperature and sufficient light in the daytime case.
questions.markingGuide: Day: photosynthesis and respiration both occur; if photosynthesis exceeds respiration, net CO₂ enters and O₂ leaves. Night: photosynthesis stops, respiration continues, net O₂ enters and CO₂ leaves. Assume adequate water, suitable temperature and sufficient light in the daytime case.

questions.content: Explain the sequence from waterlogged soil to reduced root function. Use soil air spaces, diffusion, oxygen and aerobic respiration.
questions.answerKey: Water fills air spaces, slowing oxygen delivery because diffusion is slower through water. Oxygen available to root cells falls, limiting aerobic respiration and the energy transfer needed for normal cell activities such as active transport.
questions.markingGuide: Water fills air spaces, slowing oxygen delivery because diffusion is slower through water. Oxygen available to root cells falls, limiting aerobic respiration and the energy transfer needed for normal cell activities such as active transport.

questions.content: A leaf’s carbon-dioxide uptake by photosynthesis is 2, 5 and 9 units at three light levels. Respiratory release is 5 units at each. Calculate net uptake and interpret the middle level.
questions.answerKey: Net uptake = 2−5 = −3, 5−5 = 0, 9−5 = 4 units. The first means net release of 3 units; the middle is a compensation condition with balanced active processes; the third means net uptake.
questions.markingGuide: Net uptake = 2−5 = −3, 5−5 = 0, 9−5 = 4 units. The first means net release of 3 units; the middle is a compensation condition with balanced active processes; the third means net uptake.

questions.content: State the positive iodine-test result for starch.
questions.markingGuide: A blue-black colour.

questions.content: What does Benedict’s test detect in the usual school method?
questions.markingGuide: Reducing sugars.

questions.content: Why is a negative Benedict’s result not proof that a food contains no carbohydrate?
questions.answerKey: Other carbohydrates, such as starch or non-reducing sugars, may not give that result under the stated method.
questions.markingGuide: Other carbohydrates, such as starch or non-reducing sugars, may not give that result under the stated method.

questions.content: State the positive biuret-test result.
questions.answerKey: A lilac or purple colour indicating protein.
questions.markingGuide: A lilac or purple colour indicating protein.

questions.content: What indicates lipids in a properly performed emulsion test?
questions.answerKey: A milky or cloudy white emulsion.
questions.markingGuide: A milky or cloudy white emulsion.

questions.content: Why must ethanol be kept away from flames?
questions.markingGuide: It is flammable.

questions.content: Distinguish positive and negative controls in a nutrient test.
questions.answerKey: A positive control contains the target nutrient and should respond; a negative control lacks it and should not respond.
questions.markingGuide: A positive control contains the target nutrient and should respond; a negative control lacks it and should not respond.

questions.content: A glucose control fails to respond in a Benedict’s test. What should be done before interpreting unknowns?
questions.answerKey: Check and repeat the prescribed method and reagents with a working control; do not trust unknown negatives yet.
questions.markingGuide: Check and repeat the prescribed method and reagents with a working control; do not trust unknown negatives yet.

questions.content: Which vascular tissue is commonly traced by coloured water in a cut-stem experiment?
questions.markingGuide: Xylem.

questions.content: Does a potometer directly measure water vapour leaving leaves? Explain.
questions.answerKey: No. It measures water uptake, which estimates transpiration with limitations.
questions.markingGuide: No. It measures water uptake, which estimates transpiration with limitations.

questions.content: State two controls when comparing potometer uptake in still and moving air.
questions.answerKey: Leaf area and light, temperature or humidity should be comparable.
questions.markingGuide: Leaf area and light, temperature or humidity should be comparable.

questions.content: Calculate beats per minute for 22 pulses in 20 seconds.
questions.markingGuide: 22 × 60/20 = 66 beats per minute.

questions.content: Why avoid using the thumb to count a wrist pulse?
questions.answerKey: The observer may confuse the thumb’s own pulse with the measured pulse.
questions.markingGuide: The observer may confuse the thumb’s own pulse with the measured pulse.

questions.content: Calculate uptake rate for 1.2 mL in 6 minutes.
questions.markingGuide: 1.2/6 = 0.2 mL per minute.

questions.content: Why should a pulse investigation record the delay between activity and counting?
questions.answerKey: Pulse rate can change during recovery, so unequal delays make comparisons less fair.
questions.markingGuide: Pulse rate can change during recovery, so unequal delays make comparisons less fair.

questions.content: Interpret a supplied nutrient table: water is negative in every test; starch reference and sample A turn blue-black with iodine; glucose reference and sample B give orange Benedict’s results; protein reference and A give purple biuret results. Report conclusions for A and B and identify what is unknown.
questions.answerKey: A contains detectable starch and protein. B contains detectable reducing sugar. The controls behaved as expected. Untested nutrients, amounts and overall food safety remain unknown; negative or unreported tests must not be invented.
questions.markingGuide: A contains detectable starch and protein. B contains detectable reducing sugar. The controls behaved as expected. Untested nutrients, amounts and overall food safety remain unknown; negative or unreported tests must not be invented.

questions.content: Plan a teacher-supervised plant water-uptake comparison in still and moving air. Include one changed variable, three controls, a rate calculation, repeats and a limitation.
questions.answerKey: Change air movement; keep leaf area, temperature and light or humidity comparable. Measure uptake volume over equal intervals and calculate volume/time. Use matched shoots or repeated trials with appropriate recovery. Recognise uptake is an estimate of transpiration and leaks can bias readings. Teacher prepares the apparatus safely.
questions.markingGuide: Change air movement; keep leaf area, temperature and light or humidity comparable. Measure uptake volume over equal intervals and calculate volume/time. Use matched shoots or repeated trials with appropriate recovery. Recognise uptake is an estimate of transpiration and leaks can bias readings. Teacher prepares the apparatus safely.

questions.content: Write a pulse-investigation mini-report from supplied counts: resting 17 beats in 15 s; immediately after gentle activity 25 in 15 s; after recovery 18 in 15 s. Include rates, conclusion, two controls and one limitation.
questions.answerKey: Rates are 68, 100 and 72 beats/min. This individual’s measured rate increased after activity and moved towards baseline during recovery. Keep counting interval, posture and timing comparable; report the actual recovery delay. A single individual and possible counting error limit generalisation. The figures are classroom data, not a diagnosis.
questions.markingGuide: Rates are 68, 100 and 72 beats/min. This individual’s measured rate increased after activity and moved towards baseline during recovery. questions.content: Classify 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O by the reactant–product pattern.
questions.answerKey: Combination: two reactants form one product.
questions.markingGuide: Combination: two reactants form one product.

questions.content: Classify Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.
questions.answerKey: Displacement: zinc replaces copper in the compound.
questions.markingGuide: Displacement: zinc replaces copper in the compound.

questions.content: Why can magnesium burning be both combination and combustion?
questions.answerKey: It forms one product from multiple reactants and reacts energetically with oxygen; the categories describe different aspects.
questions.markingGuide: It forms one product from multiple reactants and reacts energetically with oxygen; the categories describe different aspects.

questions.content: Name the products of complete hydrocarbon combustion.
questions.markingGuide: Carbon dioxide and water.

questions.content: State one hazardous product of incomplete combustion.
questions.markingGuide: Carbon monoxide.

questions.content: Why does no visible smoke not prove combustion gases are safe?
questions.answerKey: Harmful gases such as carbon monoxide can be colourless and invisible.
questions.markingGuide: Harmful gases such as carbon monoxide can be colourless and invisible.

questions.content: Balance C + O₂ → CO.
questions.markingGuide: 2C + O₂ → 2CO.

questions.content: Balance CH₄ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O.
questions.markingGuide: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.

questions.content: Distinguish digestion from cellular respiration.
questions.answerKey: Digestion breaks large food molecules into absorbable smaller ones; respiration transfers usable energy through reactions inside cells.
questions.markingGuide: Digestion breaks large food molecules into absorbable smaller ones; respiration transfers usable energy through reactions inside cells.

questions.content: What does hydrolysis mean in digestion?
questions.answerKey: Water participates in breaking bonds in larger molecules.
questions.markingGuide: Water participates in breaking bonds in larger molecules.

questions.content: What are the final protein digestion products in the introductory summary?
questions.markingGuide: Amino acids.

questions.content: Explain exothermic reaction.
questions.answerKey: A reaction transferring energy to its surroundings.
questions.markingGuide: A reaction transferring energy to its surroundings.

questions.content: Does a faster reaction necessarily release more total energy from the same reactant amounts? Explain.
questions.answerKey: No. Rate is energy or material change per time, while total energy depends on the overall chemical change and amounts.
questions.markingGuide: No. Rate is energy or material change per time, while total energy depends on the overall chemical change and amounts.

questions.content: Why are enzymes described as biological catalysts?
questions.answerKey: They accelerate reactions in living systems without being consumed overall.
questions.markingGuide: They accelerate reactions in living systems without being consumed overall.

questions.content: Build a comparison chart for combination, decomposition and displacement with one balanced equation and a reason for each classification.
questions.answerKey: Combination: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, multiple reactants give one product. Decomposition: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, one reactant gives two products. Displacement: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu, zinc replaces copper.
questions.markingGuide: Combination: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, multiple reactants give one product. Decomposition: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, one reactant gives two products. Displacement: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu, zinc replaces copper.

questions.content: Correct this explanation: “Digestion burns food using oxygen in the stomach, and a faster enzyme always creates more energy.” Include digestion, respiration and rate.
questions.answerKey: Digestion uses mechanical processes and enzyme-catalysed reactions to form absorbable molecules; it is not fuel combustion in the stomach. Aerobic cellular respiration uses oxygen in energy-transferring cellular reactions. Enzymes change rate without creating energy or necessarily changing total energy transferred.
questions.markingGuide: Digestion uses mechanical processes and enzyme-catalysed reactions to form absorbable molecules; it is not fuel combustion in the stomach. Aerobic cellular respiration uses oxygen in energy-transferring cellular reactions. Enzymes change rate without creating energy or necessarily changing total energy transferred.

questions.content: Using the supplied equation 2C + O₂ → 2CO, count atoms on both sides, identify whether combustion is complete or incomplete, and write a safety implication.
questions.answerKey: Each side has two C and two O atoms. It represents incomplete combustion because carbon monoxide forms rather than all carbon becoming carbon dioxide. Fuel equipment needs safe use and appropriate ventilation; never use the equation as a reason to generate carbon monoxide experimentally.
questions.markingGuide: Each side has two C and two O atoms. It represents incomplete combustion because carbon monoxide forms rather than all carbon becoming carbon dioxide. Fuel equipment needs safe use and appropriate ventilation; never use the equation as a reason to generate carbon monoxide experimentally.

questions.content: What is a minimal pair?
questions.answerKey: Two words that differ in one sound and have different meanings.
questions.markingGuide: Two words that differ in one sound and have different meanings.

Which word has /iː/: lip or leap?
questions.markingGuide: Leap.

questions.answerKey: The vowels also differ in quality or tongue position.
questions.markingGuide: The vowels also differ in quality or tongue position.

questions.content: Describe the opening consonant in thin.
questions.answerKey: /θ/: air passes between the tongue tip and upper front teeth without voice vibration.

questions.content: Which word starts with /ð/: this or tin?
questions.markingGuide: This.

questions.content: Mark the stronger syllable in begin using capitals.
questions.markingGuide: be-GIN.

questions.content: How many syllables are represented in TA-ble?
questions.markingGuide: Two.

questions.content: Give the common stress pattern for record used as a noun.
questions.answerKey: RE-cord; stress on the first syllable.
questions.markingGuide: RE-cord; stress on the first syllable.

questions.content: Give the common stress pattern for record used as a verb.
questions.answerKey: re-CORD; stress on the second syllable.

questions.content: Are one and won minimal pairs? Explain.
questions.answerKey: No. They are homophones with the same pronunciation, so they have no sound contrast.

questions.content: Complete: “We ___ two games yesterday.”
questions.markingGuide: Won.

questions.content: Complete: “I need ___ clean cup.”
questions.markingGuide: One.

questions.content: Why should a listener write the word heard before seeing a word card?
questions.answerKey: It checks what was understood without being influenced by the spelling on the card.
questions.markingGuide: It checks what was understood without being influenced by the spelling on the card.

questions.content: What is an honest description of this chapter’s pronunciation material?
questions.answerKey: It is a text guide; a teacher, partner or other actual speech model supplies listening.
questions.markingGuide: It is a text guide; a teacher, partner or other actual speech model supplies listening.

questions.content: Create six word cards using ship/sheep, lip/leap and thin/tin. Ask a partner to read each in a sentence while you write the word heard. Submit the record and a correction plan.
questions.answerKey: A suitable record lists six intended words, six responses, any mismatches and a targeted practice step.
questions.markingGuide: 1 mark for all cards; 2 for six responses; 1 for comparing responses; 2 for a specific correction plan.

questions.content: Prepare a two-minute teaching demonstration of TA-ble, be-GIN and noun/verb record. Write your script and stress marks, then perform it to a partner.
questions.answerKey: The demonstration explains stress as prominence, accurately marks the four forms, and gives meaningful sentences.
questions.markingGuide: 2 marks for accurate stress; 2 for explanations and sentences; 2 for clear delivery and a recorded partner response.

questions.content: Write a six-sentence story containing both one and won. Underline the two words and explain why each spelling fits.
questions.answerKey: An original coherent story uses one as a number and won as past-tense win, then explains each choice.
questions.markingGuide: 2 marks for correct homophones; 2 for connected sentences; 2 for meaning-based explanations.

questions.content: What is the main purpose of the announcement?
questions.answerKey: To give arrangements and instructions for Thursday’s reading-club meeting.
questions.markingGuide: To give arrangements and instructions for Thursday’s reading-club meeting.
questions.passage:
Original announcement script: “Good morning, Form One. Our reading club will meet on Thursday at 3:30 in Room Four because the library is being cleaned. Bring a notebook and one book that you are willing to discuss; do not bring money. A book exchange is suggested for next month, but it has not been approved. If you cannot attend, tell Salma before lunch on Thursday. The meeting will finish at 4:15 so that members can catch the school bus. Thank you.”

Original follow-up dialogue script: “Juma: Did she say we should pay for the exchange? Rehema: No. She said not to bring money, and the exchange is only a proposal. Juma: I will be at the clinic on Thursday afternoon. Rehema: Then tell Salma before lunch. Juma: Can I send my book with you? Rehema: Ask Salma whether that is acceptable; the announcement did not explain it.” Notice how Rehema distinguishes stated information from a question that needs further checking.

questions.content: On which day does Neema usually help?

questions.passage: Original story, “The missing sign”: Every Saturday, Neema helps at the village reading room. One wet morning she found two visitors waiting outside the old store. The following Saturday, new visitors reached the hall without asking for help.

Seller: Yes. They are two thousand shillings each. Customer: That is twenty-four thousand altogether. Could you offer a lower price for twelve? Seller: I can sell the twelve for twenty-two thousand. Customer: Thank you. Does that include a bag? Seller: Yes, one paper bag. Customer: We can pay twenty-one thousand. Would you accept that? Seller: I am sorry; twenty-two thousand is my lowest total. Customer: Then we will take six today at the usual price. Seller: Certainly; that is twelve thousand.”

Location descriptions should establish a reference point. Imagine a service centre with a reception desk just inside the entrance, a photocopy counter to the left of reception and a payment desk opposite the counter. “The payment desk is opposite the photocopy counter” names both the place sought and its reference feature. Left and right depend on orientation; tell a visitor to face reception first. Use near, beside, behind and between only when the arrangement actually supports them.

questions.content: How many seedlings were planted?
questions.markingGuide: Forty.
questions.passage:
Original oral-source script A, gardener: “We planted forty bean seedlings on Monday. By Friday, thirty-four were standing upright; six had wilted. The bed beside the wall stayed damp longer than the bed beside the path. I think the path bed needs mulch, but we have not tested that idea. Please keep the gate closed because goats entered last term. I can demonstrate mulching on Wednesday after class.” This is a text script for a human reader, not recorded audio.

Original oral-source script B, student observer: “Our group counted thirty-five upright seedlings on Thursday, before Friday’s hot afternoon. We noticed that two watering cans leak. We have not measured how much water they lose. We recommend repairing the cans before buying more. Wednesday after class clashes with our debate practice, but two members can attend the gardener’s demonstration and report back. We should compare the two beds for a week before deciding whether mulch helps.” This second source is also original text for reading aloud.

questions.content: Amina na Sudi walikuwa wanapeleka nini?
questions.answerKey: Vitabu kwenye kona ya kusoma ya kijiji.
questions.markingGuide: Vitabu kwenye kona ya kusoma ya kijiji.
questions.passage: Hadithi asilia, “Kikapu cha vitabu”: Siku ya Jumatano, Amina na Sudi walipeleka vitabu kwenye kona ya kusoma ya kijiji. Walipofika darajani, waliona maji yamefunika sehemu ya njia. Sudi alitaka kupita pembeni, lakini Amina alikumbuka onyo la kutokaribia mkondo wakati wa mvua. Walisimama mbali na maji na kumpigia mlezi wao simu. Mlezi aliwaelekeza watumie njia ya sokoni yenye daraja salama. Walifika wakiwa wamechelewa kwa dakika ishirini, lakini vitabu vilikuwa vikavu. Amina aliwaeleza wasomaji sababu ya kuchelewa. Baadaye, watoto walichora ramani ya njia salama na kuiweka ukutani. Siku iliyofuata, kikundi kingine kilitumia ramani hiyo kufika bila kukaribia maji.

questions.markingGuide: Mia moja na ishirini.
questions.passage:
Hati asilia ya habari ya kusomwa kwa sauti; hii ni matini, si rekodi ya sauti: “Mratibu: Katika wiki iliyopita, wanafunzi walikusanya chupa mia moja na ishirini kutoka eneo la shule. Sabini zilipatikana karibu na uwanja, thelathini karibu na kantini na ishirini nyuma ya madarasa. Mlezi: Idadi hizo zinaonesha mahali pa kuanzia, lakini hatujui kama chupa zote zilitupwa wiki hiyo. Mwanafunzi: Ninapendekeza vyombo vitatu vya kukusanyia chupa viwekwe karibu na uwanja. Mhasibu: Tuna pesa za kununua vyombo viwili tu kwa sasa. Mratibu: Basi kamati ichunguze bei na njia ya kupata chombo cha tatu. Tusifanye ununuzi leo.”

Mwendelezo wa hati asilia: “Mwanafunzi: Je, chupa zitauzwa ili kupata fedha? Mlezi: Bado hatujathibitisha mnunuzi wala bei. Kwanza tutauliza wakusanyaji wawili wenye huduma inayoruhusiwa. Mratibu: Rehema na Doto watauliza bei za vyombo na kuleta taarifa Ijumaa. Mimi nitawasiliana na wakusanyaji kabla ya kikao hicho. Tumeamua kuanza kuhesabu chupa kila siku kutoka Jumatatu ijayo ili tujue mabadiliko. Mhasibu: Nitaandaa daftari lenye tarehe, eneo na idadi. Mlezi: Chupa zilizovunjika zishughulikiwe na mtu mzima mwenye vifaa vinavyofaa; wanafunzi wasiziokote kwa mikono.”

questions.content: Kwa nini vijana walipendekeza boksi linalotembea?
questions.answerKey: Kijiji hakikuwa na jengo la maktaba na vitabu vya shule havingeazimwa kwa wote.

Matini asilia, “Maktaba inayotembea”, sehemu ya kwanza: Kijiji cha Mwangaza hakikuwa na jengo la maktaba. Watu waliotaka kusoma walitegemea vitabu vichache shuleni, ambavyo havingeazimwa kwa wote. Baada ya mkutano wa wazazi, kikundi cha vijana kilipendekeza boksi la vitabu litembezwe kutoka kitongoji kimoja kwenda kingine. Walipata vitabu sitini vya hadithi, kilimo na afya vilivyotolewa kwa hiari. Hakuna aliyedai kuwa boksi hilo lingechukua nafasi ya maktaba kamili; walitaka kuanza na huduma iliyowezekana kwa rasilimali walizokuwa nazo. Wazee wawili walipendekeza kila eneo liwe na mlezi wa boksi na daftari la kuazima.

Matini asilia, sehemu ya pili: Mwezi wa kwanza, boksi lilipelekwa katika vitongoji vitatu, likikaa wiki moja kila eneo na wiki moja kituoni kwa ukaguzi. Daftari lilionesha mikopo arobaini na miwili ya vitabu, lakini baadhi ya watu waliazima zaidi ya kitabu kimoja. Hivyo, mikopo hiyo haikumaanisha wasomaji arobaini na wawili tofauti. Watoto walipenda hadithi zenye michoro. Baadhi ya wakulima waliomba vitabu vyenye maelezo mafupi na picha kubwa kwa kuwa walikuwa na muda mdogo wa kusoma jioni. Mlezi alikusanya maombi hayo badala ya kuhitimisha kuwa watu hawapendi kusoma vitabu virefu katika hali zote.

Matini asilia, sehemu ya tatu: Tatizo lilijitokeza mvua iliponyesha siku ya kuhamisha boksi. Vijana walichelewesha safari na vitabu vikafika siku moja baada ya ratiba. Msomaji mmoja alilalamika kuwa hakupewa taarifa. Kamati ilikubali kasoro hiyo, ikaweka utaratibu wa kutuma ujumbe kwa walezi wa vitongoji mapema kila ratiba ilipobadilika. Pia iliamua kutafuta kifuniko kisichopitisha maji. Hata hivyo, hakukuwa na ushahidi wa gharama ya kifuniko bora; vijana walipewa kazi ya kulinganisha bei tatu kabla ya ununuzi. Mabadiliko hayo yalilenga kutatua tatizo maalumu badala ya kuficha kuchelewa kulikotokea.

Matini asilia, sehemu ya nne: Mwishoni mwa miezi mitatu, baadhi ya wanakijiji walitaka kununua vitabu vipya vyote vya hadithi, kwa sababu watoto walionekana kuvitumia sana. Iliamua kuongeza kisanduku cha maoni na kuandika pia vipindi vya usomaji wa pamoja. Kwa maoni yangu kama msimulizi, nguvu ya mradi haikuwa kutokosea kabisa, bali kukubali mapungufu na kubadili utaratibu kwa taarifa mpya. Hata hivyo, mafanikio ya kijiji kimoja hayathibitishi kwamba mpango huu utatosha kila mahali.

questions.content: Tunu na Kito wanataka kutumia nini?
questions.markingGuide: Mpira.
questions.passage: Hati asilia ya mazungumzo ya marafiki: “Tunu: Umeona mpira? Kito: Upo kwa mlezi. Tuombe kabla ya mazoezi. Tunu: Sawa; nitamuuliza kama tunaweza kuutumia hadi saa kumi na moja. Kito: Ukiruhusiwa, niambie, nami nitawaita wenzetu.” Hati asilia ya ombi kwa mlezi: “Tunu: Shikamoo, mlezi. Naomba tuutumie mpira kwa mazoezi hadi saa kumi na moja, ikiwa uwanja uko wazi. Tunu: Asante; basi tutamaliza na kurudisha mpira kabla ya saa kumi na nusu.” Hizi ni hati za maandishi kwa maigizo, si sauti iliyorekodiwa.
